source: Written 2026-10-22 by Claude Sonnet from our own summaries of the NC 2026 standards, and solved blind by Claude Opus (Claude Code agents, not runAi: no ai_runs rows), code-checked by lintQuestion; "checked" questions await a platform admin.

notes.NC26.M2.ANFR.1: Area-model questions give the four part areas in words; solving quadratic equations is left out as outside this standard.
notes.NC26.M2.ANFR.2: Text-only: tables and graphs are written out as lists of values, points or descriptions of shape. Types are told apart by constant first differences (linear), ratios (exponential), second differences (quadratic) or products (reciprocal); the tables were classified by code in the build script. No technology needed.
notes.NC26.M2.ANFR.3: Text-only: no graphs are shown, so features are asked from equations, tables of values and described situations. Technology is not needed: zeros, vertices and ranges are found by factoring, vertex form or symmetry. Reciprocal functions are asked as evaluation, domain, range and asymptotes of f(x)=k/(x-h)+c.
notes.NC26.M2.ANFR.6: Technology results are given as text (reported crossing points, tables of values) or the systems are solved by hand with exact roots, so every key is exact. Systems are always a parabola with a line (or a horizontal line), or a context that reduces to one. Pass A flags: none (all checked).
notes.NC26.M2.RMM.1: Process-heavy standard, so about 60 percent of the questions are choice; numeric questions are used wherever a model can be evaluated or built.
notes.NC26.M2.SDSR.2: Mostly choice questions (about two thirds) because telling statistical from non-statistical questions, posing questions and spotting bias are judgments about a described study; the numeric ones cover counting variables and questions, nonresponse, the size of a call-in poll's bias, and stratified or systematic sample sizes. Designing a study, regression and technology are not part of this standard.
notes.NC26.M2.SDSR.3: The standard has two halves: judging a dataset or source, and building models from it. Credibility and choosing variables are asked as choice questions about a described situation, each written so only one option is defensible; splitting by a third variable is asked with group means, rates, group-specific best-fit lines (given, not computed) and residuals, all answerable by hand. No picture or software is needed.
notes.NC26.M2.SDSR.4: Text-only: every plot is given as a list of points or values, and shapes (U-shaped, two clusters, bubble sizes, stacked segments, dual axes) are described in words. Non-standard displays are written out as their data or their layout, then asked about. Creating a display is asked as which display to choose. Software is not needed: slopes, residuals and means are all by hand.
notes.NC26.M2.SDSR.5: Regression is done by technology in class, so the fitted equation, r or r squared is given and the student predicts, finds residuals or interprets. Residual plots are described in words (random scatter, a U-shape), not drawn, and r is never computed from raw data.
notes.NC26.M2.SGMR.1: Everything is on the coordinate plane with points written as (x, y). Rotations are about the origin only; dilations are centered at the origin except where a center is given; scale factors are positive. Non-rigid transformations are taken to mean dilations. Pass A had no flags.
notes.NC26.M2.SGMR.2: Text-only: triangles are given by their sides and angles, never by a picture; the letters of similar or congruent triangles are said to be in matching order. The summary's "developing the similarity criteria" is asked as which rule proves similarity, and why a rule fails (SSA, differences instead of ratios). Dilations are asked with coordinates written out. No proofs are asked, only which rule or conclusion is justified. The decision "neither" is asked with sides that are almost, but not quite, in proportion.
notes.NC26.M2.SGMR.3: Triangles are described by their sides and angles in words, with no figure. Trigonometric values are exact (30, 45, 60 degrees, 3-4-5 style triangles) or given in the question with the rounding stated, so no calculator is needed.
notes.NC26.M2.ANFR.4: 69 new questions across six skills; none flagged in pass A. Technology and graph-reading are avoided; the graph-crossing wording in one factored-form question is stated in words.
notes.NC26.M2.ANFR.5: 69 new questions on nine skills. Technology questions give what a graphing tool would show (intersection or crossing points, or that a graph never reaches the x-axis) and ask for the interpretation, so all can be answered by hand.
notes.NC26.M2.SDSR.1: Text-only: tables are written as counts and percentages; no diagrams. Technology-based work is avoided; all answers are exact by hand.
notes.NC26.M2.SDSR.6: Mostly choice questions (23 of 30): the standard is about describing, evaluating and critiquing a statistical investigation, which is tested best by choosing among written conclusions. Numeric questions cover non-response, estimating from a sample, margins of error, a truncated axis, and percent claims. Skills: bias in sampling or wording (4), study design and limits (4), conclusions the data support (5), margin of error (4), graphs and statistics in the media (5), causal and numerical claims (4), the order and content of a report (4).
notes.NC26.M2.SGMR.4: Covers naming ratios, missing sides, missing angles, 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles, elevation and depression, and Pythagorean ladder problems. Where a non-special angle is used (40, 35, 53, 25, 40 degrees) the needed trig value is quoted in the stem, so the side questions work by hand; four angle questions (the 3-4 triangle, the 13-foot ramp, the 9-41 triangle) need a calculator inverse key and are rounded to the nearest degree, with the key well clear of a rounding boundary. Rounded numeric keys have an empty compute because the rounded answer is not an exact result.

questions.skill: Order of the modeling cycle
questions.stem: A team has stated its problem and listed the quantities and assumptions it will use. According to the modeling cycle, what should the team do next?
choices: Announce the final answer and stop working on the whole problem
Compare the model's predictions with real data
Build a model, such as an equation, from those quantities
Revise the model because it did not fit the data
questions.answer: Build a model, such as an equation, from those quantities
questions.solution: The modeling cycle runs: state the problem, name the quantities and assumptions, build a model, use the model, test it against data, then revise and explain. The team has finished the first two steps, so the next step is to build a model.

solve.answer: Build a model, such as an equation, from those quantities
solve.work: Modeling cycle: identify the problem, name quantities and assumptions (formulate), then build/compute a model, then interpret, validate against data, revise. Having stated the problem and listed quantities and assumptions, the next step is to build a model from them. Announcing the answer skips steps; revising and comparing with data come after a model exists.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: Which of these questions can be answered by building and using a mathematical model?
choices: How many boxes are needed to pack 240 books if each box holds 12 books?
Which story in the school library is the most exciting one to read?
Is reading a book at home more enjoyable than watching a movie at home with family?
Which cover color will make students feel happiest about reading in the library?
questions.answer: How many boxes are needed to pack 240 books if each box holds 12 books?
questions.solution: A model needs quantities that can be measured or counted. Only the packing question has numbers to work with. The other questions are matters of opinion.

solve.answer: How many boxes are needed to pack 240 books if each box holds 12 books?
solve.work: Only A is quantitative: 240/12 = 20 boxes. B, C, D are matters of taste/opinion.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: A team wants to model how long it takes to fill a swimming pool with a hose. Which two quantities does the model need?
choices: The number of swimmers who will use the pool and the temperature of the water in it
The age of the pool and the number of people who will swim in it
The price of the water per gallon and the number of hours the hose was used last year
The volume of the pool and the rate at which the hose delivers water
questions.answer: The volume of the pool and the rate at which the hose delivers water
questions.solution: Filling time depends on how much water the pool holds and how fast the hose delivers it: time = volume divided by rate. The other quantities do not change how long it takes.

solve.answer: The volume of the pool and the rate at which the hose delivers water

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A taxi charges a flat fee of 3 dollars plus 2 dollars for each mile. A model of the cost in dollars of a ride of $m$ miles is $C = 3 + 2m$. According to the model, what does a 7-mile ride cost, in dollars?
questions.solution: Put $m = 7$ into the model: $C = 3 + 2 \times 7 = 3 + 14 = 17$. The ride costs 17 dollars.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: Maya has 40 dollars and saves 15 dollars each week. Which equation models the total $S$, in dollars, that she has after $w$ weeks?
questions.solution: She starts with 40 dollars and adds 15 dollars for each week, so the total is 40 plus 15 times $w$: $S = 40 + 15w$.

solve.work: Starts with 40, adds 15 each week: S = 40 + 15w. Check w = 0 gives 40, w = 1 gives 55.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A plant is 5 cm tall now and grows 2 cm each day. A model of its height in centimeters after $d$ days is $h = 5 + 2d$. After how many days does the model say the plant is 25 cm tall?
questions.solution: Solve $5 + 2d = 25$. Subtract 5 from both sides: $2d = 20$. Divide by 2: $d = 10$ days.

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A model predicts that 150 people will come to a concert. In fact, 135 people come. By how many people is the prediction off?
questions.solution: Compare the prediction with what happened: $150 - 135 = 15$. The prediction is off by 15 people.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: A model for the water left in a tank is $w = 50 - 5t$, where $w$ is in gallons and $t$ is in minutes. What does the number 5 mean in this situation?
choices: The tank holds a total of 5 gallons when it is full
Water leaves the tank at a rate of 5 gallons each minute
Water is added to the tank at a rate of 5 gallons each minute
The tank is completely empty after 5 minutes
questions.answer: Water leaves the tank at a rate of 5 gallons each minute
questions.solution: In $w = 50 - 5t$, each minute $t$ takes away 5 gallons from the starting 50. So 5 is the rate at which water leaves, in gallons per minute.

solve.answer: Water leaves the tank at a rate of 5 gallons each minute
solve.work: w = 50 - 5t: w decreases by 5 gallons for each minute, so water leaves at 5 gallons per minute. 50 is the starting amount; empty at t = 10, not 5.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: A team models how much pizza a class of 20 students will eat. They decide, "Every student will eat exactly 3 slices." In the modeling cycle, what is this decision best called?
choices: A measurement of what each student really ate
A prediction of the model's final answer
A test of the model against some real data
An assumption that simplifies the problem
questions.answer: An assumption that simplifies the problem
questions.solution: Nobody has measured what the students will eat. The team is choosing a simple rule to treat as true so that it can build a model. Such a choice is an assumption.

solve.answer: An assumption that simplifies the problem
solve.work: Fixing every student at 3 slices is a simplifying assumption.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: A team models the water a hiking group needs. It assumes each hiker drinks 3 bottles of water per day. Under this assumption, how many bottles does a group of 12 hikers need for a 2-day trip?
questions.solution: Each hiker needs 3 bottles a day, and there are 12 hikers: $12 \times 3 = 36$ bottles a day. For 2 days: $36 \times 2 = 72$ bottles.

solve.work: 3 bottles per hiker per day x 12 hikers x 2 days = 72 bottles.

questions.skill: Order of the modeling cycle
questions.stem: Which step of the modeling cycle comes first?
choices: Identify the problem to be solved
Test the model against some new data
Revise the model if it does not fit
Explain the results to others
questions.answer: Identify the problem to be solved
questions.solution: A team cannot build or test anything until it knows what question it is trying to answer, so the cycle starts by identifying the problem.

solve.answer: Identify the problem to be solved
solve.work: Modeling cycle starts with identifying the problem.

questions.skill: Order of the modeling cycle
questions.stem: A team's model gave predictions that did not match real data. What should the team do next in the modeling cycle?
choices: Keep the model as it is and ignore the data
Revise the model, then test it again
Change the data so they match the predictions
Stop, since a model can never be changed
questions.answer: Revise the model, then test it again
questions.solution: When predictions and data disagree, the cycle sends the team back to revise the model (for example its assumptions), and then to test it again.

solve.answer: Revise the model, then test it again
solve.work: A mismatch with data means revise the model and test again.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: Which question can be answered by building a mathematical model?
choices: Which season of the year is the most fun for most of the people who live in our town?
Which song should the whole class sing at the graduation ceremony at the end of the year?
What is the nicest name for a new puppy that has just joined a family with two children?
How many 2-pound bags of seed are needed for a field that needs 18 pounds of seed?
questions.answer: How many 2-pound bags of seed are needed for a field that needs 18 pounds of seed?
questions.solution: Only the seed question is about quantities that can be measured and related with math (bags, pounds and the field). The others are matters of taste.

solve.answer: How many 2-pound bags of seed are needed for a field that needs 18 pounds of seed?
solve.work: 18/2 = 9 bags: quantitative. Others are taste/opinion. B.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: Which is a clearly stated problem a model could solve?
choices: Find the number of 6-passenger vans needed to carry 54 students
Make the field trip a good one that all of the students will enjoy
Decide whether the students will be happy about going on the field trip
Choose a nice place to go on the field trip for the whole class
questions.answer: Find the number of 6-passenger vans needed to carry 54 students
questions.solution: A clear problem names the unknown and the given numbers. Only the vans problem does: it asks for a number, using 54 students and 6 passengers per van.

solve.answer: Find the number of 6-passenger vans needed to carry 54 students
solve.work: 54/6 = 9 vans: clearly stated quantitative problem. A.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: A team wants to find how many weeks it will take to save 300 dollars by saving 25 dollars each week. What is the unknown quantity in this problem?
choices: The 25 dollars saved each week
The number of weeks
The 300 dollars to be saved
The number of dollars in one week's pay
questions.answer: The number of weeks
questions.solution: The team already knows 300 dollars and 25 dollars per week. What they do not know, and want to find, is the number of weeks.

solve.answer: The number of weeks
solve.work: 300 and 25 are known; the number of weeks is unknown.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: A team models how long a bike ride to school takes. Which two quantities does the model need?
choices: The color of the bike and the age of the rider
The price of the bike and the name of the school
The number of gears and the brand of the helmet
The distance to school and the speed of the bike
questions.answer: The distance to school and the speed of the bike
questions.solution: Travel time depends on distance and speed. The other quantities do not change how long the ride takes.

solve.answer: The distance to school and the speed of the bike

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: A team assumes a printer prints 20 pages each minute. Under that assumption, how many pages does it print in 6 minutes?
questions.solution: 20 pages per minute for 6 minutes is $20 \times 6 = 120$ pages.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: Which statement is an assumption a team might make to simplify a model of a race?
choices: Each runner keeps the same speed for the whole race
The race track used for the race is exactly 400 meters long
Mia finished the race in 70 seconds, which was her best time
The race started at 9:00 in the morning
questions.answer: Each runner keeps the same speed for the whole race
questions.solution: An assumption is something the team decides to treat as true to keep the model simple. Keeping a steady speed is such a choice; the other statements are facts about the race.

solve.answer: Each runner keeps the same speed for the whole race
solve.work: Constant speed is a simplifying assumption; B, C, D are facts/data.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A plumber charges 40 dollars for a visit plus 25 dollars for each hour of work. Which equation models the total charge $T$, in dollars, for $h$ hours of work?
questions.solution: The visit fee of 40 dollars is paid once, and 25 dollars is added for each hour, so $T = 40 + 25h$.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A club has 8 members now and gains 3 new members every month. Using a linear model, how many members will it have after 5 months?
questions.solution: The model is $M = 8 + 3m$. For $m = 5$: $8 + 15 = 23$ members.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A team models a culture that starts with 3 thousand bacteria and doubles every hour. Using an exponential model, how many thousand bacteria are there after 4 hours?
questions.solution: The model is $N = 3 \times 2^t$. For $t = 4$: $3 \times 16 = 48$ thousand.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A model for the distance in miles that a cyclist rides is $d = 12t$, where $t$ is the time in hours. According to the model, how far does the cyclist ride in 5 hours?
questions.solution: $d = 12 \times 5 = 60$ miles.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: The model $w = 20 - 4t$ gives the liters of water $w$ left in a bucket after $t$ minutes. After how many minutes does the model say the bucket is empty?
questions.solution: Set $20 - 4t = 0$. Then $4t = 20$ and $t = 5$ minutes.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A model for a phone battery is $b = 100 - 8t$, where $b$ is the percent of charge and $t$ is the time in hours. According to the model, what percent of charge is left after 5 hours?

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A model for the cost of printing is $C = 0.10p + 5$, where $p$ is the number of pages and $C$ is the cost in dollars. According to the model, what does it cost to print 60 pages, in dollars?

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A model predicts that a lunch stand will sell 48 sandwiches on Friday. The stand actually sells 52. By how many sandwiches is the prediction off?
questions.solution: $52 - 48 = 4$ sandwiches.

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A model predicts that a bus ride will take 20 minutes. On five days the rides take 19, 21, 20, 22 and 18 minutes. What do these data suggest about the model?
choices: The model is wrong, since only one ride took exactly 20 minutes
The model fits perfectly, since every ride took exactly 20 minutes
The model is wrong, since some rides took less than 20 minutes
The model fits well, since the times are close to 20 minutes
questions.answer: The model fits well, since the times are close to 20 minutes
questions.solution: Every ride is within 2 minutes of the prediction, so the model fits well. A model does not have to match every value exactly.

solve.answer: The model fits well, since the times are close to 20 minutes
solve.work: Times are within 2 minutes of 20, so the model fits well.

questions.skill: Revise a model
questions.stem: A team predicted that a 10-kilogram bag of rice would last a family 20 days, but it lasted only 14 days. What should the team do?
choices: Keep the model as it is unchanged, because 14 days is close enough to the 20 days predicted
Change the 14 days to 20 days in the record so that the data agree with the prediction
Remove the rice from the problem, so that the team no longer needs to predict how long it lasts
Check its assumption about how much rice the family eats each day, and revise it
questions.answer: Check its assumption about how much rice the family eats each day, and revise it
questions.solution: The prediction and the data disagree, so the team should look for the assumption that caused it, here the daily amount eaten, and revise it.

solve.answer: Check its assumption about how much rice the family eats each day, and revise it
solve.work: Prediction off (20 vs 14 days): revisit the daily-consumption assumption (10/20 = 0.5 kg/day vs actual about 0.71) and revise. D.

questions.skill: Revise a model
questions.stem: A team first assumed a runner runs 8 kilometers per hour. A test shows the runner runs 10 kilometers per hour. Using the revised assumption, how many kilometers does the model say the runner covers in 3 hours?
questions.solution: The revised model is distance $= 10 \times$ time. In 3 hours: $10 \times 3 = 30$ kilometers.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: A model for a savings jar is $S = 12 + 3w$, where $S$ is the number of dollars in the jar after $w$ weeks. What does the 12 mean?
choices: The jar gains 12 dollars each week
The jar holds 12 dollars after 3 weeks
The jar will be full after 12 weeks
The jar holds 12 dollars at the start
questions.answer: The jar holds 12 dollars at the start
questions.solution: When $w = 0$, $S = 12$, so 12 dollars is the starting amount. The 3 is the amount added each week.

solve.answer: The jar holds 12 dollars at the start

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: In the model $d = 55t$ for a car's distance in miles after $t$ hours, what does 55 mean?
choices: The car travels 55 miles each hour
The car travels for 55 hours in all
The car starts 55 miles from home
The car travels 55 miles in total on its trip
questions.answer: The car travels 55 miles each hour
questions.solution: The distance grows by 55 miles for each hour, so 55 is the car's speed in miles per hour.

solve.answer: The car travels 55 miles each hour
solve.work: 55 is the rate: 55 miles per hour. B.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: Why should a team explain its assumptions when it shares a model?
choices: It makes the model's predictions come out exactly right every time that it is used
Others can then judge when the model's predictions are likely to be reliable
Every model must have exactly three assumptions, no more and no fewer than that number
It keeps other people from changing the model or using it for a different problem
questions.answer: Others can then judge when the model's predictions are likely to be reliable
questions.solution: A model is only as good as its assumptions. Stating them lets others decide whether they fit their own situation.

solve.answer: Others can then judge when the model's predictions are likely to be reliable
solve.work: Stating assumptions lets others judge when predictions are reliable. A.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: A team reports, "Our model shows a candle burns 2 cm each hour." Which detail should they also share so others can critique the model?
choices: The color of the candle and the scent that was added to its wax when made
The name of the team leader and the day of the week on which the team met
The assumption that the candle burns at the same rate the whole time
The price of the candle and the name of the store where the team bought it
questions.answer: The assumption that the candle burns at the same rate the whole time
questions.solution: To critique a model, others need to know what it assumes. The burning rate being constant is an assumption of the model.

solve.answer: The assumption that the candle burns at the same rate the whole time
solve.work: Key assumption: constant burn rate. A.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: A bakery owner says, "We waste too much bread." Which statement turns this into a problem that a mathematical model can help solve?
choices: Find how many loaves to bake daily so that few are left over and few customers are turned away
Decide whether people should buy bread from the bakery or from the grocery store each week
Find out which kind of bread the owner likes best, so the bakery can sell only that kind every day
Explain why the owner feels that so much bread is thrown away at the end of every working day of the week
questions.answer: Find how many loaves to bake daily so that few are left over and few customers are turned away
questions.solution: A model needs a goal that can be measured. Choosing the number of loaves to bake each day, balancing leftovers against unmet demand, is a quantity question. The other statements are about preferences or feelings.

solve.answer: Find how many loaves to bake daily so that few are left over and few customers are turned away
solve.work: C defines a quantity to find (loaves per day) with a measurable trade-off (leftovers vs turned-away customers). Others are opinion or explanation.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: A team models how long a cup of hot tea takes to cool to a safe temperature. Which list contains only quantities that belong in the model?
choices: The color of the cup, the brand of the tea, and the time
The tea's starting temperature, the cup's price, and the day of the week
The tea's starting temperature, the room's temperature, and the time
The room's temperature, the name of the person drinking the tea, and the time
questions.answer: The tea's starting temperature, the room's temperature, and the time
questions.solution: How fast tea cools depends on how hot it starts, how warm the room is, and how much time has passed. Color, brand, price, the day of the week and the drinker's name do not affect the cooling.

solve.answer: The tea's starting temperature, the room's temperature, and the time
solve.work: Cooling depends on the tea's starting temperature, the room (ambient) temperature and elapsed time. Every other list includes something irrelevant (person's name, cup color, brand, price, day of week).

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: Leo models his monthly phone bill by assuming he will use exactly 4 GB of data every month. Which statement describes a risk of this assumption?
choices: The model will always predict exactly the same bill that the phone company charges him each month
The model cannot be used, because a model may not include any assumptions
If his real use changes from month to month, the model's predicted bills may be wrong
The assumption lowers his actual bills, so he will pay less than the model predicts
questions.answer: If his real use changes from month to month, the model's predicted bills may be wrong
questions.solution: An assumption is a simplification. If Leo's real data use differs from 4 GB, the bills the model predicts will differ from the real bills. Models always use assumptions; the point is to know what they are and how they could fail.

solve.answer: If his real use changes from month to month, the model's predicted bills may be wrong
solve.work: If usage varies, a fixed-4 GB model mispredicts bills. A.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A scientist measures a plant. It is 14 cm tall after 2 days and 30 cm tall after 6 days. She models the height as a linear function of the number of days. According to her model, how many centimeters does the plant grow each day?
questions.solution: The growth rate of a linear model is the change in height divided by the change in time: $\frac{30 - 14}{6 - 2} = \frac{16}{4} = 4$ cm per day.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A car rental costs 35 dollars per day plus 0.20 dollars per mile driven. Which function models the total cost $C$, in dollars, of renting for 3 days and driving $m$ miles?
questions.solution: Three days at 35 dollars a day cost $3 \times 35 = 105$ dollars. The mileage charge is 0.20 dollars for each of the $m$ miles, so it is $0.2m$. The total is $C = 105 + 0.2m$.

solve.work: 3 days x 35 = 105 dollars fixed; 0.20 per mile for m miles = 0.2m. C = 105 + 0.2m.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: The height, in feet, of a ball thrown upward is modeled by $h = -16t^2 + 48t + 4$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after the throw. What height does the model give at $t = 2$ seconds?
questions.solution: Put $t = 2$ into the model: $h = -16(2)^2 + 48(2) + 4 = -64 + 96 + 4 = 36$. The model gives a height of 36 feet.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A town's population is modeled by $P = 2000 \times 1.05^t$, where $t$ is the number of years from now. How many people does the model predict after 2 years?
questions.solution: Put $t = 2$ into the model: $1.05^2 = 1.1025$, so $P = 2000 \times 1.1025 = 2205$ people.

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A team conjectures that doubling the number of workers on a job cuts the time in half. With 2 workers, painting a fence took 6 hours. With 4 workers, it took 4 hours. What does this result show?
choices: The data support the conjecture, because more workers finished sooner
The data prove the conjecture, because the time dropped by 2 hours
The data cannot be used, because a test needs at least 10 workers
The data do not support the conjecture, which would predict 3 hours
questions.answer: The data do not support the conjecture, which would predict 3 hours
questions.solution: Halving 6 hours gives 3 hours, but the job took 4 hours with twice as many workers. The result disagrees with the conjecture, so it does not support it.

solve.answer: The data do not support the conjecture, which would predict 3 hours
solve.work: Conjecture: doubling workers halves time, so 4 workers should take 6/2 = 3 hours. Observed 4 hours, so the data do not support the conjecture. 'Support because sooner' ignores the specific halving claim; data never 'prove' it.

questions.skill: Revise a model
questions.stem: A team's model predicted that 200 tickets would be sold at a school carnival, but 260 were sold. The team finds that the model left out tickets bought at the door. What is the best next step in the modeling cycle?
choices: Keep the model unchanged, since one event is not enough to question it
Revise the model to include door sales, then test it again with new data
Delete the 60 extra tickets from the data so that the model fits the carnival's sales
Report the model as correct and explain the difference between 200 and 260 as bad luck
questions.answer: Revise the model to include door sales, then test it again with new data
questions.solution: The team has found a reason the model was off: door sales were missing. The cycle says to revise the model to fix that, and then test the new version on fresh data. Throwing away data or ignoring the error does not improve the model.

solve.answer: Revise the model to include door sales, then test it again with new data
solve.work: Missing variable found: revise the model to include door sales and retest. C.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: A student fits a straight line to a child's heights at ages 2 through 10 and uses it to predict the same child's height at age 40. Which is the best critique of this use of the model?
choices: The model is wrong because heights can never be modeled by a straight line
The model was built from ages 2 to 10, so it may not apply far outside that range
The model is fine, because a model that fits well for some ages fits for all ages
The model is valid only if the heights were measured in centimeters
questions.answer: The model was built from ages 2 to 10, so it may not apply far outside that range
questions.solution: A model is supported by the data it was built from. Predicting far beyond that range is extrapolation and is unreliable; people stop growing, so a line that rises through childhood does not describe adults.

solve.answer: The model was built from ages 2 to 10, so it may not apply far outside that range
solve.work: Extrapolating a linear fit from ages 2-10 to age 40 is invalid because growth stops; the model applies only near the data's range. Lines can model height over a short range, and units do not matter.

questions.skill: Order of the modeling cycle
questions.stem: Four steps of a modeling project are listed: (1) build an equation, (2) state the problem, (3) test the predictions against data, (4) list the quantities and assumptions. Which order fits the modeling cycle?
questions.solution: State the problem (2), list the quantities and assumptions (4), build the equation (1), then test the predictions (3).

solve.work: State problem (2), list quantities/assumptions (4), build equation (1), test (3): 2,4,1,3.

questions.skill: Order of the modeling cycle
questions.stem: Which step must be finished before a team can write an equation for its model?
choices: Testing the model against new data
Revising the model after finding a mismatch
Explaining the finished model to the class
Naming the quantities and assumptions
questions.answer: Naming the quantities and assumptions
questions.solution: An equation is built from the quantities and assumptions. Testing, revising and explaining all come after a model exists.

solve.answer: Naming the quantities and assumptions
solve.work: Before formulating an equation, the quantities and assumptions must be named. C.

questions.skill: Order of the modeling cycle
questions.stem: A team has just revised its model after a test. What does the modeling cycle say to do next?
choices: Test the revised model against data again
Declare the first model correct after all
Skip testing, because revised models are always right
Choose a brand-new problem and start over
questions.answer: Test the revised model against data again
questions.solution: A revised model is a new model, so it has to be tested again. The cycle can repeat until the model works well enough.

solve.answer: Test the revised model against data again
solve.work: After revising, test the revised model again.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: The principal says, "Our school is too crowded at lunch." Which statement turns this into a problem a model can help solve?
choices: Find which lunch food the students like the most, so that the school can serve it every day
Decide which students should sit together at lunch, so that friends are always at the same table
Find how many students should eat in each lunch period so that every student has a seat
Find how loud the cafeteria is on average during lunch, so that the noise can be turned down
questions.answer: Find how many students should eat in each lunch period so that every student has a seat
questions.solution: A model needs a measurable unknown connected to the concern. The number of students per lunch period is related to the number of seats, so it addresses crowding directly.

solve.answer: Find how many students should eat in each lunch period so that every student has a seat
solve.work: Crowding -> how many students per lunch period so all have seats. D.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: A gym wants to know whether it should add a second shift of classes. Which question could a model answer, once the team collects data?
choices: Which exercise do the members enjoy the most overall, and which class would they most like to take?
Is the music in the gym too loud for the members, and which songs would they like to hear instead?
What color should the walls of the gym be painted, and which color will the members like best?
How many members are in the building at each hour of the day, and when is the building full?
questions.answer: How many members are in the building at each hour of the day, and when is the building full?
questions.solution: Counting members hour by hour gives numbers a model can use to decide whether a second shift is needed. The other questions are about opinions or looks.

solve.answer: How many members are in the building at each hour of the day, and when is the building full?
solve.work: Hourly occupancy and when capacity is reached is measurable and bears on adding a shift. A.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: Which statement is too vague to be the problem for a model?
choices: Improve how well our town works for people who ride bikes
Find the length of bike lane needed so every house is within 1 kilometer of a lane
Find how many bike racks a school needs if 40 percent of 600 students ride
Find how many minutes a ride from the park to the library takes at 12 kilometers per hour
questions.answer: Improve how well our town works for people who ride bikes
questions.solution: A good problem names what is to be found. The other three each name a measurable unknown; "improve how well the town works" does not.

solve.answer: Improve how well our town works for people who ride bikes
solve.work: "Improve how well our town works" has no measurable quantity.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: A team models a school's daily electricity use by assuming it is the same on every day of the year. Which fact shows this assumption is poor?
choices: The school has more than one classroom, and each classroom has its own set of lights
The school is closed on weekends and in summer, when much less electricity is used
The school's electricity is measured in kilowatt-hours on a meter near the front office
The school uses at least some electricity on every school day throughout the whole year
questions.answer: The school is closed on weekends and in summer, when much less electricity is used
questions.solution: The assumption fails if use changes a lot from day to day. Closed days with low use show that it does; the other facts do not affect it.

solve.answer: The school is closed on weekends and in summer, when much less electricity is used
solve.work: Closures on weekends/summer mean use is not constant, so the assumption is poor. A.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: A team models the cost of a school trip. It assumes the trip needs 4 bus rentals at 150 dollars each and a lunch at 6 dollars for each of 80 students. Under these assumptions, what is the total cost, in dollars?
questions.solution: Buses: $4 \times 150 = 600$ dollars. Lunches: $80 \times 6 = 480$ dollars. Total: $600 + 480 = 1080$ dollars.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: In the model $d = 3t$ for the distance $d$ in miles a hiker walks in $t$ hours, which quantity does the model assume stays the same?
choices: The time $t$ that the hiker spends walking
The distance $d$ that the hiker has covered
The hiker's speed, 3 miles per hour
The hour of the day at which the hike started
questions.answer: The hiker's speed, 3 miles per hour
questions.solution: In the model, $t$ and $d$ change together. The number 3, the speed, is fixed, so the model assumes a constant speed of 3 miles per hour.

solve.answer: The hiker's speed, 3 miles per hour
solve.work: d = 3t assumes constant speed 3 mph. D.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: The length of a rectangle is 3 meters more than its width $w$. Which function models its perimeter $P$, in meters?
questions.solution: The length is $w + 3$, so $P = 2w + 2(w + 3) = 4w + 6$. The expression $w^2 + 3w$ is the area.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A member of a gym has paid 70 dollars in all after 2 months and 145 dollars in all after 5 months. The total is a linear function of the number of months and includes a one-time sign-up fee. What is the sign-up fee, in dollars?
questions.solution: The monthly fee is $(145 - 70) \div (5 - 2) = 25$ dollars. After 2 months the monthly fees come to 50 dollars, so the sign-up fee is $70 - 50 = 20$ dollars.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A savings account holds 800 dollars and earns 3 percent interest each year, added at the end of the year. Which function models the amount $A$, in dollars, after $t$ years?
choices: $A = 800 \times 3^t$
questions.solution: Each year the amount is multiplied by 1.03, so after $t$ years it is $800 \times 1.03^t$.

solve.work: Growth factor 1.03 per year: A = 800 x 1.03^t.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: Jo walks at 4 kilometers per hour for 2 hours, and then at 3 kilometers per hour for $t$ more hours. Which function models her total distance $D$, in kilometers?
questions.solution: The first part is $4 \times 2 = 8$ kilometers. The second part is $3t$ kilometers. So $D = 8 + 3t$.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A ball is dropped from a height of 100 meters. A model for its height in meters after $t$ seconds is $h = 100 - 5t^2$. According to the model, what is the height after 3 seconds?

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A model for the number of fish in a lake is $F = 1200 \times 0.95^t$, where $t$ is the number of years from now. According to the model, how many fish are in the lake after 2 years?

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: Model A for the money in one account is $A = 500 + 20t$ and model B for another account is $B = 400 + 30t$, where $t$ is the number of months. After how many months do the two models give the same amount?

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A model predicts $y = 3x + 2$. A test at $x = 4$ gives an actual value of 17. What is the actual value minus the predicted value?
questions.solution: The predicted value is $3 \times 4 + 2 = 14$. The actual value minus the predicted value is $17 - 14 = 3$.

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A team conjectures that a plant grows exactly 2 cm each day. It measures the plant's height at the end of days 1 to 4 and gets 4, 6, 8 and 13 cm. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The conjecture fits the first three days but not day 4, so the team should look into why
The conjecture is proven, since three of the four days match it and the fourth is only one day
The team should drop day 4 so that all the data fit the conjecture
The data say nothing about the conjecture, since the heights differ every day of the plant's growth
questions.answer: The conjecture fits the first three days but not day 4, so the team should look into why
questions.solution: The heights grow by 2 cm for three days and then by 5 cm. The conjecture is not supported on day 4, and the right response is to investigate, not to hide the data point.

solve.answer: The conjecture fits the first three days but not day 4, so the team should look into why
solve.work: Days 1-3: 4, 6, 8 rise by 2; day 4 rises by 5 to 13. Fits first three days, not day 4; investigate. C.

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A team has built a model of the number of visitors to a park. Which plan is the best test of the model?
choices: Check the model on the very same days that were used to build it in the first place
Collect visitor counts for new days and compare them with the model's predictions
Ask a few of the team's friends whether the model seems reasonable and sensible to them
Make sure that the model is written as an equation with clearly labeled variables
questions.answer: Collect visitor counts for new days and compare them with the model's predictions
questions.solution: A good test compares predictions with new data that were not used to build the model.

solve.answer: Collect visitor counts for new days and compare them with the model's predictions
solve.work: Validate on new data not used to build the model. B.

questions.skill: Revise a model
questions.stem: A team's first model assumed that each of 150 students recycles 2 bottles a week. Data show that each student recycles 3 bottles a week. Using the revised assumption, how many bottles does the model predict for 4 weeks?
questions.solution: Bottles per week: $3 \times 150 = 450$. For 4 weeks: $450 \times 4 = 1800$ bottles.

questions.skill: Revise a model
questions.stem: A team models a puppy's weight with a straight line fitted to its weights from 1 to 6 months. At 9 months the puppy weighs far less than the line predicts, because its growth has slowed. Which revision is best?
choices: Use a model whose growth levels off as the puppy gets older
Make the line steeper so that it follows the puppy's weights better
Keep the line and say that the puppy is unusual and not growing as it should
Remove the 9-month weight from the data so that the line fits the rest
questions.answer: Use a model whose growth levels off as the puppy gets older
questions.solution: The data show growth slowing, which a straight line cannot show. A model that levels off matches what the data show.

solve.answer: Use a model whose growth levels off as the puppy gets older
solve.work: Growth slowing calls for a model that levels off (e.g., logarithmic/logistic). B.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: A model shows that ice cream sales and swimming accidents both rise in the summer. A team says, "Ice cream sales cause swimming accidents." What is the best critique?
choices: The model is wrong, since ice cream sales cannot rise in the summer or in any other season of the year
The model proves that swimming accidents cause ice cream sales, because both rise at the same time
The model proves nothing, because the ice cream sales were not measured in dollars as they should be
Both rise in hot weather, so the model shows a relationship but not that one causes the other
questions.answer: Both rise in hot weather, so the model shows a relationship but not that one causes the other
questions.solution: Two quantities can rise together because of a third factor, here the weather. A relationship in the data does not prove one causes the other.

solve.answer: Both rise in hot weather, so the model shows a relationship but not that one causes the other
solve.work: Lurking variable hot weather; correlation is not causation. B.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: A team compares two models of the same data. Model A has a simple equation and errors of about 2. Model B has a very complicated equation and errors of about 1.9. Which is the best argument for choosing model A?
choices: Model A is nearly as accurate and much easier to understand and use
Simple models are never wrong, so a simple model is always the best one to choose
The errors of model B cannot be measured, so its accuracy cannot be compared fairly
A smaller error always means a worse model, so model B's error counts against it
questions.answer: Model A is nearly as accurate and much easier to understand and use
questions.solution: A model is judged on both accuracy and usefulness. Here the accuracy is about the same, so the easier model is the better choice.

solve.answer: Model A is nearly as accurate and much easier to understand and use
solve.work: Error 2 vs 1.9 nearly equal; simpler model easier to understand and use (parsimony). B.

questions.skill: Order of the modeling cycle
questions.stem: A team is modeling how many buses a school needs for a field trip. Which list puts these steps in an order that fits the modeling cycle?
choices: List quantities and assumptions, write the equation, state the problem, revise, compare predictions with data
State the problem, write the equation, list quantities and assumptions, revise, compare predictions with data
Write the equation, state the problem, compare predictions with data, list quantities and assumptions, revise
State the problem, list quantities and assumptions, write the equation, compare predictions with data, revise
questions.answer: State the problem, list quantities and assumptions, write the equation, compare predictions with data, revise
questions.solution: You need to know what you are solving before choosing quantities, and the quantities before writing an equation. Predictions are then compared with data, and any revision follows from that comparison.

solve.answer: State the problem, list quantities and assumptions, write the equation, compare predictions with data, revise
solve.work: Order: identify the problem, formulate (quantities and assumptions), build the model (equation), validate (compare predictions with data), revise. Only the last option has this order.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: A school wants to know how long it will take to empty a 5,000-gallon water tank with a pump that removes 40 gallons each minute. Which statement correctly names the unknown, the given quantities and the goal?
choices: Unknown: the time in minutes. Given: 5,000 gallons and 40 gallons per minute. Goal: find how long emptying takes.
Unknown: the tank volume. Given: the time and 40 gallons per minute. Goal: find how much water the tank holds.
Unknown: the pump rate. Given: 5,000 gallons and the time. Goal: find how fast the pump works, in gallons per minute.
Unknown: the number of pumps. Given: 5,000 gallons and 40 gallons per minute. Goal: find how many pumps to buy.
questions.answer: Unknown: the time in minutes. Given: 5,000 gallons and 40 gallons per minute. Goal: find how long emptying takes.
questions.solution: The question asks for a time, so time is the unknown. The tank size (5,000 gallons) and the pump rate (40 gallons per minute) are given. The goal is to find the time needed to empty the tank.

solve.answer: Unknown: the time in minutes. Given: 5,000 gallons and 40 gallons per minute. Goal: find how long emptying takes.
solve.work: Unknown = time in minutes; given 5000 gal and 40 gal/min; goal how long emptying takes (125 min). B.

questions.skill: Revise a model
questions.stem: A team models the cartons of 12 eggs a cafeteria needs for 240 breakfasts, assuming each breakfast uses 1.5 eggs on average. A test shows the true average is 2 eggs per breakfast. When the model is revised, how many more cartons does it call for than the first model?
questions.solution: First model: $240 \times 1.5 = 360$ eggs, and $360 \div 12 = 30$ cartons. Revised model: $240 \times 2 = 480$ eggs, and $480 \div 12 = 40$ cartons. The revised model needs $40 - 30 = 10$ more cartons.

solve.work: First model: 240 x 1.5 = 360 eggs, 360/12 = 30 cartons. Revised: 240 x 2 = 480 eggs, 480/12 = 40 cartons. Difference 40 - 30 = 10 cartons.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A print shop's price is a linear function of the number of copies. It charges 3 dollars for 10 copies and 7 dollars for 50 copies. Using a linear model, how many dollars does the shop charge for 130 copies?
questions.solution: The rate is $\frac{7 - 3}{50 - 10} = 0.1$ dollars per copy. From 10 to 130 copies is 120 more copies, which add $120 \times 0.1 = 12$ dollars to the 3 dollars. The price is $3 + 12 = 15$ dollars.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A farmer has 100 meters of fence to enclose a rectangular pen of width $w$ meters, using all of the fence. Which function models the area $A$, in square meters, of the pen?
questions.solution: The fence goes around all four sides, so $2w + 2L = 100$ and the length is $L = 50 - w$. The area is width times length: $A = w(50 - w)$.

solve.work: Perimeter 2w + 2L = 100, so L = 50 - w. Area A = w(50 - w). Other options: 50w ignores the constraint; w(100 - w) uses L = 100 - w; 2w(50 - w) doubles the area.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A store models its daily revenue, in dollars, from selling a toy at a price of $p$ dollars by $R = p(60 - 2p)$. According to the model, what price, in dollars, gives the greatest revenue?
questions.solution: Expand: $R = 60p - 2p^2$. This is a parabola that opens downward, so its greatest value is at the vertex, $p = \frac{60}{2 \times 2} = 15$. A price of 15 dollars gives the greatest revenue (450 dollars).

solve.work: R = 60p - 2p^2, a downward parabola with zeros p = 0 and p = 30; vertex at p = 15. R(15) = 15 x 30 = 450 dollars, the maximum.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: The value of a car, in dollars, is modeled by $V = 20000 \times 0.9^t$, where $t$ is its age in years. According to the model, how many dollars does the car lose in value during its first year?
questions.solution: At $t = 0$ the value is 20000. At $t = 1$ it is $20000 \times 0.9 = 18000$. The car loses $20000 - 18000 = 2000$ dollars.

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A team's linear model predicts weekly sales of 15, 18, 21 and 24 for weeks 1 to 4. The actual sales were 15, 19, 25 and 31. What do the differences between actual and predicted sales suggest?
choices: The model fits well, because the first prediction matched the actual sales exactly
Sales are growing more slowly than the model predicts, so the line should be made much flatter
Sales grow faster than the linear model predicts, so another kind of model may fit better
The differences look random, so the model needs no change and no further testing
questions.answer: Sales grow faster than the linear model predicts, so another kind of model may fit better
questions.solution: The actual minus predicted differences are 0, 1, 4 and 7. They grow steadily, so the model underestimates more and more. That points to growth faster than a straight line, so another model may fit better.

solve.answer: Sales grow faster than the linear model predicts, so another kind of model may fit better
solve.work: Residuals actual-predicted: 0, 1, 4, 7, increasing; actual increments 4, 6, 6 exceed model 3. Growth faster than linear; consider another model. B.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: A team builds a model of daily lunch demand from last week's data. They defend it by saying, "It is correct, because it matches last week's data exactly." Which is the best response?
choices: Matching the data used to build a model is not a test of it; check it on new data
A model that matches its data exactly is correct, so no further testing is needed
An exact match shows the model is too simple, so it should be made more complicated
Real data never fit a model exactly, so the match shows that the data must be wrong
questions.answer: Matching the data used to build a model is not a test of it; check it on new data
questions.solution: A model is built to fit its data, so a good fit proves little. The real test is whether it predicts new data that it was not built from.

solve.answer: Matching the data used to build a model is not a test of it; check it on new data
solve.work: Fitting the data the model was built from is not validation; it must be tested on new data. The other responses are false claims.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: A model for the number of fish in a pond is $F = 200 \times 1.2^t$, where $t$ is the number of years. A critic says it will fail for large $t$. Which is the best reason?
choices: It shows the fish population decreasing, but real populations always increase
It uses an exponent, and models of animal populations are not allowed to use exponents
It starts with 200 fish, and a model of a population must always start with exactly 1 fish
It grows without limit, but the pond can support only a limited number of fish
questions.answer: It grows without limit, but the pond can support only a limited number of fish
questions.solution: Because 1.2 is greater than 1, the model keeps growing and eventually passes any number. A pond has only so much space and food, so the real population levels off and the model stops describing it.

solve.answer: It grows without limit, but the pond can support only a limited number of fish
solve.work: 1.2^t grows without bound; a pond has limited carrying capacity. A. (B false: the model increases.)

questions.skill: Order of the modeling cycle
questions.stem: A team is modeling how many seats a theater needs. It has stated the problem, named its quantities and assumptions, and built an equation. Which list gives the remaining steps in an order that fits the modeling cycle?
choices: Test against data, then use the equation to make predictions, explain the results, revise if needed
Use the equation to make predictions, test them against data, revise if needed, explain the results
Explain the results to the class, revise the model if needed, make predictions, test against data
Revise the model, test it against data, use the equation to make predictions, explain the results
questions.answer: Use the equation to make predictions, test them against data, revise if needed, explain the results
questions.solution: A model must first be used to make predictions. Those are then tested against data, the model is revised if the test shows a problem, and the results are explained.

solve.answer: Use the equation to make predictions, test them against data, revise if needed, explain the results
solve.work: After formulating: compute/predict, validate against data, revise if needed, report. A.

questions.skill: Order of the modeling cycle
questions.stem: Which statement about the modeling cycle is true?
choices: It runs once in a fixed order and ends when the first equation is written
Testing against data must happen before the problem is even stated
It can repeat: testing may send a team back to revise its assumptions or its model
Revising is allowed only before any model has been built, and never after any test has been done
questions.answer: It can repeat: testing may send a team back to revise its assumptions or its model
questions.solution: The word cycle means the steps can be repeated. A failed test is a reason to go back and revise, and then test again.

solve.answer: It can repeat: testing may send a team back to revise its assumptions or its model
solve.work: The cycle is iterative: testing can lead back to revising. B.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: A team studies a 600-liter rain barrel. The garden uses 45 liters from it each day and 15 liters of rain run into it each day. Which statement best states the problem of how long the water will last?
choices: Find the number of days until the 600 liters are used up, when only 45 liters leave each day and no rain falls
Find the number of days until the 600 liters are used up, when 45 liters leave and 15 liters enter each day
Find the number of liters left in the barrel after one day, when 45 liters leave and 15 liters of rain enter
Find the number of days until the 600 liters are used up, when 60 liters leave each day
questions.answer: Find the number of days until the 600 liters are used up, when 45 liters leave and 15 liters enter each day
questions.solution: The unknown is a number of days. Each day the barrel loses 45 liters and gains 15 liters, so the statement must include both flows. Ignoring the rain, or adding it instead of subtracting it, changes the problem.

solve.answer: Find the number of days until the 600 liters are used up, when 45 liters leave and 15 liters enter each day
solve.work: Net loss 45-15 = 30 L/day; 600/30 = 20 days. C states the problem correctly; A wrongly says 60 L leave, B only one day, D ignores rain.

questions.skill: Identify the problem to be modeled
questions.stem: A team's notes say: (1) Each cabin holds 6 campers. (2) Find how many cabins are needed for 70 campers. (3) Campers do not share bunks with other cabins. Which sentence states the problem itself, rather than a given quantity or an assumption?
choices: Each cabin holds 6 campers
Campers do not share bunks with other cabins
Find how many cabins are needed for 70 campers
Seventy campers will each need a bunk of their own
questions.answer: Find how many cabins are needed for 70 campers
questions.solution: The problem is the question to be answered: how many cabins. The other sentences give a quantity or make an assumption.

solve.answer: Find how many cabins are needed for 70 campers
solve.work: (2) is the problem: find cabins for 70 campers (ceil(70/6) = 12). D.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: A team finds the number of people a ferry carries in a day by multiplying the capacity per trip, the fraction of seats filled, and the number of trips per day. Which quantity is NOT needed?
choices: The capacity of the ferry per trip
The fraction of the seats that are filled
The number of trips the ferry makes in a day
The price of a ticket
questions.answer: The price of a ticket
questions.solution: The number of people carried is capacity times fraction filled times trips. The price of a ticket would matter for money collected, not for people carried.

solve.answer: The price of a ticket
solve.work: Product of capacity, fraction filled, trips; price not used.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: A team assumes a dripping faucet drips 1 drop every 2 seconds, and that 20 drops make 1 milliliter. Under these assumptions, how many milliliters drip in 1 hour (3,600 seconds)?
questions.solution: In 3,600 seconds there are $3600 \div 2 = 1800$ drops. Then $1800 \div 20 = 90$ milliliters.

questions.skill: Name quantities and assumptions
questions.stem: Two teams model the time to paint a fence. Team A assumes the painter never rests. Team B assumes the painter rests 10 minutes in every hour. Which statement is true?
choices: Team B's assumption is more realistic and will likely give a longer time
Team A's model must be right, because a simpler model is always more accurate
Both models give the same time because they paint the same fence
Team B's model will give a shorter time, because it adds a rest break each hour
questions.answer: Team B's assumption is more realistic and will likely give a longer time
questions.solution: Adding rest time makes the total time longer, and people do rest, so Team B's assumption is more realistic. Simpler does not mean right.

solve.answer: Team B's assumption is more realistic and will likely give a longer time
solve.work: Resting 10 min per hour is more realistic and lengthens total time. C.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A farmer wants to fence a rectangular pen with an area of 600 square meters. Let $w$ be the width in meters. Which function models the amount of fence $F$, in meters, needed to go all the way around?
choices: $F = w + 2 \times \frac{600}{w}$
$F = 2w + 2 \times 600 \times w$
questions.solution: The length is $\frac{600}{w}$. The perimeter is $2w + 2 \times \frac{600}{w} = 2w + \frac{1200}{w}$.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A tank is draining at a constant rate. After 3 minutes it holds 90 liters, and after 8 minutes it holds 40 liters. Using a linear model, how many liters did the tank hold when it started draining?
questions.solution: The rate is $(90 - 40) \div (8 - 3) = 10$ liters per minute. In the first 3 minutes the tank lost 30 liters, so it started with $90 + 30 = 120$ liters.

questions.skill: Build a model
questions.stem: A sample of 640 grams of a substance loses half of its mass every 3 days. Using a model with this assumption, how many grams remain after 12 days?
questions.solution: 12 days is $12 \div 3 = 4$ halvings. The mass is $640 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4 = 640 \div 16 = 40$ grams.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A model says the number of buses needed equals the number of students divided by 48, rounded up to the next whole number. According to the model, how many buses are needed for 250 students?
questions.solution: $250 \div 48$ is about 5.2. Rounding up to a whole bus gives 6 buses.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A model for the temperature in degrees of a cooling drink is $T = 20 + 60 \times 0.5^{t/10}$, where $t$ is the time in minutes. According to the model, what is the temperature after 20 minutes?
questions.solution: For $t = 20$, the exponent is $20 \div 10 = 2$. So $T = 20 + 60 \times 0.25 = 20 + 15 = 35$ degrees.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A model for the height in feet of a rocket $t$ seconds after it is launched from the ground is $h = -16t^2 + 96t$. According to the model, at what time in seconds does the rocket return to the ground?
questions.solution: Set $-16t^2 + 96t = 0$, so $-16t(t - 6) = 0$. The rocket is on the ground at $t = 0$ and at $t = 6$ seconds.

questions.skill: Analyze a model
questions.stem: A store models its daily sales of scarves by $S = 400 - 25p$, where $p$ is the price in dollars. The team says the model should not be used for prices above 16 dollars. What is the best reason?
choices: Above 16 dollars the model gives sales greater than 400
Above 16 dollars the model says sales rise as the price rises
Above 16 dollars the model gives negative sales, which is impossible
Above 16 dollars the model gives the same sales for every price, which is not realistic
questions.answer: Above 16 dollars the model gives negative sales, which is impossible
questions.solution: At $p = 16$, $S = 400 - 400 = 0$. For a higher price the model gives a negative number of scarves sold, so it no longer makes sense.

solve.answer: Above 16 dollars the model gives negative sales, which is impossible
solve.work: S = 400 - 25p = 0 at p = 16; for p > 16, S < 0, impossible. D.

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A model predicts weekly sales of $S = 12 + 5w$ for week $w$. The actual sales in weeks 1, 2, 3 and 4 were 18, 21, 27 and 30. What is the total of the four actual values minus the total of the four predicted values?
questions.solution: The predictions are 17, 22, 27 and 32, which total 98. The actual sales total $18 + 21 + 27 + 30 = 96$. So $96 - 98 = -2$.

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A team conjectures that the area of a square doubles when its side length doubles. It tests a side of 3 (area 9) and a side of 6 (area 36). What does the test show?
choices: The conjecture is true, since 36 is greater than 9 and the area has certainly increased
The conjecture is true, since 6 is double 3 and the side length doubled as stated
The conjecture is false for this case, since the area became 4 times as large
The test shows nothing yet, since only one pair of squares was tried and more are needed
questions.answer: The conjecture is false for this case, since the area became 4 times as large
questions.solution: When the side doubles from 3 to 6, the area goes from 9 to 36, which is 4 times as large, not double. One counterexample is enough to show a conjecture false.

solve.answer: The conjecture is false for this case, since the area became 4 times as large
solve.work: Area 9 -> 36 is 4 times, not double; one counterexample refutes the conjecture. D.

questions.skill: Test a model against data
questions.stem: A model predicts the values 10, 20 and 30 for three tests. The actual values are 12, 18 and 33. What is the largest difference, ignoring sign, between an actual value and its prediction?
questions.solution: The differences are $|12 - 10| = 2$, $|18 - 20| = 2$ and $|33 - 30| = 3$. The largest is 3.

questions.skill: Revise a model
questions.stem: A team's first model said a car uses 6 liters of fuel per 100 kilometers. Tests show the car actually uses 8 liters per 100 kilometers. For a 450-kilometer trip, how many more liters does the revised model predict than the first model?
questions.solution: The difference is 2 liters per 100 kilometers. For 450 kilometers: $2 \times 4.5 = 9$ liters.

questions.skill: Revise a model
questions.stem: A team's first model for a plant's height in centimeters after $d$ days is $h = 4 + 3d$. At day 6 the plant measures 25 cm. The team revises the model to a line through the starting height of 4 cm at day 0 and the 25 cm at day 6. What is the new slope, in centimeters per day?
questions.solution: The slope is the change in height divided by the change in time: $(25 - 4) \div 6 = 3.5$ centimeters per day.

questions.skill: Revise a model
questions.stem: A team's model predicts too many snack sales on rainy days, but is accurate on all other days. Which revision best uses this evidence?
choices: Lower the predictions for every day, rainy or not
Add a lower sales assumption for rainy days only
Raise the predictions for rainy days
Remove the rainy days from the problem
questions.answer: Add a lower sales assumption for rainy days only
questions.solution: The evidence points to rainy days, so the revision should change only rainy-day predictions, and lower them.

solve.answer: Add a lower sales assumption for rainy days only
solve.work: Overpredicts only on rainy days: lower predictions for rainy days only.

questions.skill: Revise a model
questions.stem: A team revised its model three times. Each time, it tested the revised model on the same 6 data points that it used to decide on the revision. What is the weakness in this process?
choices: A model should be revised only once, and revising it three times is too many
Testing on data points always makes a model worse, so models should not be tested at all
The final model has never been tested on data it was not adjusted to fit
Six data points can never be used to revise a model, since six is too few for any model
questions.answer: The final model has never been tested on data it was not adjusted to fit
questions.solution: A model adjusted to fit certain data will naturally fit them. To know whether it works, it must be tested on new data.

solve.answer: The final model has never been tested on data it was not adjusted to fit
solve.work: Testing on the same data used to tune the model is circular; it has never been checked on fresh data. C.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: A model of a class's test scores is $S = 70 + 2h$, where $h$ is the hours spent studying. A student says it shows that 20 hours of study earns a score of 110 on a 100-point test. What is the best critique?
choices: The model is fine, since it fits the data for small $h$ so it fits for all $h$
The model gives a score above the highest possible score, so it does not apply for large $h$
The model must be wrong for every value of $h$, since test scores cannot be modeled with a line at all
Scores should go down as the hours of study go up, so the model should have a negative slope
questions.answer: The model gives a score above the highest possible score, so it does not apply for large $h$
questions.solution: At $h = 20$ the model gives 110, which is impossible on a 100-point test. The model can be useful for small $h$ but not for large $h$.

solve.answer: The model gives a score above the highest possible score, so it does not apply for large $h$
solve.work: S(20) = 70 + 40 = 110 > 100: model fails for large h (domain limit). D.

questions.skill: Explain and critique a model
questions.stem: Two teams model next year's school enrollment from the same past data. Team 1 assumes enrollment grows by the same number of students each year. Team 2 assumes it grows by the same percent each year. What is a fair way to decide between the models?
choices: Choose the model that predicts the larger enrollment, since a larger number is safer to plan for
Choose the model whose assumption is easier to say aloud, since it is easier to explain to others
Test each model's predictions against enrollment data that neither team used to build it
Choose the model built by the team with more members, since more people checked the work behind it
questions.answer: Test each model's predictions against enrollment data that neither team used to build it
questions.solution: A fair decision depends on how well each model predicts new data. Size of prediction, wording and team size say nothing about accuracy.

solve.answer: Test each model's predictions against enrollment data that neither team used to build it
solve.work: Fair comparison: test predictions on holdout data neither team used. A.

questions.skill: Factor x^2 + bx + c
questions.stem: Which is the factored form of $x^2+5x+6$?
questions.solution: Look for two numbers that multiply to $6$ and add to $5$: they are $2$ and $3$. So $x^2+5x+6=(x+2)(x+3)$.

solve.work: Need two numbers with product 6 and sum 5: 2 and 3. (x+2)(x+3) = x^2+5x+6. Others: (x+1)(x+6)=x^2+7x+6; (x+5)(x+6)=x^2+11x+30; (x-2)(x-3)=x^2-5x+6.

questions.skill: Factor out the greatest common factor
questions.stem: Which is $6x+15$ written with its greatest common factor taken out?
questions.solution: The greatest common factor of $6$ and $15$ is $3$. Divide each term by $3$: $6x\div 3=2x$ and $15\div 3=5$. So $6x+15=3(2x+5)$.

solve.work: GCF of 6x and 15 is 3: 6x+15 = 3(2x+5). Others expand to 6x-15, 6x+45, 6x+90.

questions.skill: Factor a difference of squares
questions.stem: Which is the factored form of $x^2-25$?
questions.solution: $x^2-25=x^2-5^2$ is a difference of squares, so it factors as $(x-5)(x+5)$. Check: $(x-5)(x+5)=x^2+5x-5x-25=x^2-25$.

questions.skill: Area model for factoring
questions.stem: A rectangle is made of four smaller pieces with areas $x^2$, $2x$, $3x$ and $6$ square units. The rectangle is $x+3$ units long and $x+b$ units wide. What is $b$?
questions.solution: The pieces add to $x^2+5x+6=(x+2)(x+3)$. The sides are $x+3$ and $x+2$, so the width is $x+2$ and $b=2$.

solve.work: Total area x^2+2x+3x+6 = x^2+5x+6. (x+3)(x+b) = x^2+(3+b)x+3b, so 3b = 6 and 3+b = 5, b = 2. Pieces x*x, 2*x, 3*x, 3*2 match.

questions.skill: Complete the square: find the constant
questions.stem: What number must be added to $x^2+6x$ to make a perfect square trinomial?
questions.solution: Take half of the coefficient of $x$ and square it: $\left(\frac{6}{2}\right)^2=3^2=9$. Then $x^2+6x+9=(x+3)^2$.

solve.work: Half of 6 is 3, squared is 9: x^2+6x+9 = (x+3)^2.

questions.skill: Perfect square trinomials
questions.stem: Which is $(x+4)^2$ multiplied out?
questions.solution: $(x+4)^2=(x+4)(x+4)=x^2+4x+4x+16=x^2+8x+16$. The middle term is twice $4x$, which is $8x$.

questions.skill: Factor x^2 + bx + c
questions.stem: In the factorization $x^2+9x+20=(x+4)(x+c)$, what is $c$?
questions.solution: The constants multiply to $20$, so $4\cdot c=20$ and $c=5$. Check: $4+5=9$, which matches the middle term.

questions.skill: Factor out the greatest common factor
questions.stem: The expression $4x^2+8x$ can be written as $4x(x+c)$. What is $c$?
questions.solution: Divide each term by $4x$: $4x^2\div 4x=x$ and $8x\div 4x=2$. So $4x^2+8x=4x(x+2)$ and $c=2$.

questions.skill: Perfect square trinomials
questions.stem: Which of these is a perfect square trinomial?
questions.solution: A perfect square trinomial has the form $x^2+2ax+a^2$. For $x^2+10x+25$, $a=5$: $2a=10$ and $a^2=25$, so it equals $(x+5)^2$.

solve.work: x^2+10x+25 = (x+5)^2. x^2+10x+10 and x^2+10x+5 would need 25; x^2+5x+25 would need 10x. Only one is a perfect square.

questions.skill: Multiply binomials and polynomials
questions.stem: Which is $(x+1)(x+9)$ written as a trinomial?
questions.solution: Multiply each term: $x \cdot x = x^2$, $x \cdot 9 + 1 \cdot x = 10x$, and $1 \cdot 9 = 9$. The trinomial is $x^2+10x+9$.

questions.skill: Multiply binomials and polynomials
questions.stem: A rectangle is $x$ units wide and $x+5$ units long. Its area is $x^2+kx$ square units. What is $k$?
questions.solution: Distribute: $x(x+5) = x^2 + 5x$, so $k = 5$.

questions.skill: Multiply binomials and polynomials
questions.stem: The expression $3(x+4)$ is multiplied out and written as $3x+k$. What is $k$?
questions.solution: Distribute the 3 to both terms: $3 \cdot x + 3 \cdot 4 = 3x + 12$. So $k = 12$.

questions.skill: Factor x^2 + bx + c
questions.stem: Two numbers multiply to 12 and add to 7. What is the larger of the two numbers?
questions.solution: The pairs that multiply to 12 are 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4. Only 3 and 4 add to 7. The larger is 4.

questions.skill: Factor x^2 + bx + c
questions.stem: Which is $x^2+7x+10$ factored?
questions.solution: Find two numbers that multiply to 10 and add to 7: 2 and 5. So $x^2+7x+10 = (x+2)(x+5)$.

questions.skill: Factor x^2 + bx + c
questions.stem: The trinomial $x^2-7x+12$ factors as $(x-3)(x-?)$. What is the ?
questions.solution: The two numbers multiply to 12 and add to $-7$, so both are negative: $-3$ and $-4$. The ? is 4.

questions.skill: Factor out the greatest common factor
questions.stem: What is the greatest common factor of $8x$ and $12$?
questions.solution: The factors of 8 are 1, 2, 4, 8 and of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The greatest shared one is 4. The 12 has no $x$, so $x$ is not common.

solve.work: GCF of 8 and 12 is 4; x is not in 12. GCF = 4.

questions.skill: Factor out the greatest common factor
questions.stem: Which is $5x+20$ with its greatest common factor taken out?
questions.solution: Both terms are multiples of 5: $5x = 5 \cdot x$ and $20 = 5 \cdot 4$. So $5x+20 = 5(x+4)$.

questions.skill: Factor out the greatest common factor
questions.stem: Taking out the common factor of $7x-14$ gives $7(x-?)$. What is the ?
questions.solution: $7x - 14 = 7 \cdot x - 7 \cdot 2 = 7(x - 2)$. The ? is 2.

questions.skill: Factor a difference of squares
questions.stem: The expression $x^2-36$ factors as $(x-6)(x+?)$. What is the ?
questions.solution: A difference of squares $a^2-b^2$ factors as $(a-b)(a+b)$. Here $a = x$ and $b = 6$, so $x^2-36 = (x-6)(x+6)$.

questions.skill: Factor a difference of squares
questions.stem: Which of these is a difference of squares?
questions.solution: A difference of squares is one perfect square minus another: $9x^2 = (3x)^2$ and $4 = 2^2$, so $9x^2-4 = (3x)^2-2^2$.

questions.skill: Area model for factoring
questions.stem: An area model for $(x+2)(x+5)$ has four parts with areas $x^2$, $5x$, $2x$ and one more part with no $x$. What is the area of that last part?
questions.solution: The last part is the product of the two constants: $2 \cdot 5 = 10$.

questions.skill: Area model for factoring
questions.stem: A rectangle is split into four parts with areas $x^2$, $4x$, $3x$ and 12. Which product gives the area of the whole rectangle?
questions.solution: Put $x^2$ and 12 on a diagonal. The side lengths are $x+4$ and $x+3$: the parts are $x \cdot x$, $4 \cdot x$, $3 \cdot x$ and $4 \cdot 3$.

questions.skill: Area model for factoring
questions.stem: A rectangle is $x+6$ long and $x+1$ wide. Its area is $x^2+bx+6$. What is $b$?
questions.solution: The four parts are $x^2$, $6x$, $x$ and 6. The two $x$ parts total $6x + x = 7x$, so $b = 7$.
