questions.solution: There are $36 - 6 = 30$ outcomes where the numbers differ. The sum is 7 for (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2) and (6, 1), and all 6 have different numbers. So the probability is $\frac{6}{30} = \frac{1}{5}$.

solve.work: 36 ordered outcomes, 6 doubles, so 30 with different numbers. Sum 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) = 6, all with different numbers. 6/30 = 1/5.

questions.skill: Conditional probability from the formula
questions.stem: For events $A$ and $B$, $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \text{ or } B) = 0.6$. What is $P(A | \text{not } B)$?
questions.solution: $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.5 + 0.3 - 0.6 = 0.2$, so $P(A \text{ and not } B) = 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3$. Also $P(\text{not } B) = 0.7$. Then $P(A | \text{not } B) = \frac{0.3}{0.7} = \frac{3}{7}$.

questions.skill: Conditional probability from the formula
questions.stem: At a cafe, 80% of the customers buy a snack and 50% buy a drink. Among the customers who buy a drink, 60% also buy a snack. What is the probability that a customer who buys a snack also buys a drink?
questions.solution: The share who buy both is $0.5 \times 0.6 = 0.3$. Among the 80% who buy a snack, the share who also buy a drink is $\frac{0.3}{0.8} = \frac{3}{8}$.

questions.skill: Conditional probability from the formula
questions.stem: For events $A$ and $B$, $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.15$ and $P(B | A) = 0.3$. What is $P(A)$?
questions.solution: From $P(B | A) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(A)}$, we get $P(A) = \frac{0.15}{0.3} = 0.5$.

questions.skill: Conditional probability from the formula
questions.stem: For events $A$ and $B$ with $P(A \text{ and } B) > 0$ and $P(A) = P(B)$, which statement must be true?
choices: $A$ and $B$ are independent
$A$ and $B$ cannot happen together
$P(A | B) = P(B | A)$
questions.answer: $P(A | B) = P(B | A)$
questions.solution: Both conditional probabilities have the same top, $P(A \text{ and } B)$, and the same bottom, because $P(A) = P(B)$. So they are equal. The events need not be independent, they do happen together, and $P(A | B)$ need not be 1.

solve.answer: $P(A | B) = P(B | A)$
solve.work: P(A|B) = P(AB)/P(B) and P(B|A) = P(AB)/P(A); with P(A)=P(B) these are equal. The others need not hold (they can happen together since P(AB)>0; independence and P(A|B)=1 not forced).

questions.skill: Interpreting a conditional probability
questions.stem: A report states that $P(A | B) = 0.4$. What can be said about $P(B | A)$?
choices: It must also equal 0.4, because conditional probabilities are symmetric
It must equal 0.6, because the two probabilities add up to 1
It must be smaller than 0.4, because the event $B$ comes first
It cannot be found from $P(A | B)$ alone; more information is needed
questions.answer: It cannot be found from $P(A | B)$ alone; more information is needed
questions.solution: $P(B | A) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(A)}$, which also depends on $P(A)$ and $P(B)$. Different values give different answers, so $P(A | B)$ alone is not enough.

solve.answer: It cannot be found from $P(A | B)$ alone; more information is needed
solve.work: P(B|A) = P(A|B)P(B)/P(A) depends on P(A), P(B); it cannot be found from P(A|B) alone.

questions.skill: Interpreting a conditional probability
questions.stem: In a group of 2,000 people, 5% have a certain condition. A test is positive for 90% of the people who have the condition and for 10% of the people who do not. Of the people who test positive, what fraction have the condition?
questions.solution: There are $2000 \times 0.05 = 100$ people with the condition, and 90 of them test positive. The other 1,900 people include $1900 \times 0.10 = 190$ positives. So $\frac{90}{90 + 190} = \frac{9}{28}$ of the positives have the condition.

solve.work: Have it: 5% of 2000 = 100; positive 90. Without: 1900; positive 10% = 190. Positive total 280. Fraction 90/280 = 9/28.

questions.skill: Interpreting a conditional probability
questions.stem: A clinic records 100 patients. Of the 40 who received a new treatment, 30 recovered. Of the 60 who did not, 30 recovered. Which statement is correct?
choices: $P(\text{recovered} | \text{treated}) = 0.5$, which is less than $P(\text{recovered} | \text{not treated}) = 0.75$
$P(\text{recovered} | \text{treated}) = 0.3$, which is equal to $P(\text{recovered} | \text{not treated}) = 0.3$
$P(\text{recovered} | \text{treated}) = 0.75$, which is greater than $P(\text{recovered} | \text{not treated}) = 0.5$
$P(\text{recovered} | \text{treated}) = 0.3$, which is less than $P(\text{recovered} | \text{not treated}) = 0.5$
questions.answer: $P(\text{recovered} | \text{treated}) = 0.75$, which is greater than $P(\text{recovered} | \text{not treated}) = 0.5$
questions.solution: Among the 40 treated patients, $\frac{30}{40} = 0.75$ recovered. Among the 60 patients who were not treated, $\frac{30}{60} = 0.5$ recovered. The same count, 30, is out of different group sizes.

solve.answer: $P(\text{recovered} | \text{treated}) = 0.75$, which is greater than $P(\text{recovered} | \text{not treated}) = 0.5$

questions.skill: Testing independence with the product rule
questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A) = 0.7$ and $P(B) = 0.4$. What is the probability that exactly one of $A$ and $B$ happens?

questions.skill: Testing independence with the product rule
questions.stem: For events $A$ and $B$, $P(A) = 0.3$, $P(B) = 0.5$ and $P(\text{neither } A \text{ nor } B) = 0.4$. Which statement is correct?
choices: Independent, because $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.15$, which equals $0.3 \times 0.5$
Not independent, because $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.4$ but $0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15$
Not independent, because $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.8$ but $0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15$
Not independent, because $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.2$ but $0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15$
questions.answer: Not independent, because $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.2$ but $0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15$
questions.solution: $P(A \text{ or } B) = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6$, so $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.3 + 0.5 - 0.6 = 0.2$. Independence would need $0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15$, so the events are not independent.

solve.answer: Not independent, because $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.2$ but $0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15$
solve.work: P(A or B) = 1-0.4 = 0.6. P(A and B) = 0.3+0.5-0.6 = 0.2 != 0.15, not independent. Last option.

questions.skill: Testing independence with the product rule
questions.stem: A part must pass three independent inspections. The probabilities of passing them are 0.9, 0.8 and 0.5. What is the probability that the part fails at least one inspection?
questions.solution: The part passes all three with probability $0.9 \times 0.8 \times 0.5 = 0.36$. Failing at least one is the opposite: $1 - 0.36 = 0.64 = \frac{16}{25}$.

questions.skill: Testing independence with the product rule
questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A) = 0.4$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. What is $P(\text{not } A \text{ and } B)$?
questions.solution: Because $A$ and $B$ are independent, so are "not $A$" and $B$. $P(\text{not } A) = 0.6$, so the probability is $0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.3$.

questions.skill: Independence from a two-way table
questions.stem: In a survey of 200 people, 80 prefer brand X. 32 of the people who prefer brand X are under 25. Preferring brand X is independent of being under 25. How many of the 200 people are under 25?
questions.solution: Among the people who prefer brand X, $\frac{32}{80} = 40\%$ are under 25. By independence, 40% of all 200 people are under 25, which is $0.4 \times 200 = 80$.

questions.skill: Independence from a two-way table
questions.stem: Of 100 students, 36 like both math and science, 24 like only math, 24 like only science and 16 like neither. Are liking math and liking science independent?
choices: No, because only 36 of the 100 students like both math and science, fewer than half of them
Yes, because the number who like only math equals the number who like only science, 24 in each case
No, because the number who like neither, 16, is different from the number who like both
Yes, because 60% like math, 60% like science, and 0.6 times 0.6 equals 0.36, the share who like both
questions.answer: Yes, because 60% like math, 60% like science, and 0.6 times 0.6 equals 0.36, the share who like both
questions.solution: The students who like math number $36 + 24 = 60$, and those who like science number $36 + 24 = 60$. If the events were independent, the share liking both would be $0.6 \times 0.6 = 0.36$, which matches the 36 students observed. So they are independent.

solve.answer: Yes, because 60% like math, 60% like science, and 0.6 times 0.6 equals 0.36, the share who like both
solve.work: Math: 36+24 = 60%; science: 36+24 = 60%; both 36% = 0.6*0.6. Independent. Last option.

questions.skill: Independence from a two-way table
questions.stem: Among 100 people, 30 are in group G and 40 like jazz. 18 are in group G and like jazz. How many more people in group G like jazz than there would be if being in group G and liking jazz were independent?
questions.solution: If independent, the number in both would be $100 \times 0.3 \times 0.4 = 12$. There are 18, which is $18 - 12 = 6$ more.

questions.skill: Sequential events with and without replacement
questions.stem: A bag holds 6 red and 4 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. Without knowing the color of the first, what is the probability that the second marble is blue?
questions.solution: The second is blue after a red first: $\frac{6}{10} \times \frac{4}{9} = \frac{24}{90}$. It is blue after a blue first: $\frac{4}{10} \times \frac{3}{9} = \frac{12}{90}$. The total is $\frac{36}{90} = \frac{2}{5}$.

questions.skill: Sequential events with and without replacement
questions.stem: A bag holds 5 red and 4 green marbles. Three marbles are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that all three are red?

questions.skill: Sequential events with and without replacement
questions.stem: A box holds 3 red, 2 blue and 5 green marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are the same color?
questions.solution: Both red: $\frac{3}{10} \times \frac{2}{9} = \frac{6}{90}$. Both blue: $\frac{2}{10} \times \frac{1}{9} = \frac{2}{90}$. Both green: $\frac{5}{10} \times \frac{4}{9} = \frac{20}{90}$. Total: $\frac{28}{90} = \frac{14}{45}$.

questions.skill: Sequential events with and without replacement
questions.stem: Two cards are dealt one after the other from a standard 52-card deck without replacement. Which statement about "the first card is an ace" and "the second card is an ace" is correct?
choices: Not independent: the second is an ace with chance $\frac{3}{51}$ after an ace but $\frac{4}{51}$ after a non-ace
Independent: each deal has 4 aces among 52 cards, whatever happened first
Independent: the deck is shuffled, so the cards come in random order
Not independent: the second is an ace with chance $\frac{4}{51}$ after an ace but $\frac{3}{51}$ after a non-ace
questions.answer: Not independent: the second is an ace with chance $\frac{3}{51}$ after an ace but $\frac{4}{51}$ after a non-ace
questions.solution: If the first card is an ace, 3 aces remain among 51 cards, so the chance is $\frac{3}{51}$. If it is not, all 4 aces remain among 51 cards, so the chance is $\frac{4}{51}$. The chances differ, so the events are not independent.

solve.answer: Not independent: the second is an ace with chance $\frac{3}{51}$ after an ace but $\frac{4}{51}$ after a non-ace
solve.work: After an ace: 3 aces in 51 left, 3/51; after a non-ace: 4 aces in 51, 4/51. Not independent. First option (the last swaps the values).

questions.skill: Independence and conditional probability: concepts
questions.stem: For events $A$ and $B$ with $0 < P(B) < 1$, which condition shows that $A$ and $B$ are independent?
choices: $P(A | B) = P(A | \text{not } B)$
$P(A | B) + P(A | \text{not } B) = 1$
$P(A | B) = P(\text{not } A | \text{not } B)$
$P(A | B) = P(B | A)$
questions.answer: $P(A | B) = P(A | \text{not } B)$
questions.solution: If the chance of $A$ is the same whether or not $B$ happens, then $B$ gives no information about $A$, so the events are independent.

solve.answer: $P(A | B) = P(A | \text{not } B)$
solve.work: With 0<P(B)<1, P(A) is a weighted average of P(A|B) and P(A|not B); P(A|B) = P(A|not B) iff both equal P(A), i.e. independence. Option 3.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: How many students are in Ms. Lee's math class on this Monday morning?
How many minutes do students at our school spend on homework each night?
What is the name of the principal of our school during this current school year?
How tall is the flagpole that stands in front of the main entrance of our school?
questions.answer: How many minutes do students at our school spend on homework each night?
questions.solution: A statistical question is one where the answers are expected to vary and data are needed to answer it. Homework time differs from student to student. The other three questions each have one answer that can simply be looked up or measured.

solve.answer: How many minutes do students at our school spend on homework each night?
solve.work: Statistical question anticipates variability across students: homework minutes. C.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Here are four questions. (A) How many students are in the math club? (B) How many minutes does it take students at our school to get to school? (C) How tall is the tallest tree in our park? (D) What are the shoe sizes of the students in our class? How many of the four are statistical questions?
questions.solution: A statistical question expects answers that vary. (B) and (D) do: travel times and shoe sizes differ from student to student. (A) and (C) each have a single answer. So 2 of the 4 are statistical.

solve.work: (A) one count: not statistical. (B) commute minutes vary by student: statistical. (C) one value (the tallest tree): not statistical. (D) shoe sizes vary across students: statistical. Count = 2.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: To learn how all students at a school feel about a new lunch menu, the principal asks only the 10 students sitting in the front row of the lunchroom. Why is this sample likely to be biased?
choices: Asking only 10 students is too many, because large samples are always biased
Lunch menus cannot be studied with a survey because tastes differ
The principal should have asked the teachers, not the students
The students in the front row may not be typical of all the students
questions.answer: The students in the front row may not be typical of all the students
questions.solution: The principal picked students who were easy to reach (a convenience sample). Students in the front row may differ from the rest, such as arriving early, so their opinions may not represent the whole school.

solve.answer: The students in the front row may not be typical of all the students
solve.work: A convenience sample of the front row may not represent all students (selection bias). The other options are false or irrelevant.

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: Which survey question is worded in a way that pushes people toward one answer?
choices: Which playground do you like better, the new one or the old one?
About how many times a week do you use the playground at the park near your home?
Don't you agree the wonderful new playground is better than the old one?
What do you like most about the playground in our town's park?
questions.answer: Don't you agree the wonderful new playground is better than the old one?
questions.solution: Words such as "Don't you agree" and "wonderful" suggest the answer the writer wants. The other questions are worded neutrally and let people answer honestly.

solve.answer: Don't you agree the wonderful new playground is better than the old one?
solve.work: "Don't you agree the wonderful new playground..." is leading/loaded. B.

questions.skill: Identify the population, the sample and the variables
questions.stem: A survey records each student's grade level, number of pets and favorite color. How many variables are recorded for each student?
questions.solution: A variable is a characteristic that is recorded for every person. Grade level, number of pets and favorite color are three different characteristics, so there are 3 variables.

solve.work: Variables: grade level, number of pets, favorite color = 3.

questions.skill: Identify the population, the sample and the variables
questions.stem: A school has 600 students. A survey asks 50 of them how they get to school. How many students are in the population being studied?
questions.solution: The population is the whole group we want to learn about: all 600 students at the school. The 50 students who are asked are the sample.

solve.work: The population is all students at the school (600); the 50 surveyed are the sample.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: Which method gives a random sample of 30 students from a school?
choices: Put every student's name in a hat and draw 30 names without looking
Ask the first 30 students who walk into the school each morning
Ask 30 students from the school band, which practices together after school
Ask 30 students who volunteer to answer when it is announced over the speaker
questions.answer: Put every student's name in a hat and draw 30 names without looking
questions.solution: In a random sample every student has an equal chance of being chosen. Drawing names from a hat does that. The other methods choose students who are early, in one group, or willing to volunteer, and so may not represent the school.

solve.answer: Put every student's name in a hat and draw 30 names without looking
solve.work: Names in a hat, draw 30 without looking: simple random sample. C.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A survey about a new town park is mailed to 100 families, and only 12 families reply. Why might the results be biased?
choices: The families who replied may think differently from those who did not
Mailed surveys are always biased, no matter how many families reply to them
The families who replied must all have been in favor of the new town park
The survey would only be fair if every family in the state replied
questions.answer: The families who replied may think differently from those who did not
questions.solution: When most people do not respond (nonresponse), the few who do may be those with stronger opinions, so they may not represent all 100 families. Replies cannot be assumed to be all in favor, and a survey does not need the whole state to be fair.

solve.answer: The families who replied may think differently from those who did not
solve.work: 12% response: nonresponse bias; responders may differ from non-responders. A.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: A radio show asks listeners to call in and vote on whether the town should build a new park. Most callers say yes. Why might this result be biased?
choices: The radio show reaches too many people, so the callers cannot be counted accurately
A vote by phone is not allowed, so none of the calls should be counted
Mainly people with strong opinions call in, so the callers may not represent the town
Most callers said yes, so a result that most people agree on is always biased for that reason
questions.answer: Mainly people with strong opinions call in, so the callers may not represent the town
questions.solution: This is a voluntary response sample: people choose whether to take part, and those with strong feelings are most likely to do so. Their views may differ from the rest of the town.

solve.answer: Mainly people with strong opinions call in, so the callers may not represent the town
solve.work: Voluntary response: those with strong opinions call. C.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A student collects each classmate's hours of sleep and score on a quiz. Which question can be answered using both of these variables?
choices: How many hours did the student's best friend sleep last night?
What is the most common number of hours of sleep among the classmates?
What was the highest score on the quiz among all of the classmates?
Do classmates who sleep more tend to score higher on the quiz?
questions.answer: Do classmates who sleep more tend to score higher on the quiz?
questions.solution: A question about two variables asks how they are related. Only the first question connects hours of sleep with quiz score. The others use one variable, or one person.

solve.answer: Do classmates who sleep more tend to score higher on the quiz?
solve.work: Using both sleep and score: whether more sleep goes with higher scores. Highest score uses one variable; most common sleep uses one; best friend's sleep last night is not in the data and is a single value.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a statistical question?
choices: How many hours do teenagers in our state sleep on school nights?
What time does the library on Oak Street close today?
How do the ages of the players on our school teams vary?
How much money do students at our school spend on lunch in a week?
questions.answer: What time does the library on Oak Street close today?
questions.solution: A statistical question expects different answers from different individuals, so it needs data. The library closes at one time today, so the question has a single answer to look up. The other three ask about groups whose values vary.

solve.answer: What time does the library on Oak Street close today?
solve.work: The library's closing time today has one answer; the others anticipate variability across individuals.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Here are four questions. (A) How many seats are in the school auditorium? (B) What was the high temperature in Raleigh today? (C) How much time do students at our school spend on their phones each day? (D) What is the price of this notebook? How many of the four are statistical questions?
questions.solution: Only (C) expects the answers to vary from student to student, so it needs data from many students. (A), (B) and (D) each have a single answer that can be looked up.

solve.work: A: one count. B: one value (today, one city). C: varies across students, statistical. D: one price. So 1.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: What makes a question a statistical question?
choices: It has one correct answer that can be looked up in a book or on a reliable web page
It asks about one person or one object on one day
It can be answered by collecting data, and the answers are expected to vary
It asks for a count, such as how many seats are in a room
questions.answer: It can be answered by collecting data, and the answers are expected to vary
questions.solution: A statistical question is answered with data, and the answers are expected to vary from one individual to the next. A question with a single fixed answer, or about one person or object, is not statistical, even if the answer is a count.

solve.answer: It can be answered by collecting data, and the answers are expected to vary
solve.work: A statistical question anticipates variability and is answered with data.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A teacher records each student's shoe size and height. Which question uses both of these variables?
choices: What is the most common shoe size among the students?
Do taller students tend to have larger shoe sizes?
What is the median height of the students?
How many students are in the data set?
questions.answer: Do taller students tend to have larger shoe sizes?
questions.solution: Only the first question relates the two variables, height and shoe size. The others use at most one of them.

solve.answer: Do taller students tend to have larger shoe sizes?
solve.work: Relationship between height and shoe size uses both.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A coach wants to know whether players who practice more tend to score more. Which two variables should the coach record for each player?
choices: The jersey number of each player and the player's height in inches
The name of each player's team and the name of the school
Hours of practice per week and points scored per game
The height of each player in inches and the age of the player in years
questions.answer: Hours of practice per week and points scored per game
questions.solution: To compare practice with scoring, the coach needs a measure of practice and a measure of scoring for every player. The other pairs have nothing to do with the question.

solve.answer: Hours of practice per week and points scored per game
solve.work: Practice hours and points per game.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A survey records each person's age group and favorite music genre. Which question uses both variables?
choices: Which music genre is the most popular among all the people surveyed?
How many people took the survey, counting all of the age groups together?
Which age group has the largest number of people in the survey?
Does the most popular music genre differ from one age group to another?
questions.answer: Does the most popular music genre differ from one age group to another?
questions.solution: Only the first question compares one variable (genre) across the groups of the other (age group).

solve.answer: Does the most popular music genre differ from one age group to another?
solve.work: Comparing genre preference across age groups uses both.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A student starts with the question "How much time do students spend on homework?" Which question adds a second variable?
choices: Does the time students spend on homework differ between grade levels?
What is the mean time students spend on homework each night?
What is the longest amount of time any one student spent on homework last night?
How many students do homework on school nights?
questions.answer: Does the time students spend on homework differ between grade levels?
questions.solution: Comparing homework time across grade levels uses homework time and grade level, two variables. The other questions still use only homework.

solve.answer: Does the time students spend on homework differ between grade levels?
solve.work: Adds grade level as a second variable.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: To estimate how many hours a week people in a town spend reading, a researcher surveys people as they leave the public library. Why is this sample likely to be biased?
choices: People who are leaving a place usually answer questions without thinking
The sample is too small, because any sample of fewer than 100 people is biased
Asking a question in person always makes the answers untrue
People leaving a library probably read more than most people do
questions.answer: People leaving a library probably read more than most people do
questions.solution: People at a library are more likely to be readers, so their reading time probably exceeds the town's typical reading time. The sample does not represent everyone.

solve.answer: People leaving a library probably read more than most people do
solve.work: Library visitors likely read more than typical residents: undercoverage/selection bias.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a voluntary response sample?
choices: An online poll that anyone visiting a web page may choose to answer
Every tenth name on a list that includes all of the students in the school
Ten names drawn from a hat holding every name
Students chosen by a computer using random numbers
questions.answer: An online poll that anyone visiting a web page may choose to answer
questions.solution: In a voluntary response sample the people choose themselves, as with an open online poll. The other methods are chosen by the researcher or by chance.

solve.answer: An online poll that anyone visiting a web page may choose to answer
solve.work: Self-selected online poll is voluntary response.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: A town wants to know how residents feel about a new bike lane. Which sample is most likely to be biased?
choices: 50 residents chosen at random from the town's list of addresses
The first 50 people who walk into a bicycle shop on Saturday
Every 100th household on the town's list of water customers
50 residents chosen by a random number generator from a list of all residents
questions.answer: The first 50 people who walk into a bicycle shop on Saturday
questions.solution: People at a bicycle shop are probably more interested in bike lanes than the typical resident. The other samples are chosen by chance from lists of residents.

solve.answer: The first 50 people who walk into a bicycle shop on Saturday
solve.work: Bike shop customers likely favor bike lanes.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: A teacher surveys the students who happen to be in the cafeteria at 10 a.m. to learn what all students think of the lunch menu. What type of sample is this?
choices: A simple random sample
A stratified sample
A convenience sample
A systematic sample
questions.answer: A convenience sample
questions.solution: The teacher chose whoever was easiest to reach, which is a convenience sample. It can be biased because not every student has a chance to be chosen.

solve.answer: A convenience sample
solve.work: Whoever happens to be there: convenience sample.

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: Which survey question is worded fairly, without pushing people toward one answer?
choices: Don't you think a longer school day would be terrible for students?
Do you favor or oppose a longer school day?
Wouldn't you agree that sensible people oppose a longer school day?
Do you want to waste even more of your time in school with a longer day?
questions.answer: Do you favor or oppose a longer school day?
questions.solution: The first question names both choices and uses neutral words. The others use loaded words or suggest the answer they want.

solve.answer: Do you favor or oppose a longer school day?
solve.work: A is neutral; B, C, D are leading.

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: The question "Do you agree that the awful new schedule should be changed?" is biased. Which word is the main reason?
choices: schedule
new
awful
changed
questions.answer: awful
questions.solution: The word "awful" shows the writer's opinion and pushes people to agree. The other words are neutral.

solve.answer: awful

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: Which question assumes something that may not be true?
choices: How often do you eat lunch in our cafeteria?
Do you usually eat lunch in our cafeteria or somewhere else?
In a typical week, how many lunches do you buy in our cafeteria?
How often do you enjoy the delicious lunches in our cafeteria?
questions.answer: How often do you enjoy the delicious lunches in our cafeteria?
questions.solution: The first question assumes the lunches are delicious and that the student enjoys them. The other questions do not assume anything about opinions.

solve.answer: How often do you enjoy the delicious lunches in our cafeteria?

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: Which of these is an example of nonresponse bias?
choices: A survey question is worded so that it suggests the answer that the writer wants
A scale gives weights that are all too high by the same amount
Only 20% of the people sent a survey reply, and they all have strong opinions
A sample is chosen from the students in just one classroom
questions.answer: Only 20% of the people sent a survey reply, and they all have strong opinions
questions.solution: Nonresponse bias happens when many of the people chosen do not answer and those who do differ from those who do not.

solve.answer: Only 20% of the people sent a survey reply, and they all have strong opinions
solve.work: Low response with self-selected strong opinions is nonresponse bias.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A survey asks students face to face how often they wash their hands. Why might the results be biased?
choices: Students who do not wash their hands cannot be reached in person
Face-to-face surveys always have to be repeated several times
Only students with clean hands would be willing to answer
People may say what sounds good instead of what they really do
questions.answer: People may say what sounds good instead of what they really do
questions.solution: When a question is about something people want to look good at, many give the answer that sounds best instead of the true one. This is response bias.

solve.answer: People may say what sounds good instead of what they really do

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A school has 40 teachers numbered 1 to 40. A systematic sample starts with teacher number 7 and then takes every 5th teacher. What is the number of the third teacher chosen?
questions.solution: The chosen numbers are 7, 12, 17, and so on. The third is $7 + 5 \times 2 = 17$.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: Which describes a stratified random sample?
choices: Choosing every tenth member from a list of the whole population, after a random start
Choosing members of the population who volunteer to answer
Dividing the population into groups, then choosing a random sample from each group
Choosing all the members of a few randomly picked groups
questions.answer: Dividing the population into groups, then choosing a random sample from each group
questions.solution: A stratified sample splits the population into groups (strata) and samples randomly within each. Every tenth member is systematic, volunteers are a voluntary sample, and whole randomly chosen groups form a cluster sample.

solve.answer: Dividing the population into groups, then choosing a random sample from each group
solve.work: Divide into strata, random sample within each.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: Why is a random sample better than a sample of volunteers?
choices: A random sample always gives exactly the same results as the whole population
A random sample is always larger than a sample of volunteers
A random sample lets the researcher pick the people who will answer most helpfully
Every member of the population has a chance to be chosen, so no group is favored
questions.answer: Every member of the population has a chance to be chosen, so no group is favored
questions.solution: Chance gives each member an opportunity to be chosen, so the sample is not tilted toward people with strong feelings. It still varies a little from the population, and it is not necessarily larger.

solve.answer: Every member of the population has a chance to be chosen, so no group is favored
solve.work: Every member has a chance, no group favored.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A company keeps a list of 1,000 customers. To choose a systematic sample of 50 customers, it picks every kth customer from the list. What is k?
questions.solution: To choose 50 customers from 1,000, take one out of every $\frac{1000}{50} = 20$ customers, so $k = 20$.

questions.skill: Identify the population, the sample and the variables
questions.stem: A researcher asks 200 of the 3,000 members of a gym how many hours a week they exercise. Which is the sample?
choices: All 3,000 members of the gym
The number of hours exercised each week
The gym where the members exercise
The 200 members who were asked
questions.answer: The 200 members who were asked
questions.solution: The sample is the part of the population that is actually studied: the 200 members who were asked. All 3,000 members are the population.

solve.answer: The 200 members who were asked

questions.skill: Identify the population, the sample and the variables
questions.stem: A survey of backpacks records four variables. Which one is a categorical variable?
choices: The brand of the backpack
The weight of the backpack in pounds
The number of books inside the backpack
The length of the shoulder strap in inches
questions.answer: The brand of the backpack
questions.solution: A categorical variable sorts things into groups, such as brands. The others are measurements or counts, which are numerical.

solve.answer: The brand of the backpack

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A school wants honest answers about how often students skip their homework. Which way of collecting the answers is most likely to give honest responses?
choices: Students fill in forms with no names and drop them in a box
The teacher asks each student aloud, in front of the whole class
Each student signs a form and hands it to the principal in person
Each student answers while the teacher watches and writes down the reply
questions.answer: Students fill in forms with no names and drop them in a box
questions.solution: People shade their answers when they feel watched or fear getting in trouble, which is response bias. Forms with no names that are dropped in a box remove that pressure. In each of the other plans an adult hears or sees who said what.

solve.answer: Students fill in forms with no names and drop them in a box
solve.work: Honesty about skipping homework is threatened by response bias when answers are identifiable. Anonymous forms dropped in a box remove that pressure; the other three all expose the student's identity to an adult or the class.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: A student wants to turn the question "How long is Leo's commute today?" into a statistical question. Which rewording works?
choices: How long was Leo's commute to school yesterday morning?
How long are the daily commutes of students at our school?
How long will Leo's commute be on the first day of next week?
What time does Leo leave home to start his commute today?
questions.answer: How long are the daily commutes of students at our school?
questions.solution: A statistical question asks about a group and expects the answers to vary. Asking about the commutes of all students at the school does that. The other three still ask about one person's commute or departure time on one day, which has a single answer.

solve.answer: How long are the daily commutes of students at our school?
solve.work: A statistical version must anticipate variability across many data values: commute lengths of students at our school. The others are single values about Leo.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A data set has, for each student, the grade level, the hours of screen time per day and the hours of sleep per night. Which question uses at least two of these variables?
choices: What is the typical amount of screen time per day for students?
Do students who have more screen time tend to get less sleep?
Which grade level has the most students in the data set?
Which numbers of hours of sleep per night are the most common?
questions.answer: Do students who have more screen time tend to get less sleep?
questions.solution: Only the first question asks how two variables, screen time and sleep, are related. The others each look at one variable by itself.

solve.answer: Do students who have more screen time tend to get less sleep?
solve.work: Screen time vs sleep uses two variables. Typical screen time uses one; most common sleep hours uses one; grade with most students uses one.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: A town surveys households about internet use by randomly choosing numbers from a landline phone directory. Which statement best explains how this sampling method can be biased?
choices: Households with landlines are chosen too often because they are called twice
Households are chosen at random from the directory, so no group can be left out
The directory is too long, so the sample will be too large to be fair
Households without a listed landline have no chance to be chosen
questions.answer: Households without a listed landline have no chance to be chosen
questions.solution: Random choice only helps among the households that can be chosen. People with only cell phones or unlisted numbers are not in the directory, so they are left out (undercoverage), and they may use the internet differently.

solve.answer: Households without a listed landline have no chance to be chosen
solve.work: Sampling frame is the landline directory, so households without a listed landline (often those relying on mobile/internet) are excluded: undercoverage.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A school has 300 freshmen and 500 seniors. To get a stratified sample, the student council takes a random 10% of the freshmen and a random 10% of the seniors. How many seniors are in the sample?
questions.solution: Ten percent of the 500 seniors is $0.10 \times 500 = 50$. So 50 seniors are in the sample (and 30 freshmen).

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: A poll asks, "Given the terrible traffic on Main Street, shouldn't the town build a bypass?" Which rewording removes the bias?
choices: Don't you think a bypass would finally solve the traffic problem?
Since many drivers are upset, how much do you want a bypass?
Do you support or oppose building a bypass around the town?
Would you rather have a bypass or keep the traffic on Main Street?
questions.answer: Do you support or oppose building a bypass around the town?
questions.solution: A fair question gives both sides equal weight and uses neutral words. "Support or oppose" does that. Each other version still suggests that the bypass is the right answer.

solve.answer: Do you support or oppose building a bypass around the town?
solve.work: Neutral wording: "Do you support or oppose building a bypass around the town?" The others keep loaded phrases (finally solve, many drivers are upset, keep the traffic).

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A teacher watches over students' shoulders as they fill in a survey that asks, "Did you cheat on a test this year?" Which kind of bias is most likely?
choices: Students may lie to avoid trouble, so the reported cheating rate looks too low
Only students who cheated will answer, so the cheating rate looks too high
Students will not understand the question being asked, so all of the answers will be random
The teacher chose the survey topic herself, so the sample of students is not random
questions.answer: Students may lie to avoid trouble, so the reported cheating rate looks too low
questions.solution: This is response bias: people give an untruthful answer because of how they are asked. With the teacher watching, students who cheated are likely to say they did not, so the rate is reported too low.

solve.answer: Students may lie to avoid trouble, so the reported cheating rate looks too low
solve.work: Lack of anonymity: response bias, students under-report cheating. D.

questions.skill: Identify the population, the sample and the variables
questions.stem: A data set has these variables for each of 80 students: favorite subject, whether the student plays a sport (yes or no), minutes of homework last night, and height in inches. How many of the variables are categorical?
questions.solution: A categorical variable puts people into groups. Favorite subject and playing a sport (yes or no) are categorical. Minutes of homework and height are measured numbers, so they are numerical. That makes 2 categorical variables.

solve.work: Favorite subject: categorical. Plays a sport (yes/no): categorical. Homework minutes: quantitative. Height: quantitative. 2 categorical.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A student wants to investigate whether students who ride the bus to school have longer trips than students who walk. Which is the best statistical question for this investigation?
choices: How do the travel times to school compare for bus riders and for students who walk?
How long did it take the student to ride the bus to school yesterday morning, in minutes?
Do students enjoy riding the bus to school more than they enjoy walking there?
How many students at the school ride the bus to school every single morning of the week?
questions.answer: How do the travel times to school compare for bus riders and for students who walk?
questions.solution: The best question names the group, the variable (travel time) and the comparison (bus riders and walkers), and it expects answers to vary. The other questions ask about one trip, about enjoyment, or about a count.

solve.answer: How do the travel times to school compare for bus riders and for students who walk?
solve.work: Compare travel-time distributions of bus riders vs walkers. A.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A survey is sent to 250 randomly chosen people, and 90 of them reply. What percent of the people chosen did not reply?
questions.solution: The number who did not reply is $250 - 90 = 160$. As a percent: $\frac{160}{250} \times 100 = 64$. With so many people not answering, nonresponse bias is a worry.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A school has four grade levels, and the student council wants a sample that fairly represents every grade level. Which plan is best?
choices: Choose students at random from the largest grade level, since it has the most students
Choose the students who volunteer to answer the survey from each grade level
Choose students at random in each grade, in proportion to the size of that grade
Choose students from each grade level who are in the school's honors classes
questions.answer: Choose students at random in each grade, in proportion to the size of that grade
questions.solution: Choosing at random within each grade (a stratified sample), with more students from larger grades, represents every grade fairly. The other plans leave out grades, rely on volunteers, or take only one kind of student.

solve.answer: Choose students at random in each grade, in proportion to the size of that grade
solve.work: Proportional stratified random sampling by grade represents every grade fairly. Only largest grade, volunteers, or honors students are biased.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Maya says "How old is my brother?" is not a statistical question, but "How old are the brothers and sisters of students at our school?" is. Why is she right?
choices: The second question uses larger numbers than the first
The second question is about a whole family instead of about a single person
The second question can be answered without collecting any data from the students at the school
The second question expects the answers to vary from one person to another
questions.answer: The second question expects the answers to vary from one person to another
questions.solution: The first question has one answer for one person. The second asks about many people whose ages differ, so the answers vary and data from many people are needed.

solve.answer: The second question expects the answers to vary from one person to another
solve.work: The second anticipates variability across many people; the first has one answer.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which question is statistical?
choices: How much does the number of absent students vary from day to day at our school?
How many students were absent from Ms. Lee's class on the first Monday of October?
How many days are there in the school year at our school this year?
On what day of the week does the school year begin at our school?
questions.answer: How much does the number of absent students vary from day to day at our school?
questions.solution: The number of absent students changes from day to day, so the question expects varying answers and needs data collected over many days. The other three have one answer each.

solve.answer: How much does the number of absent students vary from day to day at our school?
solve.work: A, B, D each have one answer; C asks about day-to-day variability.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Here are five questions. (1) How long is the school's soccer field? (2) How long do students at our school take to eat lunch? (3) What is Carla's favorite color? (4) How much do the backpacks of ninth graders at our school weigh? (5) How do the numbers of pets owned vary among families in our neighborhood? How many of the five are statistical questions?
questions.solution: Questions (2), (4) and (5) expect the answers to vary across many individuals. Question (1) is about one field and question (3) is about one person, so each has a single answer.

solve.work: (1) one length, (3) one person: not statistical. (2), (4), (5) vary across individuals: 3.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: The question "What is the price of one gallon of milk at the store on Elm Street today?" is not statistical. Which question is statistical?
choices: What is the price of two gallons of milk at the store on Elm Street today?
How do the prices of a gallon of milk vary among the stores in our county?
What will the price of one gallon of milk at the store on Elm Street be tomorrow?
Why is the milk at the store on Elm Street so expensive today?
questions.answer: How do the prices of a gallon of milk vary among the stores in our county?
questions.solution: Asking about the prices at many stores expects varying answers, so it needs data. The other questions still ask about a single store on a single day, or ask for a reason rather than for data.

solve.answer: How do the prices of a gallon of milk vary among the stores in our county?
solve.work: Only D asks about variation across many stores.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: A student is planning a project about pets. Which question should the student use, since it is a statistical question?
choices: How many pets does my cousin have?
How many legs does a dog have?
How many pets do the families on our street usually have?
How many pets were adopted from the shelter on Elm Street yesterday?
questions.answer: How many pets do the families on our street usually have?
questions.solution: The number of pets differs from family to family, so the question expects varying answers and needs data. The other questions are about one person, one fixed fact, or one place on one day.

solve.answer: How many pets do the families on our street usually have?
solve.work: B asks about many families whose answers vary; A, C, D have single answers.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A data set records, for 150 families, the household income, the number of cars and the miles driven per week. Which question compares the miles driven for groups of families made by another variable?
choices: What is the median household income of the 150 families in the data set, in dollars?
How does the typical weekly mileage differ among families with 0, 1, 2 or more cars?
How many of the 150 families own exactly two cars?
What is the range of the miles driven per week by the 150 families?
questions.answer: How does the typical weekly mileage differ among families with 0, 1, 2 or more cars?
questions.solution: Grouping families by the number of cars and comparing the miles driven uses two variables. The other questions each use only one.

solve.answer: How does the typical weekly mileage differ among families with 0, 1, 2 or more cars?
solve.work: Compares mileage across groups defined by number of cars.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A data set records each student's grade level, whether the student owns a bike, and the minutes of travel to school. Which question uses only one of these variables?
choices: Is bike ownership more common in some grade levels than in others?
Do students who own a bike have shorter travel times than the others?
What percent of the students own a bike?
How does the typical travel time change from one grade level to the next?
questions.answer: What percent of the students own a bike?
questions.solution: The percent who own a bike uses just bike ownership. Each of the other questions relates two of the variables.

solve.answer: What percent of the students own a bike?
solve.work: D uses bike ownership only; A, B, C use two variables.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A cafeteria manager records each student's grade level and whether the student buys lunch or brings lunch from home. Which question uses both variables?
choices: What percent of all the students buy lunch?
How many students are in the ninth grade?
How many students bring lunch from home on a typical day at the school?
Is buying lunch more common in some grades than in others?
questions.answer: Is buying lunch more common in some grades than in others?
questions.solution: Comparing how common buying lunch is across grades relates the two variables. The other questions use at most one.

solve.answer: Is buying lunch more common in some grades than in others?
solve.work: D relates grade and lunch choice.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: To learn how much households in a town spend on groceries each week, a researcher surveys only the shoppers at one grocery store on Tuesday mornings. Why might the results be biased?
choices: Shoppers on Tuesday mornings are always too busy to answer a survey honestly
A grocery store is not allowed to give out how much money its customers spend there
Only households that spend a very large amount of money ever shop on Tuesdays
Households whose members shop at other times or in other places are left out
questions.answer: Households whose members shop at other times or in other places are left out
questions.solution: The sample leaves out everyone who does not shop at that store at that time, such as people who work then or shop elsewhere. Their spending may differ, so the sample may not represent the town.

solve.answer: Households whose members shop at other times or in other places are left out
solve.work: Households shopping elsewhere or at other times are excluded.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: Mr. Ortiz wants to know how all students feel about the school dress code. He surveys only students who are in the detention room. Which statement is most reasonable?
choices: The opinions are likely more negative than those of all students
The opinions are likely more positive than those of all students
The opinions represent all students, because every student has the same dress code
The opinions are unbiased, because the students in the room answer one at a time
questions.answer: The opinions are likely more negative than those of all students
questions.solution: Students in detention are not typical, and some of them may be there because of the dress code, so they probably feel more negative about it than students in general.

solve.answer: The opinions are likely more negative than those of all students
solve.work: Students in detention are likely more negative about school rules; most reasonable is C.

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: A survey asks "How would you rate the new library?" with the choices excellent, very good, good and fair. What is the main problem?
choices: Three of the four choices are positive, which pushes answers toward praise
There are too many choices for people to read before they decide on an answer
The word "rate" makes people give a low rating
The choices do not include a number for each rating
questions.answer: Three of the four choices are positive, which pushes answers toward praise
questions.solution: A fair set of choices has balanced positive and negative options. Here nearly all of them are positive, which nudges people toward a good rating.

solve.answer: Three of the four choices are positive, which pushes answers toward praise
solve.work: Choices are skewed positive with no negative option.

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: A survey says "Most doctors say sugary drinks harm teens. Do you drink sugary drinks?" What is the main problem?
choices: The question asks about two different drinks at once
The first sentence pressures people to give the answer that sounds responsible
The question is too short to give researchers a useful answer about the teenagers
The question does not name a particular doctor
questions.answer: The first sentence pressures people to give the answer that sounds responsible
questions.solution: Telling people what experts say makes some answer the way that sounds approved instead of truthfully.

solve.answer: The first sentence pressures people to give the answer that sounds responsible
solve.work: Preamble pressures a socially desirable answer.

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: Two polls of 1,000 randomly chosen residents of the same town are taken. Poll A asks "Do you support a one-cent sales tax to repair roads?" and 70% say yes. Poll B asks "Do you support raising taxes?" and 35% say yes. What is the most likely explanation of the difference?
choices: Random samples of 1,000 people always give results that differ by about 35 points
Poll B must have surveyed people who were not residents of the town
The different wording of the two questions influenced the answers
Poll A had a larger sample, and a larger sample gives higher percentages
questions.answer: The different wording of the two questions influenced the answers
questions.solution: Both samples are random and large, so chance cannot explain a 35-point gap. The first question names a popular purpose and the second does not, so the wording shifted the answers.

solve.answer: The different wording of the two questions influenced the answers
solve.work: Same sample sizes, random; wording differs.

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: Which rewording of "Do you agree that cell phones are a distraction that should be banned from class?" is the least biased?
choices: Do you agree that cell phones are a useful tool that should always be allowed in class?
Given how rude and distracting phones are, should students be allowed to use them in class?
Do you agree that banning cell phones from class is unfair to students?
Do you think students should or should not be allowed to use cell phones in class?
questions.answer: Do you think students should or should not be allowed to use cell phones in class?
questions.solution: The first version offers both answers in neutral words. The others each lean toward one answer, in one direction or the other.

solve.answer: Do you think students should or should not be allowed to use cell phones in class?
solve.work: B is balanced ('should or should not').

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A school mails a survey about a new bell schedule to 300 randomly chosen families. A total of 120 families reply, and 84 of the replies favor the new schedule. What percent of the replies favor the new schedule?
questions.solution: Of the 120 replies, 84 favor the schedule: $\frac{84}{120} = 0.70$, which is 70%.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A survey of randomly chosen people has a low response rate. Which action would do the most to reduce nonresponse bias?
choices: Send the survey to twice as many people and use only the first replies
Follow up with reminders to the people who have not answered
Replace the people who did not answer with volunteers
Analyze only the responses that were received
questions.answer: Follow up with reminders to the people who have not answered
questions.solution: Reminders get answers from more of the people who were chosen, which reduces the gap between those who answered and those who did not. The other actions leave the problem or make it worse.

solve.answer: Follow up with reminders to the people who have not answered
solve.work: Following up with nonrespondents raises the response rate and reduces nonresponse bias.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A teacher asks the class to raise their hands if they finished last night's homework. About 95% raise their hands, but only about 60% had finished it. Which kind of bias is most likely?
choices: Nonresponse bias: many students did not answer at all
Sampling bias: a convenience sample was used
Response bias: students did not answer truthfully
Wording bias: the question suggests the answer
questions.answer: Response bias: students did not answer truthfully
questions.solution: Students answered in front of the teacher and classmates, and many said what looked good instead of what was true. That is response bias.

solve.answer: Response bias: students did not answer truthfully
solve.work: Everyone answered but some untruthfully: response bias.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A school has 240 sophomores and 360 juniors. The student council chooses a stratified random sample of 50 students, with each grade represented in proportion to its size. How many sophomores are in the sample?
questions.solution: Sophomores are $\frac{240}{600} = 40\%$ of the 600 students, so the sample has $0.40 \times 50 = 20$ sophomores.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A district has 40 schools. A researcher picks 4 of the schools at random and surveys every student in those 4 schools. What type of sample is this?
choices: A cluster sample
A stratified sample
A systematic sample
A convenience sample
questions.answer: A cluster sample
questions.solution: The population is split into natural groups (schools), some groups are chosen at random, and everyone in the chosen groups is surveyed. That is a cluster sample.

solve.answer: A cluster sample
solve.work: Randomly chosen whole groups: cluster sample.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A town has 60% rural residents and 40% urban residents, and the two groups may feel differently about a new tax. A researcher wants a sample of 300 residents that fairly represents both. Which plan is best?
choices: Survey the 300 residents who live closest to the town hall
Randomly choose 180 rural residents and 120 urban residents
Survey 300 volunteers who answer an advertisement on a web page
Randomly choose 300 residents from the urban area only
questions.answer: Randomly choose 180 rural residents and 120 urban residents
questions.solution: Choosing at random within each group, in proportion to its size ($60\%$ of 300 is 180 and $40\%$ is 120), represents both groups fairly. The other plans favor one place or one kind of person.

solve.answer: Randomly choose 180 rural residents and 120 urban residents

questions.skill: Identify the population, the sample and the variables
questions.stem: A survey records each student's age, height in inches, favorite sport and number of siblings. How many of these variables are numerical?
questions.solution: Age, height and number of siblings are numbers you can compute with. Favorite sport is a category, so 3 variables are numerical.

solve.work: Age, height, number of siblings are numerical; favorite sport is categorical: 3.

questions.skill: Identify the population, the sample and the variables
questions.stem: A study of 50 cars from a parking lot of 400 cars records each car's fuel efficiency in miles per gallon and its color. Which statement is correct?
choices: Fuel efficiency is a categorical variable and color is a numerical variable
Fuel efficiency is a numerical variable and color is a categorical variable
Both variables are numerical, because each car has a value for each
Both variables are categorical, because they both describe the cars
questions.answer: Fuel efficiency is a numerical variable and color is a categorical variable
questions.solution: Miles per gallon is a measured number, so it is numerical. Color sorts the cars into groups, so it is categorical.

solve.answer: Fuel efficiency is a numerical variable and color is a categorical variable

questions.skill: Tell statistical from non-statistical questions
questions.stem: Six questions are listed. (1) How many students are enrolled at our school today? (2) How long do students at our school take to eat lunch? (3) What is the tallest building in our city? (4) How do the ages of the players on our school's teams vary? (5) What was the score of last night's game? (6) Which pets do students in our grade own? How many of the six are statistical questions?
questions.solution: A statistical question expects different answers from one person or item to the next, so data must be collected. Questions 2, 4 and 6 do. Questions 1, 3 and 5 each have a single answer that can simply be looked up. So 3 of the 6 are statistical.

solve.work: Statistical questions anticipate variability. (1) one count today: not statistical. (2) lunch times vary across students: statistical. (3) one building: not. (4) ages vary: statistical. (5) one score: not. (6) pets vary across students: statistical. Count = 3.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: A weather club wants a question to investigate with data. Which of these is a statistical question about temperature?
choices: What was the high temperature in our town on March 3 of last year?
What is the highest temperature ever recorded in our town since records were first kept?
What was the high temperature in our town on the day Priya was born?
How did the daily high temperatures in our town vary during last March?
questions.answer: How did the daily high temperatures in our town vary during last March?
questions.solution: A statistical question asks about many values that vary, here the daily highs over a whole month. The other three each ask for one number on one day, or one record, which has a single answer.

solve.answer: How did the daily high temperatures in our town vary during last March?
solve.work: Variability of daily highs over March is statistical. B. Others have single answers.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A data set has, for each of 200 houses in a town, the price, the square footage, the number of bedrooms and the neighborhood. Which question can be answered with this data?
choices: Do houses with a red front door sell for more than other houses?
Do house prices tend to differ from one neighborhood to another?
What will the typical house price in the town be in ten years?
How many people live in a typical house in each neighborhood?
questions.answer: Do house prices tend to differ from one neighborhood to another?
questions.solution: The data record price and neighborhood, so we can compare prices across neighborhoods. Door color, future prices and the number of people living in each house are not in the data set, so the other questions cannot be answered with it.

solve.answer: Do house prices tend to differ from one neighborhood to another?
solve.work: Price and neighborhood are both in the data, so comparing prices across neighborhoods is answerable. Door color and residents per house are not recorded; future prices cannot be answered from the data.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: A radio call-in poll about a new stadium found that 85% of the callers were in favor. A random sample of residents found that 55% were in favor. By how many percentage points does the call-in poll overstate support, compared with the random sample?
questions.solution: The difference is $85 - 55 = 30$ percentage points. A call-in poll is a voluntary response sample, so people with strong feelings are overrepresented, and it can give a misleading picture. The random sample is the better guide.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: To estimate how many hours a week people in a city exercise, a researcher surveys people as they leave a gym. Which statement is correct?
choices: The estimate is likely too low, since people leaving a gym are tired and exercise less
The estimate is likely too high, since gym members probably exercise more than others
The estimate is unbiased, since everyone in the sample was asked the same question
The estimate is unbiased as long as the researcher surveys at least 1,000 people
questions.answer: The estimate is likely too high, since gym members probably exercise more than others
questions.solution: People at a gym are not typical of the whole city: they exercise more than most, so the estimate is biased high. Asking everyone the same question, or surveying more people with the same method, does not fix a biased way of choosing the sample.

solve.answer: The estimate is likely too high, since gym members probably exercise more than others
solve.work: Surveying people leaving a gym over-represents people who exercise, so the estimate is likely too high. Larger samples do not fix selection bias; same question does not remove it.

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: A survey asks, "Do you want school to start later and lunch to be longer?" What is the main problem with this question?
choices: It uses strong, emotional words that push students toward answering yes to the question
It asks for opinions, and opinions cannot be collected in a survey
It is a question about one student only, so it cannot be a statistical question
It asks about two different things at once, so one answer cannot fit both
questions.answer: It asks about two different things at once, so one answer cannot fit both
questions.solution: A student who wants a later start but not a longer lunch cannot answer honestly with a single yes or no. Each topic should be asked about in its own question. The wording is not loaded, and opinions can be surveyed.

solve.answer: It asks about two different things at once, so one answer cannot fit both
solve.work: Double-barreled question: two things at once. C.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A team weighs backpacks on a scale that always reads 3 pounds too high. The team records the weights of 40 backpacks. Which statement about the data is true?
choices: The average is not biased, because some weights are too high and some are too low
The bias will go away if many more backpacks are weighed on the same scale, because errors average out
Every recorded weight is too high, so the average is biased even with many backpacks
The individual weights are biased, but the average of all of the weights is not biased
questions.answer: Every recorded weight is too high, so the average is biased even with many backpacks
questions.solution: This is measurement bias: the scale makes every weight 3 pounds too large, so the average is 3 pounds too large as well. Weighing more backpacks on the same scale repeats the same error and does not remove it.

solve.answer: Every recorded weight is too high, so the average is biased even with many backpacks
solve.work: Systematic +3 lb error: every reading high, mean biased by 3 regardless of sample size. A.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A list has the names of 600 students, numbered 1 to 600. A systematic sample takes every 12th student, starting with student number 5. What is the number of the fourth student chosen?
questions.solution: The students chosen are 5, 17, 29, 41, and so on, adding 12 each time. The fourth student chosen is number $5 + 3 \times 12 = 41$.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A school has 1,200 students: 480 in grade 9, 420 in grade 10 and 300 in grade 11. A stratified sample of 120 students is chosen with each grade represented in proportion to its size. How many grade 10 students are in the sample?
questions.solution: Grade 10 is $\frac{420}{1200} = 0.35$ of the school, so it should be 35% of the sample: $0.35 \times 120 = 42$ students. (The sample then has 48 from grade 9, 42 from grade 10 and 30 from grade 11.)

questions.skill: Identify the population, the sample and the variables
questions.stem: A researcher selects 120 of the 4,800 students in a district and records, for each, the length of the bus ride and the school attended. Which statement correctly names the population and the sample?
choices: Population: all 4,800 students in the district; sample: the 120 students selected
Population: the 120 students selected; sample: all 4,800 students in the district
Population: the bus ride lengths; sample: the schools attended by the students
Population: all students in the state; sample: the 4,800 students in the district
questions.answer: Population: all 4,800 students in the district; sample: the 120 students selected
questions.solution: The population is the whole group we want to learn about, the 4,800 students in the district. The sample is the part of it that is actually studied, the 120 students. The bus ride length and the school are variables, not groups of people.

solve.answer: Population: all 4,800 students in the district; sample: the 120 students selected
solve.work: Population: all 4,800 district students; sample: the 120 selected. The variables (bus ride length, school) are neither.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A survey of 500 randomly chosen students received 300 replies, and 240 of those replies were yes (80%). Suppose none of the 200 students who did not reply would have said yes. What percent of all 500 students chosen would then say yes?
questions.solution: In that case only the 240 who replied yes would say yes. Out of all 500 students chosen, that is $\frac{240}{500} \times 100 = 48$ percent, far below the 80% among the replies. This shows how much nonresponse can change a result.

solve.work: Yes answers: 240 of 300 repliers; non-repliers add 0 yes. 240/500 = 0.48 = 48%.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which statement about statistical questions is true?
choices: Their answers are expected to vary, so data from many individuals are needed
They must always ask for the mean or the median of a set of numbers from a survey
They must always involve exactly two variables measured on every individual
They can be answered only by giving a survey to the whole population
questions.answer: Their answers are expected to vary, so data from many individuals are needed
questions.solution: The defining feature is variability: the answers are expected to differ, so data from many individuals are collected. A statistical question may use any summary, one variable or several, and the data may come from many sources.

solve.answer: Their answers are expected to vary, so data from many individuals are needed
solve.work: Statistical questions anticipate variability, so data from many individuals are needed.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Here are six questions. (A) How do the numbers of hours students at our school spend volunteering vary by grade level? (B) What is the median number of siblings among students in our class? (C) How many siblings does Jordan have? (D) How much does the typical ninth grader at our school weigh? (E) What is the capital of North Carolina? (F) In which month do the most students at our school have birthdays? How many of the six are statistical questions?
questions.solution: Questions (A), (B), (D) and (F) each need data from many students whose values vary. Question (C) is about one person and question (E) has one fixed answer, so neither is statistical.

solve.work: A, B (median of class data), D (typical weight), F (birth months vary, need data) are statistical; C and E are not. 4.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: Isabel wants to find out whether travel times to school differ by how students travel and by grade level. Which variables should she record for each student?
choices: Minutes of travel time, method of travel and grade level
Method of travel and grade level only, to count how many students use each method
Minutes of travel time and grade level only, to compare the times of the grades
Minutes of travel time and the name of the school only, since every student has one
questions.answer: Minutes of travel time, method of travel and grade level
questions.solution: To compare travel time by both method and grade level she needs all three variables for each student. Each of the other lists leaves one out.

solve.answer: Minutes of travel time, method of travel and grade level
solve.work: Needs travel time, method and grade.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A data set records, for each of 200 houses in a town, the price, the square footage and the neighborhood. Which question uses all three variables?
choices: Do houses with more square footage tend to have higher prices in this town?
Does the link between a house's size and its price differ by neighborhood?
Which neighborhood has the highest typical price for the houses in it?
What is the typical price of a house in the town, with all houses counted together?
questions.answer: Does the link between a house's size and its price differ by neighborhood?
questions.solution: Comparing the size-price relationship across neighborhoods uses price, size and neighborhood. The others use two variables or one.

solve.answer: Does the link between a house's size and its price differ by neighborhood?
solve.work: B: size-price relationship by neighborhood uses all three. A uses two, C uses two, D one.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A data set contains, for each of 300 students, the grade level, the hours of exercise per week and the resting heart rate. Which question can NOT be answered with these data?
choices: Do students who exercise more tend to have lower resting heart rates?
Does the typical resting heart rate differ from one grade level to the next?
Do students who eat breakfast every day have lower resting heart rates?
Do older grade levels tend to exercise more hours per week than younger ones?
questions.answer: Do students who eat breakfast every day have lower resting heart rates?
