questions.solution: The data say nothing about breakfast, so that question needs a variable that was not recorded. The other three use variables in the data set.

solve.answer: Do students who eat breakfast every day have lower resting heart rates?
solve.work: Breakfast is not recorded, so A cannot be answered.

questions.skill: Pose a statistical question about two or more variables
questions.stem: A data set has 6 variables recorded for each person. A student wants to investigate how one variable relates to another, looking at one pair of variables at a time. How many different pairs of variables are there?
questions.solution: Choose 2 of the 6 variables, where the order does not matter: $\frac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$ pairs.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: An online vote on a new school mascot receives 1,200 votes, and 900 of them are for the dragon. A random sample of 500 students finds that 240 of them prefer the dragon. By how many percentage points does the online vote overstate the preference for the dragon, compared with the random sample?
questions.solution: The online vote gives $\frac{900}{1200} = 75\%$. The random sample gives $\frac{240}{500} = 48\%$. The difference is $75 - 48 = 27$ percentage points.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: Two random samples of 40 students are taken from the same school. The mean amount of sleep is 6.8 hours in one sample and 7.3 hours in the other. Which is the best explanation of the difference?
choices: The sample with the lower mean must have been chosen in a biased way, because the means are different
Random samples vary by chance, so two of them can differ even when neither is biased
Both samples must be biased, because two fair samples would give identical means
A random sample of 40 students can never be fairly compared with another
questions.answer: Random samples vary by chance, so two of them can differ even when neither is biased
questions.solution: Different random samples give somewhat different results just by chance. That variation is not bias, which is a built-in tendency to miss the true value in one direction.

solve.answer: Random samples vary by chance, so two of them can differ even when neither is biased

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: A radio station's online poll gets 20,000 responses from listeners who chose to vote. A polling company surveys 400 randomly chosen adults in the same town. Which is the better basis for estimating what the town's adults think?
choices: The online poll, because a larger sample is always more accurate than a smaller one
The online poll, because listeners who vote are the people most affected
The random sample of 400, because a large voluntary sample can still be biased
Neither, because a sample of 400 people is too small for a town
questions.answer: The random sample of 400, because a large voluntary sample can still be biased
questions.solution: A big sample does not fix bias. The people who volunteer are not typical of the town, while a random sample gives every adult a chance to be chosen.

solve.answer: The random sample of 400, because a large voluntary sample can still be biased
solve.work: Voluntary response is biased regardless of size; random 400 is better.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: Which sample would most likely give an estimate of the mean height of all students at a school that is too high?
choices: Every tenth student on the school's alphabetical roster
30 students chosen with a random number generator
One student chosen at random from each homeroom
The members of the school's basketball team
questions.answer: The members of the school's basketball team
questions.solution: Basketball players tend to be taller than other students, so a sample made of them overestimates the mean. The other methods are random and have no such tendency.

solve.answer: The members of the school's basketball team
solve.work: Basketball players are taller than average.

questions.skill: Spot bias in how a sample is chosen
questions.stem: A study of how long small businesses last looks only at businesses that are open today. Why is the study likely to be biased?
choices: Businesses that closed are left out, so lifetimes will look longer than they really are
Businesses that are still open are always the smallest ones in the town
Owners of businesses that are open today will probably report their lifetimes dishonestly
The study includes too many businesses to be summarized in one number
questions.answer: Businesses that closed are left out, so lifetimes will look longer than they really are
questions.solution: Businesses that failed early are missing from the sample, so the ones that remain have lasted longer than the typical business.

solve.answer: Businesses that closed are left out, so lifetimes will look longer than they really are
solve.work: Survivorship bias: closed businesses left out, lifetimes look longer.

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: Which survey question has NO wording problem?
choices: In the past week, how many times did you eat lunch in the school cafeteria?
Like most students, do you eat lunch in the school cafeteria?
How many times this week did you eat in the cafeteria and the library?
Isn't it true that most students you know eat lunch in the school cafeteria?
questions.answer: In the past week, how many times did you eat lunch in the school cafeteria?
questions.solution: The first question is specific, neutral and asks about one thing. The others suggest what most students do, or ask about two things at once.

solve.answer: In the past week, how many times did you eat lunch in the school cafeteria?
solve.work: A is clear; B double-barreled, C and D leading.

questions.skill: Spot bias in the wording of a question
questions.stem: One poll asks "Do you favor the new law, which will protect children from harm?" Another asks "Do you favor the new law, which will limit personal freedom?" Which statement is correct?
choices: Only the first question is biased, because it mentions children and harm
Both questions are biased, in opposite directions, so neither is fair
Only the second question is biased, because it mentions freedom
Neither question is biased, because both ask about the same law
questions.answer: Both questions are biased, in opposite directions, so neither is fair
questions.solution: Each question describes the law in loaded words that favor one side, one in favor and the other against. Asking about the same law does not make either one neutral.

solve.answer: Both questions are biased, in opposite directions, so neither is fair
solve.work: Each wording leans a different way; both biased.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A fitness app counts steps but misses the first 100 steps of every walk. The app records the steps of 5,000 walks. Which statement is correct?
choices: Totals are correct on average, because 5,000 walks is a very large sample
Totals are too low, but the problem goes away with more walks
Totals are too high, because the app starts counting too soon
Every total is too low, a measurement bias that more walks will not fix
questions.answer: Every total is too low, a measurement bias that more walks will not fix
questions.solution: The app undercounts by 100 steps each time, so every recording is low. Collecting more data does not remove a consistent error in the measuring tool.

solve.answer: Every total is too low, a measurement bias that more walks will not fix
solve.work: Systematic undercount by 100 per walk; a larger sample does not remove it.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A survey is sent to 400 randomly chosen residents and 140 reply. Of the 140 replies, 112 say yes. Suppose half of the 260 residents who did not reply would also have said yes. What percent of all 400 chosen residents would then say yes?
questions.solution: The 260 who did not reply would add $260 \div 2 = 130$ yes answers. In all there would be $112 + 130 = 242$ yes answers out of 400, and $\frac{242}{400} = 0.605$, which is 60.5%.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: A survey about household income is sent to a random sample of residents, but mostly high-income households send it back. What is the likely effect on the median income estimated from the returned surveys?
choices: It will likely be too high, because of nonresponse bias
It will likely be too low, because of response bias
It will likely be correct, because the households were chosen at random
It cannot be affected, because a median ignores extreme values
questions.answer: It will likely be too high, because of nonresponse bias
questions.solution: The households that answered differ from the ones that did not, and they are richer, so the estimate is pushed up. Random selection does not protect against nonresponse.

solve.answer: It will likely be too high, because of nonresponse bias
solve.work: High-income households overrepresented among replies: estimate too high, nonresponse bias.

questions.skill: Spot nonresponse, response and measurement bias
questions.stem: Survey A is sent to 1,000 randomly chosen people and 8% reply. Survey B is sent to 100 randomly chosen people and 90% reply. Which statement is the most reasonable?
choices: Survey A is more trustworthy, because it was sent to more people than survey B
Survey B may be more trustworthy, since survey A's low response rate could bias it
Both are equally trustworthy, because both samples were chosen at random
Neither can be trusted, because a survey sent to fewer than 1,000 people is always biased
questions.answer: Survey B may be more trustworthy, since survey A's low response rate could bias it
questions.solution: With only 8% replying, the people who answered survey A may differ from those who did not. Survey B heard from nearly everyone it asked, so it has far less nonresponse bias.

solve.answer: Survey B may be more trustworthy, since survey A's low response rate could bias it
solve.work: 8% response rate risks nonresponse bias; B may be more trustworthy.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A list has 1,500 students. A systematic sample starts with student number 14 and then takes every 25th student on the list. What is the number of the last student chosen?
questions.solution: The chosen numbers are $14 + 25k$. The largest one not above 1,500 has $k = 59$, since $14 + 25 \times 59 = 1{,}489$ and the next one would be 1,514.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A school has 990 students: 450 in grade 9, 330 in grade 10 and 210 in grade 11. A stratified sample of 99 students is chosen with each grade represented in proportion to its size. How many more grade 9 students than grade 11 students are in the sample?
questions.solution: The sample is $\frac{99}{990} = 10\%$ of each grade: 45 from grade 9, 33 from grade 10 and 21 from grade 11. The difference is $45 - 21 = 24$.

questions.skill: Choose a sampling method that reduces bias
questions.stem: A researcher divides a school's students by grade, then in each grade surveys the first students who walk into the cafeteria. What is the main flaw?
choices: Dividing the students by grade makes the sample impossible to analyze correctly afterward
The students should be chosen from only one grade, not from all of them
Grouping by grade is fine, but students within each grade are not chosen at random
A sample is biased unless it contains exactly the same number from each grade
questions.answer: Grouping by grade is fine, but students within each grade are not chosen at random
questions.solution: Grouping by grade is a good idea, but within each grade the first students to arrive are a convenience sample. They should be chosen at random.

solve.answer: Grouping by grade is fine, but students within each grade are not chosen at random
solve.work: Strata fine but within-strata selection is convenience, not random.

questions.skill: Identify the population, the sample and the variables
questions.stem: In a poll of 1,200 randomly chosen North Carolina voters, 54% favor a new law. Which statement is correct?
choices: The 54% is a parameter, because it describes the whole population of voters in the state who favor it
The 54% is the exact percent of all the voters in the state who favor the law
The 54% is a statistic from the sample that estimates the percent of all voters in the state
The 54% is a variable, and the 1,200 voters polled are the population
questions.answer: The 54% is a statistic from the sample that estimates the percent of all voters in the state
questions.solution: A number computed from a sample is a statistic. It estimates, but is not necessarily equal to, the parameter, the percent among all voters in the state.

solve.answer: The 54% is a statistic from the sample that estimates the percent of all voters in the state
solve.work: 54% is a sample statistic estimating the population proportion.

questions.skill: Identify the population, the sample and the variables
questions.stem: A researcher surveys 80 randomly chosen students from each of the 3 high schools in a district, 240 students in all, to learn the opinions of all the students in the district. What is the population?
choices: The 240 students who were surveyed
The 80 students chosen at each of the schools
The 3 high schools that were visited
All of the students in the district
questions.answer: All of the students in the district
questions.solution: The population is the whole group the researcher wants to learn about: all of the students in the district. The 240 students are the sample.

solve.answer: All of the students in the district
solve.work: Population is all students in the district.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: A gauge records the depth of a river at one bridge. Which question about the river is a statistical question?
choices: How deep is the river at the bridge right now?
What was the river's depth at the bridge last Monday?
What was the river's depth at the bridge at 8 a.m. today?
How does the river's depth vary over a year?
questions.answer: How does the river's depth vary over a year?
questions.solution: A statistical question is answered with data that are expected to vary. Depth over a year takes many different values. The other three ask for one measurement at one moment, so each has a single answer.

solve.answer: How does the river's depth vary over a year?
solve.work: The three single-time questions each have one reading as an answer. How the depth varies over a year expects variability across many readings: statistical.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: who is behind it
questions.stem: You want to know how many hours of sleep teenagers usually get. Which source is the most credible?
choices: An online poll on an energy-drink company's page that 400 of its followers chose to answer
A blog post by an unnamed writer who gives no data and no source for the claim
A message a friend forwarded that says "most teens sleep only five hours a night" and gives no source
A national health agency's survey of 5,000 randomly chosen teens, with its methods published
questions.answer: A national health agency's survey of 5,000 randomly chosen teens, with its methods published
questions.solution: A large random sample, collected by an agency with no reason to favor an answer and with published methods, is the most trustworthy. The other sources have self-chosen respondents, no data, or no known source.

solve.answer: A national health agency's survey of 5,000 randomly chosen teens, with its methods published
solve.work: Large random national sample with published methods. B.

questions.skill: Compare group means after splitting
questions.stem: The test scores of the morning class are 60, 70 and 80. The test scores of the afternoon class are 80, 90 and 100. When the data are split by class time, what is the mean score of the afternoon class?
questions.solution: Add the afternoon scores and divide by how many there are: $\frac{80+90+100}{3}=\frac{270}{3}=90$.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: who is behind it
questions.stem: Which of these is a warning sign that the results of a study may be biased?
choices: The study names who collected the data and describes in detail how they did it
The study was paid for by a company that sells the product being tested
The people in the study were chosen at random from a large group
The study was reviewed by experts who did not work on it or on the product
questions.answer: The study was paid for by a company that sells the product being tested
questions.solution: A study paid for by a company with something to sell may be shaped, on purpose or not, to favor the company. Naming the collectors and methods, random selection and independent review are signs of a trustworthy study.

solve.answer: The study was paid for by a company that sells the product being tested
solve.work: Funding by the product's seller is a conflict of interest. D.

questions.skill: Split data by a third variable: why and how
questions.stem: Weight and height were measured for a group of dogs and cats. When weight is plotted against height, the points form two separate clouds. Which third variable would best explain the two clouds?
choices: the type of animal (dog or cat)
the weight of each animal
the height of each animal
the order in which the animals were measured
questions.answer: the type of animal (dog or cat)
questions.solution: Dogs and cats follow different patterns, so splitting the data by the type of animal separates the clouds. Weight and height are the two variables already plotted, and the measuring order has nothing to do with the animal.

solve.answer: the type of animal (dog or cat)
solve.work: Height and weight are the plotted variables; measurement order is irrelevant. Species (dog or cat) separates the clouds.

questions.skill: Combine group means into an overall mean
questions.stem: In a class of 10 students, 4 are in the band and 6 are not. The band students have a mean GPA of 3.5, and the other students have a mean GPA of 3.0. What is the mean GPA of all 10 students?
questions.solution: Find the total for each group: $4\times 3.5=14$ and $6\times 3.0=18$. The total is $32$, and $32\div 10=3.2$.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: evidence and method
questions.stem: A news article says "Studies show that most students prefer online homework," but it never names the study. What is the best first step in judging the claim?
choices: Accept the claim as true, since it appeared in a news article read by many people
Count how many times the article was shared online and trust it if the number is large
Find the original study and check who ran it and how the data were collected
Read only the headline, which gives the main point of the claim
questions.answer: Find the original study and check who ran it and how the data were collected
questions.solution: A claim is only as good as the study behind it. Finding the original study lets you check who ran it, who was asked, and how. How popular or how well placed the article is says nothing about the data.

solve.answer: Find the original study and check who ran it and how the data were collected
solve.work: Find the original source and check methods. B.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that matter for a question
questions.stem: A farmer wants to know whether the amount of rain affects how tall the corn grows. Which variable is the response variable, the one that may depend on the other?
choices: the amount of rain
the price of the corn seed
the name of the farm
the height of the corn
questions.answer: the height of the corn
questions.solution: The question asks whether the height of the corn changes with the rain, so the height is the response. The amount of rain is the explanatory variable.

solve.answer: the height of the corn
solve.work: Rain is explanatory; corn height may depend on rain, so it is the response.

questions.skill: Split data by a third variable: why and how
questions.stem: What is the main reason to split a dataset by a third variable?
choices: It makes the dataset smaller, so a computer can read it faster and give a quicker answer
The groups may follow different patterns, so a separate model for each can fit better
It lets you throw away the points that do not match the overall trend in the data
It always makes the correlation for the whole dataset closer to 1, whatever the data are
questions.answer: The groups may follow different patterns, so a separate model for each can fit better
questions.solution: If the groups behave differently, one model for everyone fits none of them well. Splitting by the third variable lets each group have its own model. It is not a way to delete points or to force a correlation.

solve.answer: The groups may follow different patterns, so a separate model for each can fit better
solve.work: Splitting lets each group have its own model when the groups follow different patterns. The others are false (speed, always raising r, discarding points).

questions.skill: Compare group means after splitting
questions.stem: Team Red scored 10, 12 and 14. Team Blue scored 9, 9 and 15. Which team has the greater mean score?
choices: Team Red, with a mean of 12
Team Blue, because it has the highest single score of 15
Team Blue, with a mean of 12
The two teams have equal means
questions.answer: Team Red, with a mean of 12
questions.solution: Red: $\frac{10+12+14}{3}=12$. Blue: $\frac{9+9+15}{3}=\frac{33}{3}=11$. Red has the greater mean, even though Blue has the single highest score.

solve.answer: Team Red, with a mean of 12
solve.work: Red: 36/3 = 12. Blue: 33/3 = 11. Red has the greater mean, 12.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that matter for a question
questions.stem: A school records five columns for each student: name, minutes of exercise per week, locker number, resting heart rate and favorite color. A coach asks whether students who exercise more tend to have a lower resting heart rate. Which two columns does the question need?
choices: The student's name and the student's locker number
Minutes of exercise and resting heart rate
Locker number and favorite color
The student's favorite color and resting heart rate
questions.answer: Minutes of exercise and resting heart rate
questions.solution: The question is about exercise and heart rate, so only those two columns matter. Name, locker number and favorite color have nothing to do with the question.

solve.answer: Minutes of exercise and resting heart rate
solve.work: Need minutes of exercise and resting heart rate. C.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: who is behind it
questions.stem: You want the typical price of homes sold in your county last year. Which source is the most credible?
choices: A real estate agent's ad that says homes here "sell for a fortune" and gives no sale prices at all
An anonymous comment on a social media post saying that "everyone knows" what the homes cost
The county records office, which lists every recorded sale and explains how it counted them
A text from a friend who heard that a neighbor sold a house for a very high price last week
questions.answer: The county records office, which lists every recorded sale and explains how it counted them
questions.solution: The county office is the official record keeper, has no reason to push a price up or down, and shows how it counted. The other sources give no data or have a reason to exaggerate.

solve.answer: The county records office, which lists every recorded sale and explains how it counted them
solve.work: Official county records listing every sale with a stated method are the most credible; the others are anonymous, biased or hearsay.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: who is behind it
questions.stem: A company that sells bottled water says its water is "healthier than any other brand." Why should you be careful with this claim?
choices: The company earns more if people believe it, so it may show only the results that favor its water
The company is too large to keep accurate records, so none of the numbers it reports can be right
Bottled water cannot be tested in any laboratory, so no company could know such a thing about it
A company is not allowed to share numbers about its own products with the people who might buy them
questions.answer: The company earns more if people believe it, so it may show only the results that favor its water
questions.solution: A source that gains from a claim may report only the favorable evidence. That is a reason to check the evidence, not proof that the claim is false.

solve.answer: The company earns more if people believe it, so it may show only the results that favor its water
solve.work: The seller has a financial interest in the claim, so it may cherry-pick favorable results. Other options are false statements.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: who is behind it
questions.stem: A news article quotes an expert on how much sleep teenagers need. Which detail best shows the expert is a credible source?
choices: The expert has many followers online and appears on television shows nearly every week of the year
The expert speaks with great confidence and never admits that anything about sleep is uncertain
The expert is described in the article as famous and has been quoted in many other news articles
The expert studies sleep in teenagers for a living and says which groups pay for the research
questions.answer: The expert studies sleep in teenagers for a living and says which groups pay for the research
questions.solution: Credibility comes from relevant training and openness about who pays for the work, not from fame, followers or confident speech.

solve.answer: The expert studies sleep in teenagers for a living and says which groups pay for the research
solve.work: Relevant expertise plus disclosure of funding signals credibility; fame, confidence and followers do not.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: evidence and method
questions.stem: Which feature of a report makes its findings easiest for other people to check?
choices: The report is long and uses many technical words to describe how all of the work was done
The data and the way they were collected are posted so that anyone can look at them
The report has many colorful charts and photographs that make each of its points very clear
The report has been shared by thousands of people online during the last few days or weeks
questions.answer: The data and the way they were collected are posted so that anyone can look at them
questions.solution: Findings can be checked only if the data and the method are available. Length, pictures and popularity say nothing about whether the results are correct.

solve.answer: The data and the way they were collected are posted so that anyone can look at them
solve.work: Posting the data and methods lets others check (reproduce) the findings.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: evidence and method
questions.stem: An ad says "9 out of 10 users love our app." What is the most important thing to find out first?
choices: How many colors the app uses and whether the ad has a catchy tune that is easy to remember
How many users were asked, how they were chosen, and exactly what they were asked
Whether the name of the app is short and whether many of its users tell their friends about it
Whether the ad was shown on a very large screen at a time when many people were watching it
questions.answer: How many users were asked, how they were chosen, and exactly what they were asked
questions.solution: A percentage means little until you know the size of the group, how it was chosen and what question it answered.

solve.answer: How many users were asked, how they were chosen, and exactly what they were asked
solve.work: Sample size, how users were chosen and the exact question determine whether 9 out of 10 means anything.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: how the sample was chosen
questions.stem: A school has 1,200 students and wants to know what they think of the new lunch menu. Which sample is best?
choices: The 100 students who are first in line at the cafeteria on one Monday and who all buy lunch
The 100 students who are on the school newspaper staff, since they are good at answering questions
The 100 students who volunteered after the principal asked for volunteers over the loudspeaker
100 students picked by a random draw from the list of every student in the school
questions.answer: 100 students picked by a random draw from the list of every student in the school
questions.solution: A random draw from the whole list gives every student the same chance, so the sample is likely to resemble the school. The other samples leave out or favor certain students.

solve.answer: 100 students picked by a random draw from the list of every student in the school
solve.work: A simple random sample from the full list is representative; the others are convenience or voluntary samples.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: how the sample was chosen
questions.stem: A school has 800 students. A random sample of 80 of them is surveyed, and 28 say they prefer pizza. Based on the sample, about how many students in the whole school prefer pizza?
questions.solution: 28 of 80 is $\frac{28}{80} = 0.35$ of the sample. A random sample suggests the same share of the school: $0.35 \times 800 = 280$.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that matter for a question
questions.stem: A researcher asks whether the age of a used car is related to its price. The dataset has columns for ID number, age, color, price and seller's name. Which two columns does the question use?
choices: the age column and the price column of the dataset
the ID number column and the price column of the dataset
the color column and the seller's name column of the dataset
the seller's name column and the age column of the dataset
questions.answer: the age column and the price column of the dataset
questions.solution: The question is about age and price, so those are the two variables to use. ID number, color and seller are not part of the question.

solve.answer: the age column and the price column of the dataset
solve.work: The question is about age and price.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that matter for a question
questions.stem: A student wonders whether the number of hours a student works after school affects the student's grade point average. Which variable is the explanatory variable (the one that might explain the other)?
choices: the grade point average that the student earns
the name of the school that the student attends
the number of hours worked after school
the number of classes that the school offers each year
questions.answer: the number of hours worked after school
questions.solution: The explanatory variable is the one that may explain or influence the other. Here hours worked might influence the grade point average, which is the response variable.

solve.answer: the number of hours worked after school
solve.work: Hours worked might explain GPA, so hours worked is explanatory.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that matter for a question
questions.stem: A dataset has the columns ID number, age, height, weight and shoe size. A doctor asks only how height is related to weight. How many of the five columns can be left out of this question?
questions.solution: The question uses two variables, height and weight. The other $5 - 2 = 3$ columns can be left out.

solve.work: Only height and weight are needed; ID, age and shoe size (3 columns) can be left out.

questions.skill: Identify a third variable that may change or explain a pattern
questions.stem: Cities with more firefighters tend to have more fire damage. Which third variable most plausibly explains both?
choices: the color of the trucks that the city uses
the age of the person who leads the department
the number of letters in the name of the city
the size of the population of the city
questions.answer: the size of the population of the city
questions.solution: Larger cities have more people and buildings, so they need more firefighters and also have more fires and damage. Firefighters do not cause the damage.

solve.answer: the size of the population of the city
solve.work: Larger populations need more firefighters and have more fires/damage: population is the lurking variable.

questions.skill: Identify a third variable that may change or explain a pattern
questions.stem: In a group of children ages 5 to 12, shoe size and reading score are positively related. Which third variable most likely explains this?
choices: the brand of shoes each child wears
the color of each child's backpack
the age of each child in the group
the street where each child lives
questions.answer: the age of each child in the group
questions.solution: Older children have larger feet and also read better, so age is linked to both variables. Shoe size does not make a child read better.

solve.answer: the age of each child in the group
solve.work: Older children have bigger feet and read better: age.

questions.skill: Split data by a third variable: why and how
questions.stem: A scatter plot of salary against years of experience shows two separate bands, one for managers and one for staff. What would improve the model?
choices: Fit one line through all of the points and ignore the job level
Fit a separate best-fit line for the managers and for the staff
Remove all of the staff because their salaries are lower overall
Plot the years of experience against the years of experience
questions.answer: Fit a separate best-fit line for the managers and for the staff
questions.solution: When a third variable (job level) splits the data into two patterns, a separate line for each group fits better than one line for all.

solve.answer: Fit a separate best-fit line for the managers and for the staff
solve.work: Two bands by job level: split by job level and fit a line for each group.

questions.skill: Compare group means after splitting
questions.stem: Plants given fertilizer grew 12, 15 and 18 centimeters. Plants without fertilizer grew 9, 10 and 11 centimeters. After splitting by fertilizer, how many centimeters greater is the mean growth of the fertilized plants?
questions.solution: The fertilized mean is $(12+15+18) \div 3 = 15$. The other mean is $(9+10+11) \div 3 = 10$. The difference is $15 - 10 = 5$.

questions.skill: Compare group means after splitting
questions.stem: Boys in a class read for 30, 40 and 50 minutes. Girls read for 35, 40 and 45 minutes. After splitting by gender, which statement is correct?
choices: The two groups have the same mean, 40 minutes, but the boys' times are more spread out
The boys have the greater mean because the boys have the longest reading time of 50 minutes
The girls have the greater mean because the times of the girls are closer to one another
The boys have the lower mean because the boys also have the shortest reading time of 30
questions.answer: The two groups have the same mean, 40 minutes, but the boys' times are more spread out
questions.solution: Both means are 40 minutes: $(30+40+50) \div 3 = 40$ and $(35+40+45) \div 3 = 40$. The boys' times range from 30 to 50, which is more spread out.

solve.answer: The two groups have the same mean, 40 minutes, but the boys' times are more spread out
solve.work: Boys mean 120/3 = 40; girls 120/3 = 40. Boys range 20 vs girls 10, so boys more spread out.

questions.skill: Combine group means into an overall mean
questions.stem: Two groups of 5 students each took a quiz. The first group had a mean score of 40 and the second group had a mean score of 60. What is the mean score of all 10 students?
questions.solution: The groups are the same size, so the combined mean is halfway between the two means: $(40 + 60) \div 2 = 50$.

questions.skill: Use a group's own best-fit line
questions.stem: For the city center, the best-fit line for a taxi fare $f$ (in dollars) against the distance $m$ (in miles) is $f=2m+3$. What fare, in dollars, does this line predict for a trip of 6 miles?
questions.solution: Substitute $m=6$: $f = 2(6) + 3 = 15$ dollars.

questions.skill: Use a group's own best-fit line
questions.stem: The best-fit line for small dogs is $w=0.5h+2$ and for large dogs is $w=1.5h-20$, where $h$ is height in centimeters and $w$ is weight in kilograms. Which group's weight rises faster as height increases?
choices: Small dogs, since their intercept of 2 is greater than the intercept of $-20$
Large dogs, since their slope of 1.5 is greater than the slope of 0.5
Both groups equally, since both of the lines have a positive slope
Large dogs, since their intercept of $-20$ is farther from zero than 2
questions.answer: Large dogs, since their slope of 1.5 is greater than the slope of 0.5
questions.solution: The rate at which weight rises is the slope. The large dogs' slope, 1.5 kilograms per centimeter, is greater than 0.5.

solve.answer: Large dogs, since their slope of 1.5 is greater than the slope of 0.5
solve.work: Rate of increase is the slope: 1.5 > 0.5, so large dogs.

questions.skill: Find a rate within a group or combine group rates
questions.stem: A survey of 200 people is split by region. There are 80 people from the north, and 25 percent of them own a bike. How many people from the north own a bike?
questions.solution: 25 percent of 80 is $0.25 \times 80 = 20$.

questions.skill: Spot a reversal when groups are combined
questions.stem: A trend that shows up in each group of data can reverse when the groups are combined into one. What is this called?
choices: regression to the mean
sampling error
Simpson's paradox
response bias
questions.answer: Simpson's paradox
questions.solution: A trend that appears in several groups but reverses when they are combined is called Simpson's paradox.

solve.answer: Simpson's paradox
solve.work: A trend reversing on aggregation is Simpson's paradox.

questions.skill: Find a residual from a best-fit line
questions.stem: The best-fit line for a group of students is $y=3x+2$, where $x$ is the hours studied and $y$ is the score. A student in the group studied 4 hours and scored 17. What is the residual (actual $y$ minus predicted $y$)?
questions.solution: The line predicts $3(4)+2 = 14$. The residual is $17 - 14 = 3$.

questions.skill: Find a rate within a group or combine group rates
questions.stem: In Group A, 18 of 24 students passed a test. In Group B, 12 of 20 students passed. By how many percentage points is the pass rate of Group A higher than the pass rate of Group B?
questions.solution: Group A: $\frac{18}{24} = 75\%$. Group B: $\frac{12}{20} = 60\%$. The difference is $75 - 60 = 15$ percentage points.

questions.skill: Split data by a third variable: why and how
questions.stem: What does it mean to split a dataset by a third variable?
choices: Sort the cases into groups by that variable and study each group on its own
Delete every case that has a value of that variable above the average of that variable
Add the values of that variable to the values of the other two variables
Replace the two main variables by that variable and study only that one variable alone
questions.answer: Sort the cases into groups by that variable and study each group on its own
questions.solution: Splitting means grouping the cases by the values of the third variable and then looking at each group separately.

solve.answer: Sort the cases into groups by that variable and study each group on its own
solve.work: Splitting = grouping cases by the third variable and analyzing each group. D.

questions.skill: Use a group's own best-fit line
questions.stem: Weight and height were measured for dogs and cats together. After splitting the data by type of animal, the best-fit line for the dogs is $w=0.8h-10$, where $h$ is the height in centimeters and $w$ is the weight in kilograms. What weight, in kilograms, does this line predict for a dog that is 50 centimeters tall?
questions.solution: Substitute $h=50$: $w=0.8\times 50-10=40-10=30$ kilograms.

questions.skill: Find a residual from a best-fit line
questions.stem: The afternoon class has its own best-fit line, $s=4h+50$, where $h$ is the hours a student studied and $s$ is the test score. A student in this class studied 5 hours and scored 74. What is the residual (the actual score minus the predicted score)?
questions.solution: The predicted score is $4\times 5+50=70$. The residual is the actual score minus the predicted score: $74-70=4$.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: evidence and method
questions.stem: Which detail would make you MOST willing to trust a study's claim that a new fertilizer raises crop yield?
choices: The fertilizer's maker ran the study and shared only the plots that grew the very best crops
Farmers who liked the fertilizer were invited to report how much their crops grew
Plants were randomly assigned to get the fertilizer or none, and the data were published
The claim appeared in an advertisement that did not say where it came from
questions.answer: Plants were randomly assigned to get the fertilizer or none, and the data were published
questions.solution: Random assignment to treatment and comparison groups, with the data open to check, is the strongest design. The other details show selected results, a self-chosen set of reporters, or an unknown source.

solve.answer: Plants were randomly assigned to get the fertilizer or none, and the data were published
solve.work: Random assignment plus published data. B.

questions.skill: Identify a third variable that may change or explain a pattern
questions.stem: In many towns, months with higher ice-cream sales also have more sunburns. Which third variable most plausibly explains both?
choices: the number of flavors the shops sell
the number of schools in the town
the number of letters in the town's name
the average daily temperature
questions.answer: the average daily temperature
questions.solution: Hot weather leads people both to buy ice cream and to spend time in the sun. The temperature is a third variable behind both patterns, so ice cream does not cause the sunburns.

solve.answer: the average daily temperature
solve.work: Hot weather raises both ice-cream sales and sunburns: average daily temperature is the lurking variable.

questions.skill: Split data by a third variable: why and how
questions.stem: A single best-fit line for pay against hours worked, using two kinds of jobs together, has $r=0.4$. After splitting the data by job type, each job type has its own line with $r=0.95$. What does this suggest?
choices: The data must have been entered incorrectly, because splitting the data can never raise $r$ at all
Job type changes the pattern, so one line for each type fits better than one line for all
Hours worked has no effect on pay at either kind of job, because the overall $r$ is so very low
The single overall line is the better model, because it uses every point in the data
questions.answer: Job type changes the pattern, so one line for each type fits better than one line for all
questions.solution: Within each job type the relationship is very strong ($r=0.95$), so hours worked does affect pay. The overall $r$ is low because the two job types follow different lines. Separate lines are the better model.

solve.answer: Job type changes the pattern, so one line for each type fits better than one line for all
solve.work: Job type is a lurking/grouping variable; separate lines fit much better. A.

questions.skill: Combine group means into an overall mean
questions.stem: In a garden, 5 tomato plants have a mean height of 80 centimeters and 15 pepper plants have a mean height of 60 centimeters. What is the mean height of all 20 plants, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Total height of the tomato plants: $5\times 80=400$. Total height of the pepper plants: $15\times 60=900$. The mean of all 20 plants is $\frac{400+900}{20}=65$ centimeters.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: evidence and method
questions.stem: A website says the mean salary of a college's graduates is very high. Which question would best help you decide whether to trust that figure?
choices: Did every graduate report a salary, or only some who chose to answer?
Does the website show the salary figure in large, colorful charts and bold text?
How many people visited the website last month, and how long did they stay?
Does the college have a long and impressive name that sounds well known?
questions.answer: Did every graduate report a salary, or only some who chose to answer?
questions.solution: If only graduates who did well chose to report, the mean would be too high. How the figure was collected matters; its design, popularity or the college's name do not.

solve.answer: Did every graduate report a salary, or only some who chose to answer?
solve.work: Voluntary response could inflate a mean salary (high earners more likely to report). Traffic, name and chart style are irrelevant.

questions.skill: Use a group's own best-fit line
questions.stem: Best-fit lines for test score $s$ against hours studied $h$ were found separately for two groups. For girls, $s=3h+55$. For boys, $s=h+62$. For 10 hours of study, how many points higher is the girls' predicted score than the boys' predicted score?
questions.solution: Girls: $3\times 10+55=85$. Boys: $1\times 10+62=72$. The difference is $85-72=13$ points.

questions.skill: Identify a third variable that may change or explain a pattern
questions.stem: A researcher asks whether students who sleep more get better grades. Which third variable might change the pattern, and so is worth splitting the data by?
choices: the locker number of each student in the school
the color of the paper that each student's survey form was printed on
the grade level of each student (for example, 6th or 11th)
the page number on which each student's survey form was stapled
questions.answer: the grade level of each student (for example, 6th or 11th)
questions.solution: Students of different ages may differ in both sleep and grades, so the pattern could differ by grade level. A locker number or the color or page number of a form has no connection to sleep or grades.

solve.answer: the grade level of each student (for example, 6th or 11th)
solve.work: Grade level plausibly affects both sleep and grades; others are irrelevant. A.

questions.skill: Find a rate within a group
questions.stem: A dataset has 40 students. Of them, 25 are in Group A, and 20 of those 25 passed the test. When the data are split by group, what percent of Group A passed?
questions.solution: Only the 25 students in Group A count: $\frac{20}{25}=0.8=80\%$.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: evidence and method
questions.stem: A survey from 2008 is cited as showing how often teenagers use their phones today. Which concern matters most?
choices: The survey was about phones, and a survey on one topic cannot be used for a later year
The survey is cited in only one place, and a survey must appear in three places to count
The survey has a year in its title, and surveys with a year in the title are always wrong
The data are many years old, so they may not describe teenagers today
questions.answer: The data are many years old, so they may not describe teenagers today
questions.solution: Behavior such as phone use changes quickly, so old data may not describe the present. The other reasons are not real rules of good evidence.

solve.answer: The data are many years old, so they may not describe teenagers today
solve.work: Data from 2008 are old and may not describe teen phone use today.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: evidence and method
questions.stem: A company's graph of sales shows only the last three months, when sales rose. Over the past two years, sales were falling. What is the concern?
choices: A short window makes a graph too hard for readers to understand at all
A short window can hide the longer trend, so the claim may be misleading
A graph of sales must always show exactly twelve months to be fair
A rise in the last three months cannot happen when sales fell for two years
questions.answer: A short window can hide the longer trend, so the claim may be misleading
questions.solution: Choosing a short stretch of time can leave out the bigger picture. Sales can rise briefly even in a long decline, so the full period should be shown.

solve.answer: A short window can hide the longer trend, so the claim may be misleading
solve.work: Showing only a rising 3-month window hides the 2-year decline: misleading.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: how the sample was chosen
questions.stem: A radio show asks listeners to phone in and vote on whether the town should build a new stadium. Why might the vote not show what the whole town thinks?
choices: Phone calls cannot be counted exactly, so any vote taken by phone is always unreliable
The show has too many listeners, and a large number of voters makes a poll less reliable
Only listeners who care a lot choose to call, so the callers may differ from the town
A vote on a stadium is a matter of opinion, so no sample can ever be used to study it
questions.answer: Only listeners who care a lot choose to call, so the callers may differ from the town
questions.solution: People who choose to respond are a self-selected group, often those with strong feelings. A random sample would be more likely to represent the town.

solve.answer: Only listeners who care a lot choose to call, so the callers may differ from the town
solve.work: Voluntary response: only those who care strongly call, so not representative.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: how the sample was chosen
questions.stem: A random sample of 150 voters in a city of 60,000 voters finds that 90 of the 150 support a new library. Based on the sample, about how many of the city's voters support the library?
questions.solution: $\frac{90}{150} = 0.6$ of the sample support it. $0.6 \times 60{,}000 = 36{,}000$.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that matter for a question
questions.stem: A buyer wants to explain the price of houses using these columns: size, number of bedrooms, year built, listing ID and the listing agent's name. Which pair of columns is the least useful for explaining price?
choices: the listing ID and the name of the listing agent
the size of the house and the number of its bedrooms
the year built and the size of the house itself
the number of bedrooms and the year that it was built
questions.answer: the listing ID and the name of the listing agent
questions.solution: A listing ID and an agent's name are labels. They do not describe the house, so they say little about its price. The other pairs describe the house itself.

solve.answer: the listing ID and the name of the listing agent
solve.work: Listing ID and agent's name are identifiers with no explanatory value for price.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that matter for a question
questions.stem: A dataset has 8 columns. Three of them are identifiers (ID number, name and address) that say nothing about the question being studied. A scatter plot is made for each pair of the remaining columns, and each pair is plotted once. How many scatter plots are made?
questions.solution: Five columns remain. The number of pairs is $\frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10$.

questions.skill: Identify a third variable that may change or explain a pattern
questions.stem: People who carry lighters have higher rates of lung disease. Which third variable most plausibly explains both?
choices: smoking, since people who smoke often carry lighters and also have more lung disease
the brand of the lighter, since some brands cause lung disease when carried in a pocket
the shoe size of each person, since people with larger shoes have larger lungs to damage
the month a person was born, since the birth month decides where lighters are sold
questions.answer: smoking, since people who smoke often carry lighters and also have more lung disease
questions.solution: Smoking leads people to carry lighters and also raises the risk of lung disease, so it explains the pattern without lighters causing disease.

solve.answer: smoking, since people who smoke often carry lighters and also have more lung disease
solve.work: Smoking causes both lighter-carrying and lung disease.

questions.skill: Split data by a third variable: why and how
questions.stem: A researcher fits a separate best-fit line for every combination of drive type (front, rear or all-wheel) and fuel type (gas or hybrid). How many lines does the researcher fit?
questions.solution: Each of the 3 drive types combines with each of the 2 fuel types: $3 \times 2 = 6$ lines.

solve.work: 3 drive types x 2 fuel types = 6 combinations, one line each.

questions.skill: Compare group means after splitting
questions.stem: Class 1 scored 70, 75, 80 and 95. Class 2 scored 60, 65, 90 and 95. By how many points is the mean of Class 1 greater than the mean of Class 2?
questions.solution: Class 1: $320 \div 4 = 80$. Class 2: $310 \div 4 = 77.5$. The difference is $80 - 77.5 = 2.5$.

questions.skill: Compare group means after splitting
questions.stem: After splitting by school, the mean score is 82 at School P and 74 at School Q. Which statement is supported by the data?
choices: Every student at School P scored higher than every student at School Q
Students at School P scored higher on average than students at School Q
School P teaches the subject better than School Q teaches the subject
A student who moved from School Q to School P would score 8 points higher
questions.answer: Students at School P scored higher on average than students at School Q
questions.solution: A mean describes the group as a whole. It supports a statement about averages, not about every student or about the cause of the difference.

solve.answer: Students at School P scored higher on average than students at School Q
solve.work: Means only support that P's students averaged higher; no causal or individual claims.

questions.skill: Combine group means into an overall mean
questions.stem: A bookstore sells 30 hardcover books with a mean price of 20 dollars and 70 paperbacks with a mean price of 10 dollars. What is the mean price of all 100 books, in dollars?
questions.solution: Total cost is $30(20) + 70(10) = 600 + 700 = 1300$ dollars. Divide by 100 books: $1300 \div 100 = 13$.

questions.skill: Combine group means into an overall mean
questions.stem: A restaurant has 12 workers with a mean wage of 15 dollars an hour. The 4 part-time workers have a mean wage of 10 dollars an hour. What is the mean wage of the other 8 workers, in dollars an hour?
questions.solution: All 12 together earn $12 \times 15 = 180$ dollars an hour. The part-time workers earn $4 \times 10 = 40$. The other 8 earn $180 - 40 = 140$, a mean of $140 \div 8 = 17.5$.

questions.skill: Use a group's own best-fit line
questions.stem: For apartments with a pool, the best-fit line for rent $r$ (in dollars) against size $s$ (in square feet) is $r=0.8s+300$. What rent, in dollars, does the line predict for a pool apartment of 900 square feet?

questions.skill: Use a group's own best-fit line
questions.stem: For runners aged 40 and older, the best-fit line for race time $t$ (in minutes) against age $a$ (in years) is $t=0.5a+20$. What does the slope 0.5 mean for this group?
choices: Each extra minute of race time goes with a predicted increase of 0.5 year in age
Each extra year of age goes with a predicted increase of 0.5 minute in race time
A runner who is 0 years old would be predicted to run the race in 0.5 minutes
Runners in this group take 0.5 minute to run the race, whatever their age may be
questions.answer: Each extra year of age goes with a predicted increase of 0.5 minute in race time
questions.solution: The slope is the change in the predicted $t$ for each increase of 1 in $a$: 0.5 minute more for each additional year.

solve.answer: Each extra year of age goes with a predicted increase of 0.5 minute in race time
solve.work: Slope: each extra year of age goes with +0.5 minute predicted time.

questions.skill: Find a rate within a group or combine group rates
questions.stem: In 9th grade, 45 of 60 students passed an exam. In 10th grade, 30 of 50 students passed. By how many percentage points is the 9th-grade pass rate higher than the 10th-grade pass rate?
questions.solution: 9th grade: $\frac{45}{60} = 75\%$. 10th grade: $\frac{30}{50} = 60\%$. The difference is 15 percentage points.

questions.skill: Find a rate within a group or combine group rates
questions.stem: A hiking club has 40 beginners and 60 experts. 10 percent of the beginners and 50 percent of the experts finish a trail. What percent of all 100 hikers finish?
questions.solution: Beginners who finish: $0.10 \times 40 = 4$. Experts who finish: $0.50 \times 60 = 30$. In all, $34$ of 100 finish, which is 34 percent.

questions.skill: Find a residual from a best-fit line
questions.stem: The best-fit line for all the data is $y=1.5x+10$. A point in the data is $(8, 20)$. What is the residual (actual $y$ minus predicted $y$)?
questions.solution: The line predicts $1.5(8) + 10 = 22$. The residual is $20 - 22 = -2$.

questions.skill: Find a residual from a best-fit line
questions.stem: A point has a residual of $-6$ from a best-fit line. What does this mean?
choices: The actual value is 6 units above the value that the line predicts at that point
The actual value is 6 percent below the value that the line predicts at that point
The point lies 6 units to the left of the line, measured along the horizontal axis
The actual value is 6 units below the value that the line predicts at that point
questions.answer: The actual value is 6 units below the value that the line predicts at that point
questions.solution: A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value. A residual of $-6$ means the actual value is 6 units less than predicted.

solve.answer: The actual value is 6 units below the value that the line predicts at that point
solve.work: Negative residual: actual is 6 below predicted.

questions.skill: Spot a reversal when groups are combined
questions.stem: Treatment A has a higher success rate than Treatment B among mild cases and also among severe cases, yet Treatment B has the higher overall rate. What best explains this?
choices: The mix of cases differs: most of A's patients had severe cases, which are harder to treat
Treatment B must work better, because the overall rate always decides which treatment is better
The rates must have been calculated wrongly, since this result is mathematically impossible
Treatment A works only in severe cases, so the mild cases should be dropped from the comparison
questions.answer: The mix of cases differs: most of A's patients had severe cases, which are harder to treat
questions.solution: The overall rate depends on how many mild and severe cases each treatment had. If A treated mostly hard cases, its overall rate can be lower even though it does better in each kind of case.

solve.answer: The mix of cases differs: most of A's patients had severe cases, which are harder to treat
solve.work: Simpson's paradox: A treated mostly severe (hard) cases, dragging its overall rate down.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that matter for a question
questions.stem: A school asks whether a tutoring program raises math scores. Which data would be the most relevant?
choices: each student's height and weight at the start of the term, and the number of the student's bus
the number of students in each homeroom and the names of the teachers who run each homeroom in the school
each student's lunch choice and the number of library books the student borrowed in the term
each student's math score before and after the term, and whether the student joined the program
questions.answer: each student's math score before and after the term, and whether the student joined the program
questions.solution: To judge whether the program raises scores you need the scores (before and after) and who was in the program.

solve.answer: each student's math score before and after the term, and whether the student joined the program
solve.work: Pre/post math scores and program participation. D.

questions.skill: Identify a third variable that may change or explain a pattern
questions.stem: Across countries, the number of televisions per person is positively related to life expectancy. Which explanation is the most reasonable?
choices: Owning a television directly adds years to the life of each person who owns one, so more sets mean longer lives
Living longer causes people to buy more televisions, and nothing else is involved
A third variable, such as national wealth, may lead to both more televisions and better health care
The two variables cannot be related, since televisions and life expectancy are measured in different units
questions.answer: A third variable, such as national wealth, may lead to both more televisions and better health care
questions.solution: Wealthier countries have more televisions and better health care. A third variable can explain a pattern without either variable causing the other.

solve.answer: A third variable, such as national wealth, may lead to both more televisions and better health care

questions.skill: Split data by a third variable: why and how
questions.stem: A line fitted to all the data has residuals that are mostly positive for students in one program and mostly negative for students in another program. What does this suggest?
choices: The residuals should all be positive, so the data in the first program were entered incorrectly by mistake
The line is perfect, because the positive and negative residuals add up to zero overall for all students
The two programs should be combined and their sizes ignored, which makes every residual vanish
The program may be a third variable that matters, so a separate line for each program may fit better
questions.answer: The program may be a third variable that matters, so a separate line for each program may fit better
questions.solution: If the residuals separate by group, the group is related to the pattern. Fitting a line for each program can reduce the residuals.

solve.answer: The program may be a third variable that matters, so a separate line for each program may fit better
solve.work: Residual sign differs by program: program is a relevant third variable; separate lines. B.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: evidence and method
questions.stem: One small study of 12 people finds that a new diet lowers cholesterol. Why should the result be treated carefully?
choices: Small studies are never published, so a small study that is published was probably faked by its authors
Diets never change cholesterol, so any study that shows a change must contain an error
A small sample can differ from the population by chance, and no one has yet repeated the result
A study of 12 people is too large to be reliable and it should have been much smaller
questions.answer: A small sample can differ from the population by chance, and no one has yet repeated the result
questions.solution: With only 12 people, chance can produce a result that does not hold for others. Confidence grows when larger or repeated studies agree.

solve.answer: A small sample can differ from the population by chance, and no one has yet repeated the result
solve.work: Small sample, chance variation, not replicated. B.

questions.skill: Combine groups into an overall rate
questions.stem: Tutor A taught 90 beginners, and 72 of them improved. Tutor A also taught 10 advanced students, and 4 of them improved. Over all of Tutor A's students, what percent improved?
questions.solution: In all, $72+4=76$ of the $90+10=100$ students improved, which is $\frac{76}{100}=76\%$.

questions.skill: Spot a reversal when groups are combined
questions.stem: Two doctors treated easy and hard cases. Doctor K: 81 of 90 easy cases recovered, and 2 of 10 hard cases recovered. Doctor L: 19 of 20 easy cases recovered, and 32 of 80 hard cases recovered. Which statement is correct?
choices: Doctor K has the higher recovery rate within each kind of case, and Doctor K also has a higher overall rate
Doctor L has the higher recovery rate within each kind of case, and also overall
Doctor K has the higher rate overall, so Doctor K must be better in each kind of case
Doctor L has the higher recovery rate in each kind of case, but Doctor K has the higher rate overall
questions.answer: Doctor L has the higher recovery rate in each kind of case, but Doctor K has the higher rate overall
questions.solution: Easy cases: K recovers $\frac{81}{90}=90\%$ and L recovers $\frac{19}{20}=95\%$. Hard cases: K recovers $\frac{2}{10}=20\%$ and L recovers $\frac{32}{80}=40\%$. So L is higher in both kinds. Overall, K recovers $\frac{83}{100}=83\%$ and L recovers $\frac{51}{100}=51\%$. K looks better overall only because most of K's patients had easy cases.

solve.answer: Doctor L has the higher recovery rate in each kind of case, but Doctor K has the higher rate overall
solve.work: K: easy 81/90 = 90%, hard 2/10 = 20%, overall 83/100 = 83%. L: easy 19/20 = 95%, hard 32/80 = 40%, overall 51/100 = 51%. L higher in each kind, K higher overall (Simpson's paradox). D.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: evidence and method
questions.stem: Four reports claim that students who use a study app earn higher grades. Which report gives the strongest evidence?
choices: A survey run by the app's maker, in which 500 of its own users gave the app five stars and wrote kind comments
A university study of 2,000 students comparing users with non-users of similar earlier grades, with data posted
A teacher's note that the 6 students in her class who use the app did well on the last two tests she gave them
A review site, paid by the app's maker, that praises the app and shows no data behind its claim of higher grades
questions.answer: A university study of 2,000 students comparing users with non-users of similar earlier grades, with data posted
questions.solution: The university study is large, compares users with similar non-users so earlier grades do not explain the result, and shares its data. The other reports come from an interested party, from a tiny group, or from a paid site with no data.

solve.answer: A university study of 2,000 students comparing users with non-users of similar earlier grades, with data posted
solve.work: Large independent study comparing similar students with posted data. C.

questions.skill: Identify a third variable that may change or explain a pattern
questions.stem: Students who eat breakfast have higher test scores on average. A critic says family income might explain both. How could the researchers account for family income?
choices: Split the students into income groups and compare breakfast eaters with non-eaters within each group
Drop every student who skipped breakfast, then compare the scores of those who are left
Keep only the highest-scoring students and look at how often each of those students ate breakfast, then report it
Leave family income out of the analysis entirely and report the same overall averages that were found before
questions.answer: Split the students into income groups and compare breakfast eaters with non-eaters within each group
questions.solution: Comparing breakfast eaters with skippers inside each income group keeps income about the same within each comparison, so income cannot explain a difference there. The other choices throw away data or ignore the question.

solve.answer: Split the students into income groups and compare breakfast eaters with non-eaters within each group
solve.work: Stratify by income and compare within groups. C.

questions.skill: Use a group's own best-fit line
questions.stem: Used vehicles are split into two types. For sedans, the best-fit line is $p=20-a$. For trucks, it is $p=26-2a$. Here $a$ is the age in years and $p$ is the price in thousands of dollars. At what age do the two lines predict the same price?
questions.solution: Set the two predicted prices equal: $20-a=26-2a$. Add $2a$ to both sides and subtract $20$: $a=6$. At 6 years both lines predict $14$ thousand dollars.

questions.skill: Combine group means into an overall mean
questions.stem: The mean score of all 50 students in a course is 73. The 20 students in Section 1 have a mean score of 85. What is the mean score of the other 30 students?
questions.solution: All 50 students have a total of $50\times 73=3650$. Section 1 has $20\times 85=1700$. The other 30 students have $3650-1700=1950$, so their mean is $\frac{1950}{30}=65$.

questions.skill: Residuals: group line against overall line
questions.stem: A point from Group 1 is $(4, 19)$. The best-fit line for all the data is $y=2x+5$. The best-fit line for Group 1 alone is $y=3x+5$. How much smaller is the size of the residual (the distance between the actual $y$ and the predicted $y$) using the Group 1 line than using the all-data line?
questions.solution: All-data line: predicted $y=2\cdot 4+5=13$, so the residual is $19-13=6$. Group 1 line: predicted $y=3\cdot 4+5=17$, so the residual is $19-17=2$. The residual is $6-2=4$ smaller.

solve.work: All-data prediction 2*4+5 = 13, residual size 6. Group 1 prediction 3*4+5 = 17, residual size 2. 6 - 2 = 4.

questions.skill: Split data by a third variable: why and how
questions.stem: A city studies whether bike lanes reduce accidents. For each street, the data give whether it has a bike lane, its accidents per year, and its traffic volume. Busy streets tend to have more accidents and also more bike lanes. Which comparison best accounts for traffic volume?
choices: Compare the street with the most accidents to the street with the fewest accidents
Compare the traffic on streets with bike lanes to the traffic on streets without bike lanes in the city
Compare accidents on streets with and without bike lanes, among streets with similar traffic
Compare accidents on streets with and without bike lanes, using all the streets together
questions.answer: Compare accidents on streets with and without bike lanes, among streets with similar traffic
questions.solution: Busy streets would make the bike-lane streets look worse for a reason that has nothing to do with the lanes. Comparing streets with similar traffic takes volume out of the comparison. The other comparisons ignore traffic or do not compare accidents by bike lane.

solve.answer: Compare accidents on streets with and without bike lanes, among streets with similar traffic

questions.skill: Use a group's own best-fit line
questions.stem: The height $y$ in centimeters of seedlings after $x$ weeks has these best-fit lines. For seedlings that got fertilizer, $y=2x+10$. For seedlings that did not, $y=2x+4$. For any number of weeks, how many centimeters taller do the lines predict the fertilized seedlings to be?
questions.solution: The lines have the same slope, so the gap does not change with $x$. At any $x$, the difference is $(2x+10)-(2x+4)=6$ centimeters.

solve.work: Same slope 2; difference in intercepts 10 - 4 = 6 cm for any x.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: how the sample was chosen
questions.stem: A school with 1,200 students wants to estimate the percent of all its students who ride the bus. Which sample gives the most reliable estimate?
choices: The first 40 students to arrive at school in the morning, because they are easy to count
A voluntary online survey that 700 students chose to answer, because it is the largest
All 30 students in one homeroom, because they are easy to reach and to ask
A random sample of 60 students chosen by computer from the full list of 1,200
questions.answer: A random sample of 60 students chosen by computer from the full list of 1,200
questions.solution: A random sample gives every student an equal chance, so it represents the whole school. Students who arrive first, who choose to answer a survey, or who share one homeroom may differ from the rest of the school, so those samples can be biased, however large they are.

solve.answer: A random sample of 60 students chosen by computer from the full list of 1,200
solve.work: Voluntary response, one homeroom and first arrivals are all biased (self-selection, convenience; early arrivals may be bus riders). A simple random sample of 60 from the full list is unbiased, so it gives the most reliable estimate despite being smaller.

questions.skill: Spot a reversal when groups are combined
questions.stem: Men applied to two programs: 80 of 100 applicants to the easy program were admitted, and 10 of 50 applicants to the hard program. Women: 9 of 10 applicants to the easy program were admitted, and 41 of 190 applicants to the hard program. What percent of all women applicants were admitted?
questions.solution: Women admitted: $9 + 41 = 50$. Women who applied: $10 + 190 = 200$. $\frac{50}{200} = 25\%$. (Women do better in each program, yet men do better overall, because most women applied to the hard program.)

questions.skill: Spot a reversal when groups are combined
questions.stem: Player R got hits in 29 of 100 at-bats in the first half of a season and in 5 of 10 at-bats in the second half. Player S got hits in 1 of 10 at-bats in the first half and in 45 of 100 at-bats in the second half. Which statement is correct?
choices: Player S has the higher average in each half, but Player R has the higher average overall
Player R has the higher average in each half, and Player R also has the higher average overall
Player S has the higher average in each half, and Player S also has the higher average overall
Player R has the higher average in each half, but Player S has the higher average overall
questions.answer: Player R has the higher average in each half, but Player S has the higher average overall
questions.solution: First half: R $29\%$, S $10\%$. Second half: R $50\%$, S $45\%$. R is higher in each half. Overall R is $\frac{34}{110} \approx 31\%$ and S is $\frac{46}{110} \approx 42\%$, so S is higher overall.

solve.answer: Player R has the higher average in each half, but Player S has the higher average overall
solve.work: First half R .290 vs S .100; second half R .500 vs S .450: R higher in each. Overall R 34/110 = .309, S 46/110 = .418: S higher overall.

questions.skill: Combine group means into an overall mean
questions.stem: A class of 25 students has a mean score of 76.8. The boys have a mean score of 72 and the girls have a mean score of 80. How many girls are in the class?
questions.solution: Total points: $76.8 \times 25 = 1920$. If all 25 had the boys' mean, the total would be $72 \times 25 = 1800$. Each girl adds $80 - 72 = 8$ more, so $\frac{1920-1800}{8} = 15$ girls.

questions.skill: Combine group means into an overall mean
questions.stem: Three sections took the same exam. 10 students in Section 1 had a mean of 70, 20 students in Section 2 had a mean of 80, and 20 students in Section 3 had a mean of 90. What is the mean of all 50 students?

questions.skill: Combine group means into an overall mean
questions.stem: Group 1 has a mean of 60 and Group 2 has a mean of 80. The mean of the two groups combined is 66. What do you know about the sizes of the groups?
choices: Group 2 is larger, since the second group has the higher mean of the two
Group 1 is larger, since the combined mean is closer to 60 than to 80
The groups are the same size, since 66 lies between the means of 60 and 80
The groups cannot be combined, since the combined mean is not exactly 70
questions.answer: Group 1 is larger, since the combined mean is closer to 60 than to 80
questions.solution: A combined mean lies nearer the mean of the larger group. 66 is closer to 60, so Group 1 is larger. (It is 7 times 3 in proportion: $\frac{6}{20}$ of the weight is on Group 2.)

solve.answer: Group 1 is larger, since the combined mean is closer to 60 than to 80
solve.work: Weighted mean 66 is closer to 60 so Group 1 carries more weight: (66-60)/(80-66) means n1:n2 = 14:6. Group 1 larger.

questions.skill: Use a group's own best-fit line
questions.stem: The best-fit line for all the data is $y=2x+10$. The data are split into Group A and Group B, with their own lines: $y=x+14$ for Group A and $y=3x+6$ for Group B. Group A has the points $(2, 17)$, $(6, 19)$ and $(3, 14)$. Group B has the points $(2, 12)$, $(5, 25)$ and $(4, 17)$. For how many of the six points is the size of the residual strictly smaller from the point's own group line than from the all-data line?
questions.solution: A: $(2,17)$: 3 against 1. $(6,19)$: 3 against 1. $(3,14)$: 2 against 3. B: $(2,12)$: 2 against 0. $(5,25)$: 5 against 4. $(4,17)$: 1 against 1. Strictly smaller for 4 points.

solve.work: A line y=x+14: (2,17) group res 1 vs all 17-14=3 yes; (6,19) -1 vs -3 yes; (3,14) -3 vs -2 no. B line y=3x+6: (2,12) 0 vs -2 yes; (5,25) 4 vs 5 yes; (4,17) -1 vs -1 tie, not strictly, no. Count 4.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: how the sample was chosen
questions.stem: Product A has an average rating of 4.9 from 8 ratings, all posted on the day it launched. Product B has an average rating of 4.5 from 3,000 ratings posted over a year. Which statement is best?
choices: B's rating is likely more dependable, since it rests on many more ratings gathered over time
A's rating is likely more dependable, since it is higher and all of the ratings came at once
The ratings are equally dependable, since an average always shows the true quality of a product
Neither rating means anything, since every rating a customer gives is only a matter of opinion
questions.answer: B's rating is likely more dependable, since it rests on many more ratings gathered over time
questions.solution: An average from a few ratings posted together can be skewed by chance or by a few friendly reviewers. Thousands of ratings spread over a year give a steadier picture.

solve.answer: B's rating is likely more dependable, since it rests on many more ratings gathered over time
solve.work: 3,000 ratings over a year are more dependable than 8 launch-day ratings.

questions.skill: Use a group's own best-fit line
questions.stem: Two groups have best-fit lines of $y$ against $x$: $y=4x+10$ for Group P, which has 10 members, and $y=2x+30$ for Group Q, which has 30 members. At $x=5$, what is the mean of the predicted $y$-values over all 40 members?
questions.solution: Group P predicts $4(5)+10 = 30$. Group Q predicts $2(5)+30 = 40$. The mean is $\frac{10(30) + 30(40)}{40} = \frac{1500}{40} = 37.5$.

questions.skill: Find a rate within a group or combine group rates
questions.stem: A class has 200 students, 120 in Group A and 80 in Group B. The pass rate is 75 percent in Group A and 65 percent overall. What is the pass rate in Group B, in percent?
questions.solution: Passing overall: $0.65 \times 200 = 130$. Passing in Group A: $0.75 \times 120 = 90$. So $40$ of the 80 in Group B passed, which is 50 percent.

questions.skill: Find a rate within a group or combine group rates
questions.stem: In a school, 40 percent of the students are in the arts program. In the arts program, 85 percent of the students passed a test. Of the students not in the arts program, 60 percent passed. What percent of all students passed?
questions.solution: Weight the rates by the share of students: $0.4 \times 85 + 0.6 \times 60 = 34 + 36 = 70$ percent.

questions.skill: Compare group means after splitting
