questions.stem: The mean of Group A is 10 points higher than the mean of Group B. Group A has 20 members and Group B has 30 members. The mean of all 50 members is 54. What is the mean of Group B?
questions.solution: Let B's mean be $m$. Then A's mean is $m+10$ and $20(m+10) + 30m = 54 \times 50$. So $50m + 200 = 2700$ and $m = 50$.

questions.skill: Identify a third variable that may change or explain a pattern
questions.stem: Cities with more libraries also report more crimes. What is the best next step before drawing any conclusion?
choices: Close libraries in some cities, because the data show that libraries cause crime to rise there
Conclude that crime causes libraries to be built, since the cities with more crime must have built them
Look for a third variable, such as population, and compare the rates per person instead of the counts
Collect data from more cities, because only the number of cities limits what can be concluded
questions.answer: Look for a third variable, such as population, and compare the rates per person instead of the counts
questions.solution: Big cities have both more libraries and more crimes. Rates per person remove the effect of size and show whether any link remains.

solve.answer: Look for a third variable, such as population, and compare the rates per person instead of the counts
solve.work: Population is a lurking variable; compare per-capita rates.

questions.skill: Split data by a third variable: why and how
questions.stem: A dataset of 30 students is split by 10 different schools. What is the main risk of fitting a separate line for each school?
choices: Each school has only about three students, so each line may be unreliable
A separate line for each school always has a lower correlation than the single line
Splitting a dataset into groups always reverses the direction of every trend in it
A school cannot be used for splitting, since a school is not a number in the data
questions.answer: Each school has only about three students, so each line may be unreliable
questions.solution: Splitting into many groups leaves very few cases in each, so each line is based on too little data and may be misleading.

solve.answer: Each school has only about three students, so each line may be unreliable
solve.work: About 3 students per school: lines from so few points are unreliable.

questions.skill: Find a residual from a best-fit line
questions.stem: In the shade, the best-fit line for the height $h$ (in centimeters) of a plant against the weeks $w$ is $h=1.5w+4$. A plant in the shade was 11.5 centimeters tall after 6 weeks. What is the residual (actual minus predicted), in centimeters?
questions.solution: The line predicts $1.5(6) + 4 = 13$ centimeters. The residual is $11.5 - 13 = -1.5$.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: how the sample was chosen
questions.stem: A town has three neighborhoods with 2,000, 5,000 and 3,000 households. A survey chooses 150 households at random, in the same proportion from each neighborhood. How many households come from the neighborhood with 3,000 households?
questions.solution: The neighborhood holds $\frac{3000}{10000} = 30\%$ of the households, so $0.30 \times 150 = 45$ households are chosen from it.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: how the sample was chosen
questions.stem: A company emailed 400 customers a satisfaction survey. 60 customers replied, and 54 of those said they were satisfied. What percent of all 400 customers emailed are known to be satisfied?
questions.solution: $\frac{54}{400} = 0.135$, which is 13.5 percent. The other 340 customers did not reply, so nothing is known about them.

questions.skill: Spot a reversal when groups are combined
questions.stem: An analyst finds that, overall, Group X has a higher success rate than Group Y. What is the best next step before concluding that X does better?
choices: Report only the overall rates, since the overall rates rest on the largest number of cases in the whole data set
Drop the smaller group from the data, so that the two groups have the same sizes as one another in every comparison
Compare the groups within each level of a third variable, and check how group sizes differ across the levels
Average the two overall rates so that the larger group does not count for more than the smaller
questions.answer: Compare the groups within each level of a third variable, and check how group sizes differ across the levels
questions.solution: An overall comparison can hide a reversal. Comparing within the levels of a third variable shows whether the pattern holds in each.

solve.answer: Compare the groups within each level of a third variable, and check how group sizes differ across the levels
solve.work: Check for Simpson's paradox: compare within levels of a third variable and look at group sizes. B.

questions.skill: Split data by a third variable: why and how
questions.stem: Across all the vehicles in a dataset, price and odometer reading have a positive correlation, $r=0.35$. Within the cars alone $r=-0.9$, and within the trucks alone $r=-0.85$. The trucks have both higher odometer readings and higher prices. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Within each type, more miles means a lower price; the positive overall $r$ arises because trucks differ from cars
More miles goes with a higher price, because the overall correlation is positive for the whole dataset of vehicles
The overall $r$ is the correct one to report, since the cars and trucks together include every vehicle
Cars and trucks have no relationship between miles and price, since the overall $r$ of 0.35 is such a weak value
questions.answer: Within each type, more miles means a lower price; the positive overall $r$ arises because trucks differ from cars
questions.solution: In each group the relationship is strong and negative. Combining the groups hides it, because trucks have both more miles and higher prices.

solve.answer: Within each type, more miles means a lower price; the positive overall $r$ arises because trucks differ from cars
solve.work: Within each type, negative relation; the overall positive r comes from the trucks being higher on both (Simpson-like aggregation). C.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: how the sample was chosen
questions.stem: A survey was mailed to 2,000 households. Only 150 households replied, and most of those were people with strong opinions. What is the main concern?
choices: Households with strong opinions reply more truthfully, so the 150 replies are fully reliable on their own as a sample
The households that replied may differ from those that did not, so the results may not represent all households
Only 2,000 households were sent the survey, which is too many for the results to be exact in any case
A survey sent by mail always gives answers that are correct, so only the number of replies is a worry
questions.answer: The households that replied may differ from those that did not, so the results may not represent all households
questions.solution: When few people reply and the repliers are not typical, the results are biased. This is called nonresponse bias.

solve.answer: The households that replied may differ from those that did not, so the results may not represent all households
solve.work: Low response with strong opinions: nonresponse/voluntary bias. A.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: evidence and method
questions.stem: Study 1 randomly assigned 300 patients to a drug or a placebo and found no effect. Study 2 let 300 patients choose whether to take the drug and found a large effect. Which study should you trust more?
choices: Study 2, because patients who choose the drug are the ones who know best whether it works for them
Study 2, because it found an effect and a study that finds no effect is not useful
Study 1, because random assignment makes the two groups alike apart from the drug itself
Neither, because two studies that have the same size can never be compared with each other at all
questions.answer: Study 1, because random assignment makes the two groups alike apart from the drug itself
questions.solution: When patients choose, the people who take the drug may differ in other ways. Random assignment balances such differences, so Study 1 gives stronger evidence.

solve.answer: Study 1, because random assignment makes the two groups alike apart from the drug itself
solve.work: Randomized controlled trial beats self-selection. C.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that matter for a question
questions.stem: A hospital asks whether an exercise program lowers blood pressure. Its dataset has patient ID, age, program (yes or no), blood pressure before, blood pressure after, and zip code. Which analysis uses the relevant variables best?
choices: Plot the zip code against the patient ID number and look for a pattern in the points on the resulting plot
Compare the change in blood pressure for patients in the program and not in it, taking age into account
Compare the blood pressure before the program for patients who live in different zip codes around the hospital
Compare the ID numbers of the patients who joined the program with those who did not join it
questions.answer: Compare the change in blood pressure for patients in the program and not in it, taking age into account
questions.solution: The question is about the change in blood pressure and the program. Age may also matter, so it is a sensible third variable. ID and zip code are not relevant here.

solve.answer: Compare the change in blood pressure for patients in the program and not in it, taking age into account
solve.work: Change in BP by program, accounting for age (relevant variables). A.

questions.skill: Judge a source's credibility: who is behind it
questions.stem: A study of a sugary drink was paid for by the company that makes the drink. The researchers published their data, their methods and who paid, and an independent team repeated the study and got similar results. Which is the most sensible conclusion?
choices: The funder is reason enough to reject it, so the repeated result should be ignored by every reader
Funding never affects results, so the funder does not matter even when the methods are kept hidden
It earns more trust, since the methods are open and an independent team got similar results
The result can be trusted only if the maker's own scientists were the ones who repeated the study
questions.answer: It earns more trust, since the methods are open and an independent team got similar results
questions.solution: A funder is a reason to look harder, not a reason to reject a study automatically. Open data and methods let others check the work, and an independent team getting similar results is strong support. So the result earns more trust.

solve.answer: It earns more trust, since the methods are open and an independent team got similar results
solve.work: Industry funding is a possible source of bias, but open data and methods, disclosed funding and an independent replication with similar results all raise credibility. The best conclusion: it earns more trust.

questions.skill: Split the data by a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: A single best-fit line for all 60 students has a sum of squared residuals of 400. The students are then split by a third variable, and each group gets its own best-fit line, with sums of squared residuals of 90 and 70. By what percent did the total sum of squared residuals fall?
questions.solution: After the split the total is 90 + 70 = 160. The fall is 400 - 160 = 240. As a percent of 400, 240 / 400 = 0.6, which is 60 percent. A large drop like this says the third variable matters for the model.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: A teacher has two numbers for each student: the hours studied and the test score. She wants to see whether more studying goes with higher scores. Which display fits best?
choices: A pie chart
A histogram
A stem-and-leaf plot
A scatter plot
questions.answer: A scatter plot
questions.solution: Each student gives a pair of numbers, and a scatter plot shows how two numbers go together. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, and a histogram or stem-and-leaf plot shows only one variable.

solve.answer: A scatter plot
solve.work: Two quantitative variables per student, looking for an association: scatter plot. Stem-and-leaf, pie and histogram show one variable.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: A coach asked each of 60 students which sport they play: soccer, tennis or swimming. Which display shows how many students play each sport?
choices: A scatter plot with one point for each student
A bar chart with one bar for each sport
A line graph that joins the three sports
A box plot of the 60 answers from the students
questions.answer: A bar chart with one bar for each sport
questions.solution: The sports are categories, and the question is about a count in each category, so a bar chart with one bar per sport fits. A scatter plot needs two numbers, a line graph suits change over time, and a box plot needs numbers.

solve.answer: A bar chart with one bar for each sport
solve.work: One categorical variable with counts per category: a bar chart, one bar per sport. Box plot and scatter plot need numbers; a line graph joining categories is wrong.

questions.skill: Describe the direction and strength of a scatter plot
questions.stem: The points (hours of exercise per week, resting heart rate) are (1, 78), (2, 74), (3, 72), (4, 68) and (5, 65). Which statement describes the pattern?
choices: Heart rate tends to go down as exercise goes up (a negative association)
Heart rate tends to go up as exercise goes up (a positive association)
Heart rate stays about the same whatever the exercise (no association)
Heart rate first goes up and then goes down as exercise goes up (a curve)
questions.answer: Heart rate tends to go down as exercise goes up (a negative association)
questions.solution: As the hours of exercise increase from 1 to 5, the heart rate falls from 78 to 65 with no reversal. This is a negative association.

solve.answer: Heart rate tends to go down as exercise goes up (a negative association)
solve.work: Heart rate 78,74,72,68,65 falls steadily as exercise rises: negative association.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: The points (1, 4), (2, 7), (3, 10), (4, 13) and (5, 16) are plotted on a scatter plot. Which description fits the points?
choices: They lie on a straight line that falls from left to right
They lie on a curve that bends upward more and more
They lie on a straight line that rises from left to right
They are scattered with no pattern that can be seen
questions.answer: They lie on a straight line that rises from left to right
questions.solution: Each time $x$ goes up by 1, $y$ goes up by exactly 3. A constant change in $y$ puts the points on a straight line, and since $y$ increases, the line rises.

solve.answer: They lie on a straight line that rises from left to right
solve.work: y rises by 3 for each step of 1 in x (y=3x+1): points on a straight rising line.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: The vertical axis of a bar chart starts at 90 instead of 0, and the bars show values between 92 and 98. Why can this be misleading?
choices: It makes the bars look much wider than they really are on the page
It makes it impossible to tell the categories on the chart apart
It changes the actual values that each of the bars shows
Small differences between the bars look much bigger than they are
questions.answer: Small differences between the bars look much bigger than they are
questions.solution: When the axis starts at 90, a bar for 98 is drawn 8 units tall and a bar for 92 only 2 units tall, so one looks 4 times as tall as the other. The real values, 98 and 92, are close.

solve.answer: Small differences between the bars look much bigger than they are
solve.work: Truncated axis: bars of 92 and 98 show heights 2 and 8 above 90, so a 6% difference looks like 4 times. Values themselves unchanged.

questions.skill: Read values from a scatter plot or line graph
questions.stem: In a scatter plot of (hours of sleep, test score), these points are plotted: (5, 60), (6, 68), (7, 75) and (8, 83). How many of the points show a test score above 70?
questions.solution: The test scores are 60, 68, 75 and 83. Only 75 and 83 are above 70, so 2 points qualify.

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: A bubble chart shows each student as a bubble. The horizontal position is height, the vertical position is weight, and the size of the bubble shows age in years. Student B's bubble is labeled 15 and student C's bubble is labeled 9. How many years older is student B than student C?
questions.solution: The size of the bubble shows age, so B is 15 and C is 9 years old. The difference is $15-9=6$ years.

solve.work: Bubble size encodes age; B is 15, C is 9. 15-9 = 6 years.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: A scatter plot shows (temperature in degrees, ice cream cones sold): (60, 100), (70, 150), (80, 200) and (90, 250). The points lie on a line. How many more cones are sold for each 1 degree increase in temperature?
questions.solution: When the temperature goes up by 10 degrees, sales go up by 50 cones. For 1 degree, sales go up by $50\div 10=5$ cones.

solve.work: Slope = (250-100)/(90-60) = 150/30 = 5 cones per degree (each 10 degrees adds 50).

questions.skill: Read values from a scatter plot or line graph
questions.stem: A line graph shows the temperature at each hour: 20 degrees at 1 pm, 24 at 2 pm, 28 at 3 pm, 26 at 4 pm and 22 at 5 pm. By how many degrees did the temperature rise from 1 pm to its highest point?
questions.solution: The highest point on the line is 28 degrees, at 3 pm. The rise from 20 degrees is $28-20=8$ degrees.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: In a scatter plot of height (horizontal) against weight (vertical) for 30 people, each point is colored blue for an adult and red for a child. What does the color of a point show?
choices: Whether the person is an adult or a child, a third variable
The person's weight, which the vertical position already shows
The person's height, which the horizontal position already shows
How many people have exactly that height and weight
questions.answer: Whether the person is an adult or a child, a third variable
questions.solution: Height and weight are shown by the position of the point. The color adds a third variable: whether the person is an adult or a child.

solve.answer: Whether the person is an adult or a child, a third variable
solve.work: Position shows height and weight; color encodes adult vs child, a third (categorical) variable.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: A city records the noon temperature on every day of one year and wants to show how the temperature changes over the year. Which display fits best?
choices: A pie chart with one slice for each month, sized by that month's average noon temperature
A line graph with the date on the horizontal axis and the temperature on the vertical axis
A histogram that counts how many days fall in each temperature range during the year
A single box plot that sums up all 365 noon temperatures as a five-number summary
questions.answer: A line graph with the date on the horizontal axis and the temperature on the vertical axis
questions.solution: The question is about change over time, so the date goes on the horizontal axis and the points are joined in order: a line graph. A pie chart, a histogram and a box plot all lose the order of the days.

solve.answer: A line graph with the date on the horizontal axis and the temperature on the vertical axis
solve.work: Change over time of a time-ordered variable: line graph with date on x and temperature on y. Pie, single box plot and histogram lose the time order.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: Which pair of measurements is best displayed on a scatter plot?
choices: The favorite color of each of 30 students, chosen from a list of five different colors
The number of students in each of five school clubs, counted at the start of September
The score of each of 30 students on one test that the whole class took on one day
The height and the arm span of each of 30 students, both measured on the same day
questions.answer: The height and the arm span of each of 30 students, both measured on the same day
questions.solution: A scatter plot needs two numbers for each person or item. Only the height and arm span give two numbers for each student; the other pairs give one category or one number per item.

solve.answer: The height and the arm span of each of 30 students, both measured on the same day
solve.work: A scatter plot needs two quantitative variables measured on the same individuals: height and arm span of each student. Others are one variable or categorical.

questions.skill: Describe the direction and strength of a scatter plot
questions.stem: Four scatter plots have the correlation coefficients below. Which one shows the strongest negative linear association?
questions.solution: A negative association has a negative $r$, and the strongest one is the negative value closest to $-1$. That is $-0.92$. The value 0.97 is strong, but positive.

solve.work: Strongest negative: most negative r closest to -1, i.e. -0.92.

questions.skill: Describe the direction and strength of a scatter plot
questions.stem: As the age of a used car increases, its price tends to fall, and the points on a scatter plot of the two follow a tight line. Which description is best?
choices: A strong positive linear association
A strong negative linear association
A weak negative linear association
No association between age and price
questions.answer: A strong negative linear association
questions.solution: Price goes down as age goes up, so the association is negative. The points follow a tight line, so it is strong.

solve.answer: A strong negative linear association
solve.work: Price falls as age rises (negative) and points follow a tight line (strong, linear).

questions.skill: Describe the direction and strength of a scatter plot
questions.stem: A scatter plot of students' shoe sizes against their birth months looks like a patternless cloud of points. Which value of $r$ is most likely?
questions.solution: A patternless cloud means there is almost no linear association, so $r$ is close to 0.

solve.work: Patternless cloud means r near 0: r = 0.03.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: The points $(0, 5)$, $(1, 8)$, $(2, 11)$ and $(3, 14)$ lie on a line. What is the $y$-value on the line when $x=5$?
questions.solution: Each step of 1 in $x$ adds 3 to $y$, and $y=5$ at $x=0$. At $x=5$, $y=5+3\times 5=20$.

solve.work: Slope 3, intercept 5: y = 3x + 5; at x = 5, y = 20.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: A line on a scatter plot starts at $(0, 3)$ and rises 4 units for every 1 unit to the right. Which equation describes the line?
questions.solution: The slope is the rise per 1 unit to the right, which is 4, and the $y$-intercept is 3. So $y=4x+3$.

questions.skill: Describe a non-linear relationship
questions.stem: The number of bacteria in a dish is 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 at hours 1 to 5. Which description of a scatter plot of these points is best?
choices: A curve that bends upward, rising faster and faster, so the relationship is not linear
A straight line that rises by the same amount in each hour, so the relationship is linear
A curve that rises at first and then falls back down again, like the shape of a hill
A flat line that stays at the same height, since all of the numbers are positive
questions.answer: A curve that bends upward, rising faster and faster, so the relationship is not linear
questions.solution: The values double each hour: the increases are 2, 4, 8, 16, which grow. A graph that rises faster and faster is a curve, not a line.

solve.answer: A curve that bends upward, rising faster and faster, so the relationship is not linear
solve.work: Doubling each hour: exponential, curve bending upward, not linear.

questions.skill: Describe a non-linear relationship
questions.stem: In which set of points does $y$ change by the same amount each time $x$ goes up by 1?
questions.solution: In the first set $y$ goes up by 3 each time, so the points are on a line. In the others the changes are 2, 4, 8 or 3, 5, 7 or $-10$, $-5$, $-2.5$, which are not constant.

solve.work: C: 2,5,8,11 differ by 3 each time (linear). A doubles, B squares, D halves.

questions.skill: Describe a non-linear relationship
questions.stem: The points $(1, 100)$, $(2, 50)$, $(3, 25)$ and $(4, 12.5)$ fall along a curve. Each $y$-value is the one before it multiplied by the same number. What is that number?
questions.solution: Divide any $y$-value by the one before it: $50\div 100=0.5$. Check: $50\times 0.5=25$ and $25\times 0.5=12.5$.

questions.skill: Spot and judge outliers
questions.stem: The points $(1, 2)$, $(2, 4)$, $(3, 6)$, $(4, 8)$ and $(5, 30)$ are plotted. One point is far from the pattern of the others. What is the $x$-value of that point?
questions.solution: The first four points lie on the line $y=2x$. At $x=5$ the line gives 10, but the point is at 30, far away. The outlier has $x=5$.

solve.work: Others follow y = 2x; (5,30) should be (5,10). x = 5.

questions.skill: Spot and judge outliers
questions.stem: In a scatter plot, what is an outlier?
choices: A point that lies far away from the overall pattern formed by the other points
The point that has the greatest $x$-value of all of the points shown in the plot
Any point that lies exactly on a line drawn through the middle of the other points
The first point that was recorded when the data were being collected for the plot
questions.answer: A point that lies far away from the overall pattern formed by the other points
questions.solution: An outlier is a point that stands apart from the pattern of the rest of the data. Being the largest, on the line, or the first recorded does not make a point an outlier.

solve.answer: A point that lies far away from the overall pattern formed by the other points
solve.work: Outlier: a point far from the overall pattern of the others.

questions.skill: Spot and judge outliers
questions.stem: In a scatter plot of the hours of sleep that students get on a school night, one student is listed as sleeping 80 hours. What should the analyst do first?
choices: Leave it in without a check, because every value must always be used in every analysis
Delete it quietly, because a point far from the others never belongs in a data set
Check whether it is a mistake in the data, then fix it or explain why it was left out
Change it to the mean of the other values without telling the readers of the report
questions.answer: Check whether it is a mistake in the data, then fix it or explain why it was left out
questions.solution: No one sleeps 80 hours, so this is probably a data-entry error. The analyst should check it, and either correct it or say why it was removed, rather than hide the change.

solve.answer: Check whether it is a mistake in the data, then fix it or explain why it was left out
solve.work: 80 hours of sleep in a night is impossible: check for a data error, then correct or explain exclusion.

questions.skill: Read values from a scatter plot or line graph
questions.stem: A scatter plot shows the points $(1, 5)$, $(2, 9)$, $(3, 12)$, $(4, 18)$ and $(5, 20)$. How many of the points have an $x$-value greater than 2 and a $y$-value less than 19?
questions.solution: The points with $x>2$ are $(3, 12)$, $(4, 18)$ and $(5, 20)$. Of these, $(3, 12)$ and $(4, 18)$ have $y<19$. That is 2 points.

questions.skill: Read values from a scatter plot or line graph
questions.stem: A line graph shows the numbers of customers on Monday to Friday: 12, 15, 9, 14 and 18. Which day shows the biggest increase from the day before?
choices: Thursday
Tuesday
Wednesday
Friday
questions.answer: Thursday
questions.solution: The changes from the day before are Tuesday $+3$, Wednesday $-6$, Thursday $+5$ and Friday $+4$. The biggest increase is on Thursday.

solve.answer: Thursday
solve.work: Changes: Tue +3, Wed -6, Thu +5, Fri +4. Biggest increase Thursday.

questions.skill: Read values from a scatter plot or line graph
questions.stem: The points of a graph are $(1, 4)$, $(2, 7)$, $(3, 6)$, $(4, 12)$ and $(5, 15)$. Between which two neighboring values of $x$ does $y$ go down?
choices: From $x=1$ to $x=2$
From $x=3$ to $x=4$
From $x=2$ to $x=3$
From $x=4$ to $x=5$
questions.answer: From $x=2$ to $x=3$
questions.solution: The $y$-values go 4, 7, 6, 12, 15. Only the step from 7 to 6 is a decrease, which is from $x=2$ to $x=3$.

solve.answer: From $x=2$ to $x=3$
solve.work: y: 4,7,6,12,15; goes down only from x=2 (7) to x=3 (6).

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: A scatter plot shows height (horizontal) and weight (vertical) for each student. How can the plot also show each student's grade level, a third variable?
choices: Join the points of the plot with line segments, in the order in which the students were measured
Draw a second copy of the same points on top of the first, so that each student appears twice
Replace the weight axis with the grade level, so that only two of the variables are shown
Color each point by grade level, or give each grade level its own shape of point
questions.answer: Color each point by grade level, or give each grade level its own shape of point
questions.solution: Color, shape and size of the points can carry an extra variable. The other choices either add nothing or give up one of the variables.

solve.answer: Color each point by grade level, or give each grade level its own shape of point
solve.work: Encode the categorical third variable with color or point shape.

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: In a bubble chart the AREA of each bubble shows the population of a country. Country P's bubble has 3 times the area of country Q's bubble. Country Q has 5 million people. How many million people does country P have?
questions.solution: Area shows population, so 3 times the area means 3 times the population: $3\times 5=15$ million.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: In a treemap, the area of each rectangle shows an amount. The rectangle for food has an area of 4 square units and stands for 200 dollars. The rectangle for rent has an area of 12 square units. How many dollars does rent stand for?
questions.solution: Each square unit stands for $200\div 4=50$ dollars. Rent has 12 square units, so it stands for $12\times 50=600$ dollars.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot has the stem 7. Class A's leaves on this stem are 2 and 5. Class B's leaves are 0, 1 and 8. Each leaf is a ones digit, so 7 | 2 means 72. What is the highest score of class B on this stem minus the highest score of class A on it?
questions.solution: Class B's highest score on the stem is 78. Class A's is 75. The difference is $78-75=3$.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A bar graph has no title and no labels on its axes. What is the main problem for a reader?
choices: The reader cannot tell what the bars measure or what units are used
The bars have to be drawn too tall when there are no labels to limit their size
The data on the bars must have been collected in a careless way by the writer
The reader will think that all of the bars have the same height as each other
questions.answer: The reader cannot tell what the bars measure or what units are used
questions.solution: Without a title and axis labels, no one can tell what is being measured or in what units, so the graph cannot be interpreted.

solve.answer: The reader cannot tell what the bars measure or what units are used
solve.work: Without title and axis labels the reader cannot tell what is measured or in what units.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A graph of a store's monthly sales shows only the three months in which sales went up, and leaves out the nine months in which sales went down. What is the problem?
choices: It shows too few points, because a graph must always have at least twelve points
It uses months on the horizontal axis, which can never be used for a sales graph
It shows only some of the data, picked to give a false picture of the whole year
It makes the sales look lower than they were, because it leaves out the best months
questions.answer: It shows only some of the data, picked to give a false picture of the whole year
questions.solution: Showing only the good months is cherry-picking: the picture suggests sales rose all year when they mostly fell.

solve.answer: It shows only some of the data, picked to give a false picture of the whole year
solve.work: Cherry-picking: showing only months with rises gives a false picture of the year.

questions.skill: Describe the direction and strength of a scatter plot
questions.stem: Five scatter plots have the correlation coefficients $0.8$, $-0.9$, $0.15$, $-0.5$ and $0.6$. Which coefficient goes with the weakest linear association?
questions.solution: Strength depends on how far $r$ is from 0, not on its sign. The distances from 0 are 0.8, 0.9, 0.15, 0.5 and 0.6. The smallest is 0.15, so $r=0.15$ is the weakest.

solve.work: Weakest linear association = smallest |r|: |0.8|, |-0.9|, |0.15|, |-0.5|, |0.6|. Smallest is 0.15.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: For each of 200 houses, a real estate agent has the size in square feet, the price, and whether the house is in the city or in the suburbs. Which single display shows all three variables?
choices: A pie chart that splits all of the 200 houses into the city houses and the suburb houses
A scatter plot of price against size, with city and suburb houses in different colors
A histogram of the prices of all 200 houses, with no other information shown on the chart
A bar chart with one bar for the average size of all of the 200 houses in the sample
questions.answer: A scatter plot of price against size, with city and suburb houses in different colors
questions.solution: Price and size are two numbers, so they go on the two axes of a scatter plot. Using a different color for city and suburb adds the third variable. The other displays show only one or two of the variables.

solve.answer: A scatter plot of price against size, with city and suburb houses in different colors
solve.work: Size (numeric), price (numeric) and location (categorical): a scatter plot of price vs size with color for city/suburb shows all three. The others show one variable.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: Which question is best answered by comparing side-by-side box plots?
choices: Do students in grade 9 usually sleep more than students in grade 12?
How are hours of study and test scores related for the students in one class?
What share of the students in a school ride the bus to school each day?
How did the number of absences change from month to month during a year?
questions.answer: Do students in grade 9 usually sleep more than students in grade 12?
questions.solution: Side-by-side box plots compare the spread of one numeric variable (hours of sleep) across groups (grades). Study hours and scores need a scatter plot, a share needs a pie or bar chart, and change over months needs a line graph.

solve.answer: Do students in grade 9 usually sleep more than students in grade 12?
solve.work: Side-by-side box plots compare a numerical variable across groups: sleep for grade 9 vs grade 12. Bus share is a proportion; study vs score is a scatter plot; month-to-month change is a line graph.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: The points (hours of practice, number of mistakes) are (1, 9), (2, 7), (3, 5) and (4, 3), and they lie on a line. By how much does the number of mistakes change for each extra hour of practice? (Write a decrease as a negative number.)
questions.solution: From 1 hour to 4 hours, the mistakes go from 9 to 3, a change of $3-9=-6$ over 3 hours. That is $-6\div 3=-2$ per hour: 2 fewer mistakes for each extra hour.

solve.work: Mistakes 9,7,5,3: change of -2 per extra hour.

questions.skill: Describe a non-linear relationship
questions.stem: The points (0, 16), (1, 9), (2, 4), (3, 1), (4, 0), (5, 1) and (6, 4) are plotted. Which description fits the pattern?
choices: The pattern is linear and negative: $y$ gets smaller as $x$ gets larger
The pattern is linear and positive: $y$ gets larger as $x$ gets larger
The pattern is curved: $y$ falls and then rises, so it is not linear
The pattern is random: there is no relationship between $x$ and $y$
questions.answer: The pattern is curved: $y$ falls and then rises, so it is not linear
questions.solution: The $y$-values fall from 16 to 0 and then rise again, so the points follow a U-shaped curve. A straight line cannot do that. There is a clear relationship, so it is not random.

solve.answer: The pattern is curved: $y$ falls and then rises, so it is not linear
solve.work: y = (x-4)^2: 16,9,4,1,0,1,4 falls to 0 at x=4 then rises. Curved, not linear, not random.

questions.skill: Describe the direction and strength of a scatter plot
questions.stem: Two scatter plots show hours of practice (horizontal) and number of mistakes (vertical). In plot A the points follow a tight line that falls from left to right. In plot B the points also fall from left to right, but they are spread widely around the line. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both plots show a negative association, and the association in plot B is stronger
Plot A shows a negative association and plot B shows a positive association
Neither plot shows an association, because the points do not all lie on one line
Both plots show a negative association, and the association in plot A is stronger
questions.answer: Both plots show a negative association, and the association in plot A is stronger
questions.solution: Both clouds fall from left to right, so both are negative. The tighter the points are around a line, the stronger the association, so plot A is stronger.

solve.answer: Both plots show a negative association, and the association in plot A is stronger
solve.work: Both fall left to right: negative. Tighter clustering about the line (A) means stronger association.

questions.skill: Spot and judge outliers
questions.stem: The ages and heights of six children are plotted as the points (age in years, height in centimeters): (4, 100), (5, 108), (6, 115), (7, 123), (8, 130) and (9, 190). One point is far from the pattern of the others. What is the age of that child?
questions.solution: The first five points rise by about 7 or 8 centimeters per year, so at age 9 the height should be near 138. The point (9, 190) is far above that, so it is the outlier, and the child is 9.

solve.work: Heights rise about 7-8 cm per year: 100,108,115,123,130; age 9 would be about 137-138, but it is 190. Outlier age 9.

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: A scatter plot shows fuel use in liters per 100 kilometers (vertical) against engine size in liters (horizontal). The red points are cars: (1.5, 6), (2.0, 8) and (2.5, 10). The blue points are trucks: (2.0, 12), (2.5, 15) and (3.0, 18). At an engine size of 2.5 liters, how many more liters per 100 kilometers does the truck use than the car?
questions.solution: At 2.5 liters, the red car point is at 10 and the blue truck point is at 15. The difference is $15-10=5$ liters per 100 kilometers.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: A bubble chart shows four groups of students. For each group, the horizontal position is hours of study, the vertical position is the average score and the size of the bubble is the number of students. Group A: 2 hours, score 60, 30 students. Group B: 4 hours, score 75, 50 students. Group C: 6 hours, score 88, 20 students. Group D: 8 hours, score 90, 10 students. How many students are in the groups with an average score above 70?
questions.solution: The groups with an average score above 70 are B (75), C (88) and D (90). Their numbers of students are 50, 20 and 10, which add to 80.

solve.work: Average score above 70: B (75, 50 students), C (88, 20), D (90, 10). 50+20+10 = 80. A (60) excluded.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: The vertical axis of a bar chart starts at 70 instead of 0. Company A's bar stops at 100 and company B's bar stops at 80. How many times as tall as B's bar does A's bar look?
questions.solution: The drawn heights are measured from 70: A's bar is $100-70=30$ tall and B's bar is $80-70=10$ tall. A's bar looks $30\div 10=3$ times as tall, although 100 is only 1.25 times 80.

solve.work: Visible bar heights from 70: A 100-70 = 30, B 80-70 = 10. A looks 30/10 = 3 times as tall.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A graph shows that on days when more ice cream is sold at a beach, more swimmers need to be rescued. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Eating ice cream causes the swimming accidents on those days
Hot weather may explain why both ice cream sales and rescues rise
Swimming accidents cause people to buy more ice cream on those days
The data must be wrong, because unrelated things cannot rise together
questions.answer: Hot weather may explain why both ice cream sales and rescues rise
questions.solution: Hot weather brings more people to the beach, so both numbers can rise together without either causing the other. A pattern in a graph does not show cause and effect by itself.

solve.answer: Hot weather may explain why both ice cream sales and rescues rise
solve.work: Association does not imply causation; hot weather is a likely lurking variable raising both.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: A researcher has the commute times of 100 workers in each of four cities. She wants to compare the typical commute time and the spread of the times across the four cities. Which display is best?
choices: Side-by-side box plots, one for each city, drawn on the same time scale
One pie chart with four slices, where each slice shows the total commute time of a city
A scatter plot with the city name on one axis and the worker's number on the other axis
A line graph that joins the average commute times of the cities in alphabetical order
questions.answer: Side-by-side box plots, one for each city, drawn on the same time scale
questions.solution: Box plots show the median and the spread of each group, and putting them side by side on one scale makes the cities easy to compare. The other displays hide the spread or invent an order that does not exist.

solve.answer: Side-by-side box plots, one for each city, drawn on the same time scale
solve.work: Comparing center and spread of a quantitative variable across 4 groups: side-by-side box plots on a common scale.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: A researcher measured 4 variables on each student. She wants a scatter plot of every pair of different variables, with each pair shown once (so a plot of A against B is the same pair as B against A). How many scatter plots is that?
questions.solution: The pairs of 4 variables are AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD. In general there are $\frac{4\times 3}{2}=6$ pairs.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: Data for 500 students: hours of sleep, hours of screen time and grade level (9, 10, 11 or 12). A counselor wants to see how sleep and screen time are related and whether that relationship differs between grade levels. Which display is best?
choices: A pie chart with four slices, one for each grade level, sized by the number of its students
One histogram of the hours of sleep for all of the 500 students taken together as a group
A scatter plot of sleep against screen time, with the points colored by grade level
A bar chart that shows the average hours of screen time for each of the four grade levels
questions.answer: A scatter plot of sleep against screen time, with the points colored by grade level
questions.solution: Two numerical variables call for a scatter plot, and color can carry the third variable, the grade level. Each other display leaves out at least one of the three variables.

solve.answer: A scatter plot of sleep against screen time, with the points colored by grade level
solve.work: Two quantitative variables (sleep, screen time) plus a categorical third (grade): scatter plot with points colored by grade.

questions.skill: Describe the direction and strength of a scatter plot
questions.stem: Plot A has the correlation coefficient $r=-0.7$ and plot B has $r=0.5$. Which statement is correct?
choices: Plot A has the stronger linear association, and it is negative; plot B has a weaker positive one
Plot B has the stronger linear association, because 0.5 is greater than $-0.7$ and is positive
Plot A has the weaker linear association, because a negative value always means a weaker one
Neither plot shows a linear association, because both values are far from 1 and from $-1$
questions.answer: Plot A has the stronger linear association, and it is negative; plot B has a weaker positive one
questions.solution: Strength depends on how far $r$ is from 0, not on its sign. Since $|-0.7|>|0.5|$, plot A is stronger. The sign gives the direction: plot A falls and plot B rises.

solve.answer: Plot A has the stronger linear association, and it is negative; plot B has a weaker positive one
solve.work: |-0.7| = 0.7 > 0.5, so A is stronger and negative; B is weaker and positive.

questions.skill: Describe the direction and strength of a scatter plot
questions.stem: Five scatter plots have the correlation coefficients $0.9$, $-0.95$, $0.3$, $-0.5$ and $0.6$. Call a linear association strong when $r$ is at least $0.8$ or at most $-0.8$. How many of the five plots show a strong association?
questions.solution: The values 0.9 and $-0.95$ are at least 0.8 or at most $-0.8$. The other three are not. So 2 plots are strong.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: The points of a scatter plot lie on a line through $(0, 50)$ and $(10, 120)$, where $x$ is the number of years since 2010 and $y$ is the number of subscribers in thousands. If the line continues, how many thousands of subscribers does it predict at $x=15$?
questions.solution: The rate is $\frac{120-50}{10}=7$ thousand per year. At $x=15$, $y=50+7\times 15=155$.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: A line fitted to a scatter plot of used cars is $\text{price}=25000-1800\times \text{age}$, with price in dollars and age in years. Which sentence explains the number 1800?
choices: Each extra year of age goes with a predicted price about 1,800 dollars higher than before
Each extra year of age goes with a predicted price about 1,800 dollars lower
A brand-new car, with an age of 0 years, is predicted to cost only about 1,800 dollars
Each extra 1,800 dollars of price goes with a car that is about one year older than before
questions.answer: Each extra year of age goes with a predicted price about 1,800 dollars lower
questions.solution: The slope is $-1800$: for each additional year of age the predicted price changes by $-1800$ dollars, that is, it is 1,800 dollars lower.

solve.answer: Each extra year of age goes with a predicted price about 1,800 dollars lower
solve.work: Slope -1800: each extra year of age predicts a price about $1,800 lower.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: A fitted line predicts $\hat{y}=3x+12$. At $x=5$ the actual value is $y=31$. What is the residual (actual minus predicted)?
questions.solution: The predicted value is $3\times 5+12=27$. The residual is $31-27=4$.

questions.skill: Describe a non-linear relationship
questions.stem: The $y$-values at $x=0, 1, 2, 3$ are 3, 6, 12 and 24. Each $y$-value is the one before it multiplied by the same number. If the pattern continues, what is $y$ at $x=5$?
questions.solution: Each value is multiplied by 2: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96. So $y=96$ at $x=5$.

questions.skill: Describe a non-linear relationship
questions.stem: The points $(-2, 4)$, $(-1, 1)$, $(0, 0)$, $(1, 1)$ and $(2, 4)$ have a correlation coefficient of exactly $r=0$. Which statement is correct?
choices: There is no relationship of any kind, because the correlation coefficient is exactly zero
There is no linear association, but the points show a strong curved relationship
There is a strong linear association, because the points are symmetric about the $y$-axis
There is a negative association, because the first points have the larger $y$-values
questions.answer: There is no linear association, but the points show a strong curved relationship
questions.solution: These points lie exactly on the curve $y=x^2$, a strong relationship. The correlation coefficient measures only linear association, so it can be 0 even when the points follow a curve.

solve.answer: There is no linear association, but the points show a strong curved relationship
solve.work: Points lie on y = x^2: no linear association (r = 0) but a strong curved relationship.

questions.skill: Spot and judge outliers
questions.stem: The points of a scatter plot follow a tight line that rises from left to right, except for one point far above the line near the middle. What happens to $r$ if that one point is removed?
choices: It gets closer to 0, because fewer points always means that there is less of a pattern
It gets closer to 1, because the remaining points follow the line more closely
It stays exactly the same, because one point out of many cannot change the value of $r$
It becomes negative, because the removed point was pulling the line upward at its middle
questions.answer: It gets closer to 1, because the remaining points follow the line more closely
questions.solution: The outlier pulls the points away from a line and weakens the correlation. Without it the points are nearer to the line, so $r$ moves closer to 1.

solve.answer: It gets closer to 1, because the remaining points follow the line more closely
solve.work: The point far off the line weakens r; removing it leaves points tightly on a rising line, so r moves closer to 1.

questions.skill: Read values from a scatter plot or line graph
questions.stem: A line graph shows a town's population: 12,000 in 2000, 15,000 in 2005, 21,000 in 2010 and 24,000 in 2015. What is the average rate of change from 2005 to 2015, in people per year?
questions.solution: The population grew by $24000-15000=9000$ in 10 years, so the average rate is $9000\div 10=900$ people per year.

questions.skill: Read values from a scatter plot or line graph
questions.stem: A scatter plot shows the hours of sleep at various ages: 8.5 hours at age 14 and 8 hours at age 18. Estimate the hours of sleep at age 16 by assuming the line segment between those two points.
questions.solution: Age 16 is halfway between 14 and 18, so the estimate is halfway between 8.5 and 8: $\frac{8.5+8}{2}=8.25$.

solve.work: Age 16 is the midpoint of 14 and 18: (8.5 + 8)/2 = 8.25 hours.

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: A scatter plot colors girls red and boys blue. The girls' points follow $y=2x+10$ and the boys' points follow $y=3x+4$. At what value of $x$ do the two lines give the same $y$?
questions.solution: Set $2x+10=3x+4$. Then $10-4=3x-2x$, so $x=6$. (Both lines give $y=22$ there.)

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: A scatter plot shows weekly hours of study (horizontal) and test score (vertical) for students at three schools, with one color for each school. Which question can be answered only by using the colors?
choices: Does the link between study hours and score look different from school to school?
Do students who study more hours tend to have higher scores, over all of the points shown?
What are the lowest and highest test scores among all of the students in the plot?
How many students in all are shown, counting every one of the points in the plot?
questions.answer: Does the link between study hours and score look different from school to school?
questions.solution: Only the colors tell which school each student attends, so only the first question needs them. The others can be answered by looking at all the points together.

solve.answer: Does the link between study hours and score look different from school to school?
solve.work: Only the colors separate schools, so only the question comparing the relationship across schools needs them.

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: On a scatter plot of age (horizontal) against income (vertical), each point is shaded darker for more years of education. The points at the upper right are the darkest. Which conclusion do the data support?
choices: More education causes people to earn more and to grow older, in every group of people anywhere
Older people always have more years of education than younger people do, in every group
In these data, people who are older and earn more also tend to have more years of education
The shading shows that years of education have no link with either the age or the income
questions.answer: In these data, people who are older and earn more also tend to have more years of education
questions.solution: Dark points at the upper right show that older, higher-earning people tend to have more education here. Such a plot shows an association in these data, not a cause, and not a rule for everyone.

solve.answer: In these data, people who are older and earn more also tend to have more years of education
solve.work: Association only, in these data: older, higher-income people tend to have more education. No causation or "always".

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: On a vertical axis with a log scale, the gridlines are labeled 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 and are equally spaced. Point P sits on the line labeled 10, and point Q sits two gridlines higher. How many times as large as P's value is Q's value?
questions.solution: Q is on the line labeled 1,000. Each gridline up multiplies the value by 10, so two gridlines multiply it by $10\times 10=100$.

solve.work: P at 10; two gridlines higher is 1,000; 1000/10 = 100.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: A heat map shows the average number of customers for each day of the week (rows) and each hour of the day (columns). A darker cell means more customers. The darkest cell is in the Saturday row at 12 noon. Which statement is supported?
choices: Among the day-and-hour cells shown, Saturday at noon had the highest average number of customers
Saturday was the busiest day of the whole week at every one of the hours that are shown in the map
More customers visit at noon than at any other hour on every one of the days of the week
The darkest cell shows the total number of customers who visited the store in the whole week
questions.answer: Among the day-and-hour cells shown, Saturday at noon had the highest average number of customers
questions.solution: The darkest cell is the one with the largest value, so Saturday at noon had the highest average among the cells. It says nothing about every hour, every day or a weekly total.

solve.answer: Among the day-and-hour cells shown, Saturday at noon had the highest average number of customers
solve.work: Darkest cell = highest average among the day-hour cells shown: Saturday at noon.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: In a parallel coordinates plot, each student is one line through three vertical axes: math, reading and science scores. The lines of students P and Q cross between the math axis and the reading axis. What does the crossing mean?
choices: P and Q have identical scores in all three of the subjects that are shown
The two students were measured on different days of the school term
P scored higher than Q in one of the two subjects and lower in the other
P's scores and Q's scores are both outliers in the data set of the class
questions.answer: P scored higher than Q in one of the two subjects and lower in the other
questions.solution: Two lines cross between two axes when their order switches: one student is higher on the first axis and lower on the next.

solve.answer: P scored higher than Q in one of the two subjects and lower in the other
solve.work: Lines crossing between two axes means their order reverses: P higher in one subject, lower in the other.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A bar graph's vertical axis does not start at 0. The bars show 80 and 50, but the taller bar looks 3 times as tall as the shorter bar. At what value does the axis start?
questions.solution: If the axis starts at $b$, the drawn heights are $80-b$ and $50-b$, and $80-b=3(50-b)$. Then $80-b=150-3b$, so $2b=70$ and $b=35$.

solve.work: Drawn heights 80 - s and 50 - s with 80 - s = 3(50 - s) -> 2s = 70 -> s = 35.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A line graph shows a company's sales for the years 2010, 2011, 2012, 2015 and 2020, with those years spaced equally along the horizontal axis. Why is this misleading?
choices: Years should never be put on a horizontal axis, because time is not a number in a graph
Equal spacing for unequal gaps in time distorts how fast the sales appear to change
A line graph can show at most four points, and this graph is trying to show five of them
The years 2015 and 2020 are too recent to be shown together with the years before them
questions.answer: Equal spacing for unequal gaps in time distorts how fast the sales appear to change
questions.solution: The gaps are 1, 1, 3 and 5 years but are drawn as equal. A slow change over 5 years looks as fast as a change over 1 year.

solve.answer: Equal spacing for unequal gaps in time distorts how fast the sales appear to change
solve.work: Equal spacing for gaps of 1,1,3,5 years distorts apparent rates of change.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A graph puts two unrelated quantities on one chart, each with its own vertical axis scale chosen by the designer so that the two lines nearly overlap. What is the problem?
choices: Two lines on one chart always cancel out each other's changes, so nothing can be read
Different scales on one chart are never allowed, so the lines must have been drawn wrongly
Lines that overlap on a chart always show that the two quantities have identical values
Choosing the scales can make unrelated quantities look closely connected
questions.answer: Choosing the scales can make unrelated quantities look closely connected
questions.solution: With two separate scales the designer can stretch either line to match the other, which suggests a link that may not exist.

solve.answer: Choosing the scales can make unrelated quantities look closely connected
solve.work: Dual axes with chosen scales can make unrelated series look related.

questions.skill: Spot and judge outliers
questions.stem: A line is fitted to a scatter plot. The residuals have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 3. A point is called an outlier if its residual is more than 2 standard deviations from 0, above or below. Six points have the residuals $1$, $-7$, $4$, $5$, $-2$ and $8$. How many of the points are outliers?
questions.solution: Two standard deviations is 6, so a point is an outlier when its residual is above 6 or below -6. Of the six residuals, only -7 and 8 are beyond that. So there are 2 outliers.

solve.work: 2 SD = 6. Residuals with |e| > 6: -7 and 8. 1, 4, 5, -2 are within. Count = 2.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: A school counts how many students in each of two grades choose each of four lunch options. It wants to compare the percent choosing each option in the two grades, although the grades have different numbers of students. Which display is best?
choices: Two bars, one for each grade, each split into four colored percent segments
A scatter plot of grade against lunch option with one point for each student
One pie chart that adds the counts of both grades into a single circle
A line graph that joins the four lunch options in the order they are listed
questions.answer: Two bars, one for each grade, each split into four colored percent segments
questions.solution: Showing each grade as a bar split into percent segments puts the two grades on the same scale of 100 percent, so the shares can be compared even though the grades differ in size. A single combined pie chart hides the difference between the grades, and the other two displays do not suit categories.

solve.answer: Two bars, one for each grade, each split into four colored percent segments
solve.work: Comparing percents across groups of different size: a segmented (100%) bar per grade, split into the four options. A combined pie loses the grade split; scatter and line graphs do not fit categorical data.

questions.skill: Describe a non-linear relationship
questions.stem: A straight line was fitted to a scatter plot. The residuals (actual value minus predicted value) of the 7 points, from left to right, are +3, +1, -2, -4, -2, +1, +3. What does this pattern show?
choices: The residuals add up to 0, so the line is a good model for all of the data
The residuals are a mix of positive and negative, so there is no relationship
The residuals form a U shape, so the data are curved and a line fits poorly
The residuals are all fairly small, so the relationship is exactly linear
questions.answer: The residuals form a U shape, so the data are curved and a line fits poorly
questions.solution: The residuals of a least-squares line always add to 0, so that alone does not show a good fit. Here they are positive, then negative, then positive again in a U shape. A curved pattern in the residuals means the relationship is curved and a straight line misses it.

solve.answer: The residuals form a U shape, so the data are curved and a line fits poorly
solve.work: Residuals +3,+1,-2,-4,-2,+1,+3: positive at the ends, negative in the middle, a U shape, so the relationship is curved and a line is a poor model. (They sum to 0, as least-squares residuals do, which says nothing about fit.)

questions.skill: Spot and judge outliers
questions.stem: The line $y=2x+8$ passes exactly through the points $(1, 10)$, $(2, 12)$, $(3, 14)$, $(4, 16)$ and $(5, 18)$. A sixth point, $(6, 50)$, is an outlier. By how much does the actual $y$-value of the sixth point differ from the $y$-value the line gives at $x=6$ (actual minus line)?
questions.solution: At $x=6$ the line gives $2\cdot 6+8=20$. The actual value is 50, so the difference is $50-20=30$.

questions.skill: Spot and judge outliers
questions.stem: The numbers of steps, in thousands, taken in a day by five people are 6, 7, 8, 7 and 22. The value 22 is an outlier. By how much does the mean decrease when the outlier is removed?
questions.solution: With all five values the mean is $\frac{50}{5}=10$. Without 22 the mean is $\frac{28}{4}=7$. The mean decreases by $10-7=3$ thousand steps.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: In a stacked bar chart, one bar is made of three colored segments. The red segment runs from 0 to 20 on the vertical axis, the blue segment runs from 20 to 50, and the green segment runs from 50 to 65. How many units does the blue segment represent?
questions.solution: A segment in a stacked bar represents its own length, not the value at its top. The blue segment starts at 20 and ends at 50, so it represents $50-20=30$ units.

solve.work: Stacked segments: blue runs 20 to 50, so 50-20 = 30 units.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: A graph has two vertical axes. The left axis shows rainfall in centimeters from 0 to 30 and goes with the bars. The right axis shows temperature in degrees from 50 to 90 and goes with the line. In July the line is drawn higher than the top of the bar. A reader says, "The temperature was greater than the rainfall." What is wrong with this reading?
choices: A line can never be drawn higher than a bar when a graph shows two different things
Nothing is wrong, because the point drawn higher on the graph always has the larger value
The temperature axis should start at 0, and then the line would really be lower than the bar
The bar and the line use different axes and units, so their heights cannot be compared
questions.answer: The bar and the line use different axes and units, so their heights cannot be compared
questions.solution: The bar is read on the rainfall axis and the line on the temperature axis. Rainfall in centimeters and temperature in degrees are different quantities with different scales, so where they sit relative to each other on the page says nothing about which is greater.

solve.answer: The bar and the line use different axes and units, so their heights cannot be compared
solve.work: Dual-axis chart: bar read on the left (cm, 0-30), line on the right (degrees, 50-90). Different scales and units, so relative heights do not compare the quantities.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A pie chart of the favorite pets of 80 students labels the slices dogs 45 percent, cats 40 percent and fish 25 percent. Taken at face value, how many more students than the 80 surveyed do the labeled slices add up to?
questions.solution: The labels add to $45+40+25=110$ percent, which is 10 percent too much. Ten percent of 80 is 8, so the labels stand for 88 students, which is 8 more than the 80 surveyed. The slices of a pie chart must add to 100 percent.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A news graphic shows the values 10 and 20 as circles. The circle for 10 has a diameter of 2 centimeters and the circle for 20 has a diameter of 4 centimeters. Why is this display misleading?
choices: The larger circle has only twice the area of the smaller one, so it looks too small
The larger circle has 4 times the area of the smaller, but its value is only 2 times as large
Circles cannot be used to show numbers at all, so only bars should ever be used for values
The diameters are not in the same ratio as the values, so the circles are drawn wrongly
questions.answer: The larger circle has 4 times the area of the smaller, but its value is only 2 times as large
questions.solution: The diameters are in the ratio 2 : 4, which matches the values 10 : 20. But area grows with the square of the diameter: $\pi\cdot 1^2$ and $\pi\cdot 2^2$ are in the ratio 1 : 4. The eye reads area, so the larger circle looks 4 times as big for a value that is only 2 times as big.

solve.answer: The larger circle has 4 times the area of the smaller, but its value is only 2 times as large
solve.work: Diameters 2 and 4 are in ratio 1:2, like the values, but areas are in ratio 1:4 (pi*1^2 vs pi*2^2), so the larger value looks 4 times as big though only 2 times.

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: On a scatter plot of all students, hours of study (horizontal) against test score (vertical), the points slope downward overall. When the points are colored by class, the points of each class slope upward. Class A's points are mostly at few study hours and high scores. Class B's points are mostly at many study hours and low scores. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Within each class more study goes with higher scores; the overall slope comes from the classes differing
More study causes lower test scores, as the overall downward slope of all the points shows
The colors hide the real pattern, so only the overall slope of all the points should be trusted
There is no relationship between study hours and test scores in any group of students at all
questions.answer: Within each class more study goes with higher scores; the overall slope comes from the classes differing
questions.solution: Inside each class the trend goes up, so studying goes with higher scores there. The classes themselves differ (one studies little and scores high, the other studies a lot and scores low), and that difference makes the combined plot slope down. Splitting by class shows the real pattern.

solve.answer: Within each class more study goes with higher scores; the overall slope comes from the classes differing
solve.work: Simpson's paradox: within each class the association is positive; the overall downward slope comes from class A (few hours, high scores) and class B (many hours, low scores) differing.

questions.skill: Describe a non-linear relationship
questions.stem: A scatter plot shows $y=64, 32, 16, 8, 4$ at $x=0, 1, 2, 3, 4$, a curve that falls quickly and then levels off. A student draws a straight line through the first point $(0, 64)$ and the last point $(4, 4)$. By how much does the line's value at $x=1$ exceed the actual $y$-value at $x=1$?
questions.solution: The slope of the line is $\frac{4-64}{4-0}=-15$, so at $x=1$ the line gives $64-15=49$. The actual value is 32. The line is higher by $49-32=17$. A straight line fits a curved pattern badly.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: A scatter plot of 50,000 points forms one solid dark blob, because most of the points lie on top of each other. Which change would best show where the points are most crowded?
choices: Make every point larger, so that the individual points can be seen more clearly in the blob
Make the points partly see-through, or color each small region by how many points it holds
Join the points with line segments, in the order in which the data were collected
Remove the vertical axis, so that the shape of the blob is no longer squeezed flat
questions.answer: Make the points partly see-through, or color each small region by how many points it holds
questions.solution: Overlapping points hide density. Partly see-through points, or coloring regions by their counts (a heat map), show where there are many points. Larger points and joining lines make the overlap worse.

solve.answer: Make the points partly see-through, or color each small region by how many points it holds
solve.work: Overplotting: transparency or density shading (binned counts) reveals where points are densest. Larger points worsen it; removing an axis or joining points is wrong.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: For each of 10 years, a company has the percent of its sales that came from each of three product lines (the three percents add to 100 each year). It wants to show how the mix of sales changed over the years. Which display is best?
choices: One pie chart that shows the average percent of the three lines over all ten of the years
A scatter plot of the percent of one product line against the percent of another line
A box plot of the ten yearly percents for the first line, with no axis for the years
A bar for each year, split into three colored segments that show the percents of the lines
questions.answer: A bar for each year, split into three colored segments that show the percents of the lines
questions.solution: Each year's bar is a whole of 100 percent, and the colored segments show how the mix changes from year to year. The other displays drop the years or at least one of the product lines.

solve.answer: A bar for each year, split into three colored segments that show the percents of the lines
solve.work: Parts of a whole changing over years: one 100% stacked bar per year with three segments.

questions.skill: Choose a display for the data and the question
questions.stem: When is it appropriate to join the points of a graph with line segments?
choices: When the horizontal variable is time or another ordered scale and each point follows the one before it
When the points belong to different, unrelated people, whose order in the list does not matter at all
When the two variables have no connection to each other, so that a pattern is not wanted at all
When there are so many points that the individual points are hard to see on the page or screen
questions.answer: When the horizontal variable is time or another ordered scale and each point follows the one before it
questions.solution: Joining points with lines suggests that the value moves from one point to the next, which makes sense for a time series or another ordered scale. For unrelated individuals, a line suggests a connection that is not there.

solve.answer: When the horizontal variable is time or another ordered scale and each point follows the one before it
solve.work: Joining points is meaningful when x is time or an ordered scale and consecutive points follow each other.

questions.skill: Describe the direction and strength of a scatter plot
questions.stem: The correlation between $x$ and $y$ is $r=0.6$. Each $y$-value is then replaced by $10-3y$. What is the correlation between $x$ and the new values?
questions.solution: Multiplying $y$ by a negative number turns the direction around, so the sign of $r$ changes. Adding 10 and multiplying by 3 do not change the strength. The new correlation is $-0.6$.

solve.work: y -> 10 - 3y is a linear transformation with negative slope; |r| unchanged, sign flips: -0.6.

questions.skill: Describe the direction and strength of a scatter plot
questions.stem: For a data set, the correlation coefficient is $r=0.8$. The percent of the variation in $y$ that is accounted for by the linear relationship with $x$ is $r^2$ written as a percent. What is that percent?
questions.solution: Square the correlation: $0.8^2=0.64$, which is 64 percent.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: A line passes through the points $(2, 17)$ and $(6, 41)$ of a scatter plot. At what value of $x$ does the line reach $y=71$?
questions.solution: The slope is $\frac{41-17}{6-2}=6$. From $(2, 17)$ the line must rise $71-17=54$, which takes $54\div 6=9$ units of $x$. So $x=2+9=11$.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: In plot A, $y$ rises 30 when $x$ rises 5. In plot B, $y$ rises 42 when $x$ rises 8. Which statement about the rates of change is correct?
choices: Plot B rises faster, because its total rise of 42 is greater than the total rise of 30 in plot A
The plots rise at the same rate, because in each plot the $y$-values go up as the $x$-values go up
Plot B rises faster, at 8 units of $y$ per unit of $x$, while plot A rises only 5 units of $y$
Plot A rises faster, at 6 units of $y$ per unit of $x$, while plot B rises 5.25 units
questions.answer: Plot A rises faster, at 6 units of $y$ per unit of $x$, while plot B rises 5.25 units
questions.solution: The rate of change is rise divided by run. Plot A: $30\div 5=6$. Plot B: $42\div 8=5.25$. So plot A rises faster.

solve.answer: Plot A rises faster, at 6 units of $y$ per unit of $x$, while plot B rises 5.25 units
solve.work: A: 30/5 = 6 per unit; B: 42/8 = 5.25 per unit. A rises faster.

questions.skill: Describe a linear relationship (rate of change)
questions.stem: A line fitted to a scatter plot of (hours of practice, score) has a slope of 3 points per hour. If practice time were measured in minutes instead (60 minutes in an hour), what would the slope be, in points per minute?
questions.solution: One minute is $\frac{1}{60}$ of an hour, so the score changes by $\frac{3}{60}=0.05$ points per minute.

solve.work: 3 points per hour = 3 points per 60 minutes = 0.05 points per minute.

questions.skill: Describe a non-linear relationship
questions.stem: The $y$-values at $x=0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ are 2, 3, 6, 11 and 18. The amounts by which $y$ goes up from one $x$ to the next themselves go up by the same amount each time. If the pattern continues, what is $y$ at $x=5$?
questions.solution: The increases are 1, 3, 5 and 7, so each increase is 2 more than the one before. The next increase is 9, so $y=18+9=27$.

questions.skill: Describe a non-linear relationship
questions.stem: The number of students who have heard a rumor is small at first, then climbs quickly, and then levels off near 200 (the whole school). Which description of a scatter plot of the data is best?
choices: A straight line that rises steadily, so a single slope would describe the whole of the data
A curve that bends downward only, falling faster and faster after the first few points
A cloud of points with no pattern, since the number of students cannot be predicted
An S-shaped curve that levels off, so a straight line would fit badly at both ends
questions.answer: An S-shaped curve that levels off, so a straight line would fit badly at both ends
questions.solution: Slow growth, then fast growth, then leveling off is an S shape. A straight line cannot follow it, and it would miss badly at both ends.

solve.answer: An S-shaped curve that levels off, so a straight line would fit badly at both ends
solve.work: Slow start, rapid rise, leveling off near 200: logistic S-shaped curve; a line fits badly at the ends.

questions.skill: Spot and judge outliers
questions.stem: Nine points of a scatter plot follow a line closely. A tenth point is far to the right of all of the others and lies exactly on the same line. Which statement is correct?
choices: It is an outlier that must be deleted before any line can be fitted to the nine other points
It makes the association weaker, because it is farther from the center of the $x$-values
It shows the pattern is not linear, because it is farther away than any of the other points
It is far from the others in $x$ but fits the pattern, so $r$ stays strong or gets stronger
questions.answer: It is far from the others in $x$ but fits the pattern, so $r$ stays strong or gets stronger
questions.solution: A point can be unusual in $x$ and still follow the pattern. This point lies on the line of the others, so it supports the linear pattern and $r$ stays strong or gets stronger.

solve.answer: It is far from the others in $x$ but fits the pattern, so $r$ stays strong or gets stronger
solve.work: A high-leverage point lying on the line extends the pattern; r stays strong or increases.

questions.skill: Spot and judge outliers
questions.stem: The points $(1, 10)$, $(2, 12)$, $(3, 14)$, $(4, 16)$ and $(5, 18)$ have a mean $y$-value of 14. A sixth point, $(6, 50)$, is added. By how much does the mean of the $y$-values go up?
questions.solution: The five $y$-values add to 70. With the sixth, the sum is 120 and the mean is $120\div 6=20$. The mean goes up by $20-14=6$.

solve.work: Sum of y = 70; new mean (70+50)/6 = 20; increase 20 - 14 = 6.

questions.skill: Read values from a scatter plot or line graph
questions.stem: A line graph shows the water in a tank, in liters: 50 at minute 0, 44 at minute 2, 28 at minute 6 and 20 at minute 10. What is the average rate of decrease from minute 2 to minute 10, in liters per minute?
questions.solution: The tank lost $44-20=24$ liters in $10-2=8$ minutes, which is $24\div 8=3$ liters per minute.

questions.skill: Read values from a scatter plot or line graph
