questions.stem: A line graph of a species' population (in hundreds) has the points year 0: 30, year 3: 45, year 5: 47 and year 9: 71. During which interval did the population grow fastest on average?
choices: From year 0 to year 3
From year 5 to year 9
From year 3 to year 5
From year 0 to year 9
questions.answer: From year 5 to year 9
questions.solution: The average rates are $15\div 3=5$, $2\div 2=1$, $24\div 4=6$ and $41\div 9\approx 4.6$ per year. The fastest is year 5 to year 9.

solve.answer: From year 5 to year 9

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: In a bubble chart, the AREA of a bubble shows the number of students in a group. Bubble A has a radius of 2 cm and bubble B has a radius of 3 cm. Group A has 40 students. How many students are in group B?
questions.solution: Area is proportional to the radius squared. The areas are in the ratio $3^2:2^2=9:4$. So group B has $40\times \frac{9}{4}=90$ students.

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: The same two variables are drawn in four small scatter plots side by side, one for each season of the year, all with the same axes. What is the main advantage of this layout?
choices: Readers can see the exact value of every point without needing to read the numbers on the axes
Readers can compare how the relationship changes from season to season without points overlapping
The four plots together always show a stronger correlation than one plot of all of the points
Readers can ignore the axes, since the seasons are shown by the position of each of the plots
questions.answer: Readers can compare how the relationship changes from season to season without points overlapping
questions.solution: Small multiples give each group its own panel on a shared scale, so changes in the pattern are easy to see and the points do not cover one another.

solve.answer: Readers can compare how the relationship changes from season to season without points overlapping
solve.work: Small multiples with shared axes let the reader compare the relationship across seasons without overlap.

questions.skill: Read a third variable shown by color, size or groups
questions.stem: In a scatter plot of all 90 students, hours of practice and score show no association. Coloring the points by group shows group 1 sloping upward and group 2, of similar size, sloping downward. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Practice has no effect on the score of anyone, since the plot of all the students shows no association
One of the two colored groups must have been recorded wrongly, since the groups disagree with each other
The groups show that the data are random, because the two opposite slopes cancel each other out
The lack of an overall trend hides opposite trends in the two groups, so they should be looked at separately
questions.answer: The lack of an overall trend hides opposite trends in the two groups, so they should be looked at separately
questions.solution: Opposite slopes in two similar-sized groups can cancel, giving no trend overall. The third variable, the group, reveals a pattern that the combined plot hides.

solve.answer: The lack of an overall trend hides opposite trends in the two groups, so they should be looked at separately
solve.work: Opposite trends in two similar-sized groups cancel overall; analyze groups separately.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: A cumulative frequency graph shows how many students scored at or below each score: 12 students scored 60 or less, 30 scored 70 or less, and 54 scored 80 or less. How many students scored above 70 and up to 80?
questions.solution: Students at 80 or below: 54. Students at 70 or below: 30. Those above 70 and up to 80: $54-30=24$.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: On a graph whose vertical axis uses a log scale, the points for a quantity over time fall along a straight line that rises. What does this say about the quantity?
choices: It grows by the same amount, such as 10 units, in each equal step of time on the graph
It grows by the same percent, or the same multiple, in each equal step of time
It grows more slowly at each step, since a log scale flattens every rising pattern of points
It stays at the same value, since a straight line on a log scale has no growth in it
questions.answer: It grows by the same percent, or the same multiple, in each equal step of time
questions.solution: Equal distances on a log axis are equal multiples. A straight rising line means the quantity is multiplied by the same factor in each time step (exponential growth).

solve.answer: It grows by the same percent, or the same multiple, in each equal step of time
solve.work: Straight rising line on a log scale = constant ratio per time step: exponential growth, same percent each step.

questions.skill: Read a non-standard display
questions.stem: In a stacked bar chart, the middle segment of each bar is hard to compare from one bar to the next. Why?
choices: The middle segments are always shorter than the top and bottom ones, so they are hidden by them
The middle segments show a different variable in each bar, so no comparison of them is possible
Stacked bars can show only the total of each bar and can never show the parts of the totals
The middle segments do not start from a common baseline, so their lengths are hard to compare
questions.answer: The middle segments do not start from a common baseline, so their lengths are hard to compare
questions.solution: Only the bottom segment starts at zero. A middle segment starts wherever the segment below it ends, so the eye cannot compare its length directly with the middle segment of another bar.

solve.answer: The middle segments do not start from a common baseline, so their lengths are hard to compare
solve.work: Middle segments float on different baselines, so their lengths are hard to compare.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A news graphic shows 1,000 as a cube with an edge of 2 cm and 3,000 as a cube with an edge of 6 cm. The value is 3 times as large. How many times as large as the smaller cube is the volume of the bigger cube?
questions.solution: The edge is 3 times as long, so the volume is $3^3=27$ times as large, far more than the 3 times it should show.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A map shades each state by the total number of flu cases, and the states with the most people are the darkest. Why can this be misleading?
choices: Big states have more cases even when the rate per person is lower, so rates per person are fairer
Maps cannot show numbers of cases, because states have different shapes and sizes on the map
The darkest states must have the least careful residents, which the map does not say at all
Shading shows an average for each state, which is a different thing from a total count
questions.answer: Big states have more cases even when the rate per person is lower, so rates per person are fairer
questions.solution: Total counts follow population size. Comparing states fairly needs a rate, such as cases per 100,000 people.

solve.answer: Big states have more cases even when the rate per person is lower, so rates per person are fairer
solve.work: Totals track population; rates per person are the fair comparison.

questions.skill: Critique a misleading display
questions.stem: A histogram uses bins of unequal widths, such as 0 to 10, 10 to 20 and 20 to 60, but the bar heights are plain counts. Why can this mislead?
choices: Histograms may use only bins of equal widths, so this one has to be a different kind of graph
The narrow bins hide values, so a count in them can never be shown in a histogram
The wide bins collect more values, so they look more common than they are per unit of width
Bars of counts always show a percent, so the heights cannot be read as numbers of values
questions.answer: The wide bins collect more values, so they look more common than they are per unit of width
questions.solution: A wide bin can hold many values just because it is wide. To compare fairly, the bar heights should show density (count per unit of width) or the bins should be equal.

solve.answer: The wide bins collect more values, so they look more common than they are per unit of width
solve.work: With unequal bins, plain counts exaggerate wide bins; heights should be density (count per unit width).

questions.skill: Predicting with a fitted model
questions.stem: A quadratic model for the height of a plant, in centimeters, $t$ weeks after planting is $h(t) = -0.5t^2 + 6t + 2$. What height does the model predict after 4 weeks, in centimeters?

questions.skill: Residuals (actual minus predicted)
questions.stem: A model predicts that a family will use 40 gallons of water in a day. The family actually uses 46 gallons. A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value. What is the residual, in gallons?
questions.solution: Residual $=$ actual $-$ predicted $= 46 - 40 = 6$ gallons. It is positive because the actual value is above the prediction.

questions.skill: Interpreting the correlation coefficient r
questions.stem: A linear model for a data set has a correlation coefficient of $r = -0.95$. Which statement best describes the relationship?
choices: A weak negative linear relationship
A strong positive linear relationship
No linear relationship
A strong negative linear relationship
questions.answer: A strong negative linear relationship
questions.solution: The size of $r$, $0.95$, is close to 1, so the linear relationship is strong. The negative sign means that $y$ tends to decrease as $x$ increases.

solve.answer: A strong negative linear relationship
solve.work: r = -0.95 is negative and close to -1: strong negative linear relationship.

questions.skill: Interpreting r squared
questions.stem: A model has $r^2 = 0.81$. What does this value tell us?
choices: About 81% of the data points lie exactly on the graph of the model
About 81% of the variation in the $y$-values is explained by the model
The model's predictions will be wrong for about 81% of the data points
The $y$-values go up by 81% each time $x$ goes up by 1 unit
questions.answer: About 81% of the variation in the $y$-values is explained by the model
questions.solution: $r^2$ is the proportion of the variation in $y$ that the model accounts for. An $r^2$ of 0.81 means about 81% of the variation in the $y$-values is explained by the model; the rest is not.

solve.answer: About 81% of the variation in the $y$-values is explained by the model
solve.work: r^2 is the proportion of variation in y explained by the model: about 81%.

questions.skill: Reading residual plots
questions.stem: A quadratic model is fitted to a data set. Its residual plot shows points scattered randomly above and below zero, with no pattern. What does this suggest?
choices: A quadratic model is a reasonable fit for the data
A quadratic model is a poor fit for the data
The data have no relationship at all between the two variables
Every data point lies exactly on the curve of the model
questions.answer: A quadratic model is a reasonable fit for the data
questions.solution: When the residuals are scattered with no pattern, the model has captured the shape of the data and what is left is random variation. That supports using the quadratic model. (Points exactly on the curve would have residuals of exactly 0.)

solve.answer: A quadratic model is a reasonable fit for the data
solve.work: Random residuals with no pattern: model form is appropriate. D.

questions.skill: Choosing a linear, exponential or quadratic model
questions.stem: A bacteria count is recorded each hour: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48. Which type of model fits these counts best?
choices: Linear
Quadratic
Exponential
Logarithmic
questions.answer: Exponential
questions.solution: Each count is 2 times the one before it, a constant ratio, which is an exponential pattern. The differences (3, 6, 12, 24) are not constant, so it is not linear, and the second differences (3, 6, 12) are not constant either, so it is not quadratic.

solve.answer: Exponential

questions.skill: Outliers
questions.stem: In a scatter plot, which data point is called an outlier?
choices: A point that lies far from the overall pattern of the other points
The point with the largest $x$-value of all the data
A point that lies exactly on the graph of the model that was fitted to the data
The point whose $y$-value equals the average of the $y$-values
questions.answer: A point that lies far from the overall pattern of the other points
questions.solution: An outlier is a point that stands apart from the general pattern of the data, far from where the model or the other points would put it. Being the largest, on the graph or at the average does not make a point an outlier.

solve.answer: A point that lies far from the overall pattern of the other points
solve.work: Outlier: point far from the overall pattern. A.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: Over one summer, ice cream sales and the number of sunburns at a beach are strongly positively correlated. Which conclusion is best?
choices: Eating ice cream makes people more likely to get sunburned at the beach
Getting a sunburn makes people want to buy more ice cream at the beach
Hot weather may be causing both, so neither has to cause the other
Banning ice cream sales would greatly reduce the sunburns
questions.answer: Hot weather may be causing both, so neither has to cause the other
questions.solution: Correlation does not prove causation. A third factor, hot sunny weather, can increase both ice cream sales and sunburns. Neither one causes the other.

solve.answer: Hot weather may be causing both, so neither has to cause the other
solve.work: Lurking variable hot weather drives both. D.

questions.skill: Interpreting a model in context
questions.stem: A quadratic model for the height of a ball, in feet, is $h(t) = -16t^2 + 32t + 4$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. What does the 4 in the model tell us?
choices: The ball's greatest height is 4 feet
The ball's height at time $t = 0$ is 4 feet
The ball hits the ground at time $t = 4$ seconds
The ball rises by 4 feet during each second
questions.answer: The ball's height at time $t = 0$ is 4 feet
questions.solution: Put $t = 0$ in the model: $h(0) = -16(0)^2 + 32(0) + 4 = 4$. The constant term is the predicted height at the start, 4 feet.

solve.answer: The ball's height at time $t = 0$ is 4 feet
solve.work: h(0) = 4: initial height 4 ft. D. (Max height is h(1) = 20.)

questions.skill: Judging predictions (extrapolation)
questions.stem: A quadratic model was fitted to data about children aged 6 to 14. For which age is the model's prediction the most trustworthy?
choices: 30 years old
50 years old
80 years old
10 years old
questions.answer: 10 years old
questions.solution: A model is most reliable inside the range of the data it was built from (ages 6 to 14). Age 10 is inside that range. Predicting for 30, 50 or 80 means extrapolating far outside it, where the pattern may not continue.

solve.answer: 10 years old
solve.work: Predictions are most trustworthy inside the data's range (6 to 14). Only 10 is inside; 30, 50, 80 are extrapolation.

questions.skill: Predicting with a fitted model
questions.stem: A model for the number of bacteria in a dish is $N(t) = 5 \cdot 2^t$, where $t$ is the time in hours. How many bacteria does the model predict after 6 hours?
questions.solution: Put $t = 6$ into the model: $5 \cdot 2^6 = 5 \cdot 64 = 320$.

questions.skill: Predicting with a fitted model
questions.stem: A linear model for the cost, in dollars, of renting a bike for $x$ hours is $C(x) = 4.5x + 10$. What cost does the model predict for 12 hours, in dollars?
questions.solution: Put $x = 12$ into the model: $4.5 \cdot 12 + 10 = 54 + 10 = 64$.

questions.skill: Predicting with a fitted model
questions.stem: A quadratic model for the number of visitors to a new website, in hundreds, on day $d$ after it opens is $V(d) = d^2 - 3d + 5$. How many hundreds of visitors does the model predict on day 6?
questions.solution: Put $d = 6$ into the model: $36 - 18 + 5 = 23$.

questions.skill: Residuals (actual minus predicted)
questions.stem: A model predicts that a runner will finish a race in 52 minutes. The runner actually takes 47 minutes. The residual is the actual value minus the predicted value. What is the residual, in minutes?
questions.solution: Residual = actual minus predicted $= 47 - 52 = -5$.

questions.skill: Residuals (actual minus predicted)
questions.stem: At one data point the residual (actual minus predicted) is positive. Which statement must be true?
choices: The actual value is less than the value the model predicted.
The actual value is exactly equal to the value the model predicted.
The actual value is greater than the value the model predicted.
The actual value is greater than the value of the next data point.
questions.answer: The actual value is greater than the value the model predicted.
questions.solution: Residual = actual minus predicted. If that difference is positive, the actual value is larger than the prediction.

solve.answer: The actual value is greater than the value the model predicted.

questions.skill: Residuals (actual minus predicted)
questions.stem: A line model is $y = 3x + 2$. A data point is $(4, 15)$. What is the residual at this point (actual minus predicted)?
questions.solution: The model predicts $3(4) + 2 = 14$. The actual value is 15, so the residual is $15 - 14 = 1$.

questions.skill: Interpreting the correlation coefficient r
questions.stem: Which of these values can NOT be the correlation coefficient $r$ of a data set?
questions.solution: The correlation coefficient is always between $-1$ and $1$. So 1.2 is impossible; the other values are all possible.

questions.skill: Interpreting the correlation coefficient r
questions.stem: All the points of a data set lie exactly on one line that slopes downward. What is the correlation coefficient $r$?
questions.solution: Points exactly on a line give $|r| = 1$. The line slopes downward, so $r$ is negative: $r = -1$.

questions.skill: Interpreting r squared
questions.stem: A line fitted to a data set has $r = 0.5$. What percent of the variation in $y$ does the line explain?

questions.skill: Interpreting r squared
questions.stem: A model has $r^2 = 0.04$. Which statement best describes the model?
choices: It explains almost all of the variation in $y$ in the data.
It explains exactly 96% of the variation in $y$ in the data.
It shows a very strong negative linear relationship in the data.
It explains only a very small part of the variation in $y$.
questions.answer: It explains only a very small part of the variation in $y$.
questions.solution: $r^2 = 0.04$ means about 4% of the variation in $y$ is explained, which is very little.

solve.answer: It explains only a very small part of the variation in $y$.

questions.skill: Reading residual plots
questions.stem: Which pattern in a residual plot suggests that a line is a good model for the data?
choices: The points form a clear curve that is high at both ends and low in the middle.
The points scatter randomly above and below zero, with no pattern.
The points all lie above zero, with none at all below the horizontal axis.
The points start close to zero and then spread out into a fan shape.
questions.answer: The points scatter randomly above and below zero, with no pattern.
questions.solution: A good-fitting model leaves residuals that look like random scatter around zero. A curve, a fan or all points on one side show something the model has missed.

solve.answer: The points scatter randomly above and below zero, with no pattern.
solve.work: Random scatter about zero with no pattern indicates a good linear fit.

questions.skill: Choosing a linear, exponential or quadratic model
questions.stem: The values of $y$ for $x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ are 5, 8, 11, 14, 17. Which type of model fits best?
choices: An exponential model, because $y$ is multiplied by the same number each time.
A quadratic model, because the amounts that $y$ goes up by keep growing larger.
A linear model, because $y$ goes up by the same amount (3) each time.
None of the three, because the values of $y$ keep growing and never repeat.
questions.answer: A linear model, because $y$ goes up by the same amount (3) each time.
questions.solution: The differences are 3, 3, 3, 3: constant. That is the signature of a linear model.

questions.skill: Choosing a linear, exponential or quadratic model

questions.skill: Outliers

questions.solution: Five scores are close to 80. The score of 20 is far from all of them, so 20 is the outlier.

questions.skill: Interpreting a model in context
questions.stem: A model for a savings balance, in dollars, is $B(t) = 500(1.04)^t$, where $t$ is the time in years. What does the 1.04 tell us?
choices: Each year the balance is multiplied by 1.04, which is a growth of 4% a year.
Each year the balance goes up by 1.04 dollars, the same amount every year.
Each year the balance is multiplied by 1.04, which is a growth of 104% a year.
The balance at the very start of the model is 1.04 dollars in the account.
questions.answer: Each year the balance is multiplied by 1.04, which is a growth of 4% a year.
questions.solution: In $a \cdot b^t$, the number $b$ is the growth factor. A factor of 1.04 means 4% more each year.

solve.answer: Each year the balance is multiplied by 1.04, which is a growth of 4% a year.

questions.skill: Interpreting a model in context
questions.stem: A model for the temperature, in degrees, of a cup of tea $t$ minutes after it is poured is $T(t) = 90 - 4t$. After how many minutes does the model predict a temperature of 70 degrees?
questions.solution: Solve $90 - 4t = 70$. Then $4t = 20$, so $t = 5$ minutes.

questions.skill: Judging predictions (extrapolation)

choices: 25 degrees
30 degrees
35 degrees
60 degrees
questions.answer: 60 degrees

The model should not be used for ages so far outside the ages in the data.
The model needs only a larger slope, and then it will work for all ages.
Adults grow much faster than children, so the prediction is believable.
questions.answer: The model should not be used for ages so far outside the ages in the data.

questions.skill: Choosing a linear, exponential or quadratic model

A linear model, because the plot shows time along the horizontal axis of the graph.
questions.answer: A quadratic model, because the points rise and then fall in a curve.

questions.skill: Outliers
questions.stem: In a scatter plot, one point lies far from the pattern of all the other points. What should an analyst do first?
choices: Delete the point right away, because any point that is off the pattern must be a mistake.
Keep the point and say nothing, because one point can never change the fit.
Move the point onto the pattern of the others, so that the plot looks clearer to readers.
Check whether the point was recorded by mistake, before deciding whether to keep it.
questions.answer: Check whether the point was recorded by mistake, before deciding whether to keep it.
questions.solution: An outlier may be an error or a real, interesting value. Look into it first. Deleting or changing data without a reason is poor practice.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation

Older children tend to have larger feet and also tend to read better.
Reading better makes a child's feet grow larger than other children's feet.
Shoe size and reading score measure exactly the same thing.
questions.answer: Older children tend to have larger feet and also tend to read better.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: Which kind of study can best show that a treatment causes a change in an outcome?
choices: A survey asking people whether they used the treatment and how they feel now about their health
A scatter plot of the treatment against the outcome with a high value of $r$
An experiment in which people are randomly assigned to the treatment or to a comparison group
A study that watches only those people who chose to use the treatment on their own
questions.answer: An experiment in which people are randomly assigned to the treatment or to a comparison group
questions.solution: Random assignment makes the groups alike except for the treatment, so a difference in the outcome can be linked to the treatment.

questions.skill: Predicting with a fitted model
questions.stem: A fitted quadratic model for a cyclist's speed, in km/h, $t$ seconds after starting is $s(t) = -0.2t^2 + 3t + 4$, for $0 \le t \le 12$. What speed does the model predict at 10 seconds, in km/h?
questions.solution: $s(10) = -0.2(10)^2 + 3(10) + 4 = -0.2(100) + 30 + 4 = -20 + 30 + 4 = 14$ km/h. (10 is inside the range 0 to 12, so this is a fair prediction.)

questions.skill: Residuals (actual minus predicted)
questions.stem: A quadratic model is $f(x) = 2x^2 - 5x + 3$, and the data point $(4, 18)$ was observed. What is the residual at this point (actual minus predicted)?
questions.solution: The model predicts $f(4) = 2(16) - 20 + 3 = 15$. The actual value is 18, so the residual is $18 - 15 = 3$.

questions.skill: Residuals (actual minus predicted)
questions.stem: A data point has a residual of $-3.2$ (actual minus predicted). Which statement is true?
choices: The actual value is 3.2 more than the model's prediction
The model's prediction is 3.2 less than the actual value
The actual value is 3.2 less than the model's prediction
The correlation coefficient of the model is $r = -3.2$
questions.answer: The actual value is 3.2 less than the model's prediction
questions.solution: Residual $=$ actual $-$ predicted. A residual of $-3.2$ means actual $-$ predicted $= -3.2$, so the actual value is 3.2 below the prediction (the point is below the model's graph). A correlation coefficient can never be below $-1$.

solve.answer: The actual value is 3.2 less than the model's prediction
solve.work: actual - predicted = -3.2 -> actual = predicted - 3.2: the actual value is 3.2 less than the prediction. Options A and D describe a positive residual; B confuses residual with r.

questions.skill: Interpreting r squared
questions.stem: For a model, the correlation coefficient is $r = -0.7$. What percent of the variation in $y$ is explained by the model?
questions.solution: $r^2 = (-0.7)^2 = 0.49$, so the model explains 49% of the variation in $y$.

questions.skill: Interpreting the correlation coefficient r
questions.stem: Four data sets have these correlation coefficients. Which one shows the strongest linear relationship?
questions.solution: Strength depends on how close $r$ is to $-1$ or $1$, not on the sign. The sizes are 0.9, 0.7, 0.4 and 0.3, so $r = -0.9$ is the strongest (a strong negative relationship).

questions.skill: Reading residual plots
questions.stem: A line is fitted to a data set. Its residual plot is U-shaped: the residuals are positive at the left and right ends and negative in the middle. What does this suggest?
choices: The linear model is a good fit, so no other model is needed
The data contain exactly one outlier, located in the middle of the plot
The correlation coefficient must be exactly 0 for this data set
A curved model, such as a quadratic, would fit better than a line
questions.answer: A curved model, such as a quadratic, would fit better than a line
questions.solution: A clear pattern in the residuals means the model has missed some of the shape of the data. A U-shape says the data bend away from the line, so a curve such as a quadratic should fit better.

solve.answer: A curved model, such as a quadratic, would fit better than a line
solve.work: U-shaped residuals from a line indicate curvature; try a quadratic. B.

questions.skill: Choosing a linear, exponential or quadratic model
questions.stem: For the equally spaced $x$-values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, the $y$-values are 3, 8, 15, 24, 35. Which choice describes the best model?
choices: Linear, because the first differences are always constant
Quadratic, because the second differences are constant
Linear, because the $y$-values keep on increasing as $x$ grows
Exponential, because the $y$-values keep increasing
questions.answer: Quadratic, because the second differences are constant
questions.solution: The first differences are 5, 7, 9, 11, which are not constant, so the data are not linear. The second differences are 2, 2, 2, which are constant: that is the sign of a quadratic. The ratios of consecutive values (about 2.7, 1.9, 1.6) are not constant, so it is not exponential.

solve.answer: Quadratic, because the second differences are constant
solve.work: y = x^2 + 2x: first differences 5, 7, 9, 11; second differences 2, constant: quadratic. D.

questions.skill: Outliers
questions.stem: A scatter plot shows a strong positive linear pattern, except for one point far below the others. The point is removed and the line is fitted again. What will most likely happen to $r$?
choices: $r$ will move closer to 0
$r$ will move closer to 1
$r$ will become negative
$r$ will stay exactly the same
questions.answer: $r$ will move closer to 1
questions.solution: An outlier that sits far from the pattern weakens the correlation. Removing it leaves points that follow the line more closely, so $r$ gets closer to 1 (a stronger positive linear relationship).

solve.answer: $r$ will move closer to 1
solve.work: Removing a point far off a strong positive linear pattern makes the remaining points fit the line more tightly, so r increases toward 1.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: A study of students finds a positive correlation ($r = 0.6$) between the number of books a student owns and the student's reading score. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Buying more books for a student will raise that student's reading score by a lot
Reading well causes students to own more books, not the other way around
Books and reading scores are not related to each other at all, since $r$ is only 0.6
Students with more books tend to score higher, but books may not be the cause
questions.answer: Students with more books tend to score higher, but books may not be the cause
questions.solution: $r = 0.6$ shows that the two go up together, but a correlation alone cannot show which causes which, or whether a third factor (such as time spent reading at home) explains both. The data do show the two are related.

solve.answer: Students with more books tend to score higher, but books may not be the cause
solve.work: Positive association, but not necessarily causal (confounders such as family income). B.

questions.solution: The parabola opens downward, so its highest point is the vertex, at $p = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{60}{2(-3)} = 10$. The model predicts the greatest revenue at a ticket price of 10 dollars.

questions.skill: Interpreting the correlation coefficient r

questions.solution: $r^2 = 0.36$ means 36% is explained. The rest is $100 - 36 = 64$%.

questions.skill: Reading residual plots
questions.stem: A line is fitted to data that actually grow by doubling. What will the residual plot most likely show?
choices: A random scatter around zero, so the line is a good model for the data.
All points exactly on the horizontal axis, so the line predicts every value.
One point far from zero, so only one data value was recorded wrongly.

questions.skill: Reading residual plots

Predictions are equally precise for large and for small values of $x$ in the data.

questions.skill: Outliers
questions.stem: A quadratic model is $f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 10$. The observed points are $(1, 5)$, $(3, 1.4)$, $(4, 2)$ and $(7, 11)$. Which point is most likely an outlier?
questions.solution: Compare each point with the model's prediction: $f(1) = 5$ (residual 0), $f(3) = 1$ (residual 0.4), $f(4) = 2$ (residual 0) and $f(7) = 17$ (residual $11 - 17 = -6$). The point $(7, 11)$ is far from the model, much farther than the others, so it is the likely outlier.

solve.work: Predictions: f(1) = 5, f(3) = 1, f(4) = 2, f(7) = 17. Residuals: 0, 0.4, 0, -6. The point (7, 11) is far from the model: outlier.

questions.skill: Quadratic regression: finding the model through data
questions.stem: The points $(0, 4)$, $(1, 5)$, $(2, 8)$ and $(3, 13)$ lie exactly on a quadratic curve $y = x^2 + bx + c$. What $y$-value does this curve give at $x = 5$?

questions.skill: Interpreting a model in context
questions.stem: A quadratic regression model for the height of a model rocket, in meters, is $h(t) = -5t^2 + 30t + 2$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. What maximum height does the model predict, in meters?
questions.solution: The parabola opens downward, so the maximum is at the vertex, where $t = -\frac{30}{2(-5)} = 3$ seconds. Then $h(3) = -5(9) + 90 + 2 = -45 + 90 + 2 = 47$ meters.

questions.skill: Judging predictions (extrapolation)
questions.stem: A shop's profit, in thousands of dollars, in month $t$ is modeled by $P(t) = -2t^2 + 24t - 40$, fitted to data from months 1 to 10. A student uses the model for month 20. Which statement is best?
choices: $P(20) = -360$, and it is reliable because the model was fitted to real data from the shop's records
$P(20) = 360$, but month 20 is far outside months 1 to 10, so the prediction is unreliable
$P(20) = 360$, and it is reliable because the model was fitted to real data
$P(20) = -360$, but month 20 is far outside months 1 to 10, so the prediction is unreliable
questions.answer: $P(20) = -360$, but month 20 is far outside months 1 to 10, so the prediction is unreliable
questions.solution: $P(20) = -2(400) + 24(20) - 40 = -800 + 480 - 40 = -360$. But the model was built from months 1 to 10, and month 20 is far beyond that range (extrapolation). A quadratic keeps curving down, which is unlikely to describe a real shop that long, so the prediction should not be trusted.

solve.answer: $P(20) = -360$, but month 20 is far outside months 1 to 10, so the prediction is unreliable
solve.work: P(20) = -2(400) + 24(20) - 40 = -800 + 480 - 40 = -360. Month 20 is extrapolation outside 1-10, unreliable. C.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: A linear model relating hours studied to test score has $r^2 = 0.72$. Which statement is correct?
choices: The model explains about 72% of the variation in scores, which proves that studying causes higher scores
The model explains about 72% of the variation in scores, but this alone does not show cause and effect
The model explains about 28% of the variation in scores, but this alone does not show cause and effect
The correlation coefficient is $r = 0.72$, but this alone does not show cause and effect
questions.answer: The model explains about 72% of the variation in scores, but this alone does not show cause and effect
questions.solution: $r^2 = 0.72$ means the model explains about 72% of the variation in scores (not 28%, which is what is left over). The correlation coefficient is $r = \pm\sqrt{0.72}$, about $\pm 0.85$, not 0.72. And a strong association never proves cause and effect on its own.

solve.answer: The model explains about 72% of the variation in scores, but this alone does not show cause and effect
solve.work: r^2 = 0.72 means about 72% of the variation in scores is explained; r = sqrt(0.72) ~ 0.85, not 0.72; correlation alone does not prove causation.

questions.skill: Predicting with a fitted model
questions.stem: A model for the number of bacteria in a dish is $P(t) = 100 \cdot 2^t$, where $t$ is the time in hours. After how many hours does the model predict 3,200 bacteria?
questions.solution: Solve $100 \cdot 2^t = 3200$. Then $2^t = 32 = 2^5$, so $t = 5$ hours.

questions.skill: Predicting with a fitted model
questions.stem: A quadratic model for the height of a drone, in meters, is $s(t) = -0.5t^2 + 8t + 3$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after takeoff. The model predicts a height of 27 meters at two different times. What is the earlier of the two times, in seconds?
questions.solution: Solve $-0.5t^2 + 8t + 3 = 27$. Then $t^2 - 16t + 48 = 0$, which factors as $(t - 4)(t - 12) = 0$. The earlier time is 4 seconds.

questions.skill: Residuals (actual minus predicted)
questions.stem: A quadratic model is $f(x) = 0.5x^2 - x + 2$. The observed points are $(2, 5)$, $(4, 7)$ and $(6, 16)$. What is the mean of the three residuals (actual minus predicted)?

questions.skill: Residuals (actual minus predicted)
questions.stem: An exponential model is $f(x) = 2 \cdot 3^x$. At $x = 3$ the residual is 6 (actual minus predicted). What is the actual value of $y$ at $x = 3$?
questions.solution: The model predicts $2 \cdot 27 = 54$. Actual = predicted + residual $= 54 + 6 = 60$.

questions.skill: Interpreting the correlation coefficient r
questions.stem: All the points of a data set lie exactly on the line $y = -3x + 2$. What is the correlation coefficient $r$?
choices: $r = -3$, because $r$ is equal to the slope of the line through the points.
$r = 1$, because the points lie exactly on one line and so are perfectly related.
$r = -1$, because the points lie exactly on a line that slopes downward.
$r = 0$, because the line crosses the $y$-axis at 2 instead of at the origin.
questions.answer: $r = -1$, because the points lie exactly on a line that slopes downward.
questions.solution: For points exactly on a line, $|r| = 1$ whatever the slope is. The slope is negative, so $r = -1$.

solve.answer: $r = -1$, because the points lie exactly on a line that slopes downward.

questions.skill: Interpreting r squared
questions.stem: A line fitted to one data set has $r = 0.6$. A line fitted to a second data set has $r = 0.8$. By how many percentage points of the variation in $y$ does the second line explain more than the first?
questions.solution: $0.8^2 = 0.64$ is 64% and $0.6^2 = 0.36$ is 36%. The difference is $64 - 36 = 28$ percentage points.

questions.skill: Choosing a linear, exponential or quadratic model
questions.stem: The values of $y$ for $x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ are 1, 3, 9, 27, 81. Which type of model fits best?
choices: An exponential model, because each $y$ is 3 times the one before it.
A quadratic model, because the $y$-values rise faster and faster as $x$ grows.
A linear model, because the $y$-values always increase as $x$ goes up by 1.
None of the three, because the amounts that $y$ goes up by keep on changing.
questions.answer: An exponential model, because each $y$ is 3 times the one before it.
questions.solution: The ratio of each value to the one before is always 3, so the model is exponential. The differences (2, 6, 18, 54) are not constant and their changes (4, 12, 36) are not constant, so it is neither linear nor quadratic.

solve.answer: An exponential model, because each $y$ is 3 times the one before it.

questions.skill: Choosing a linear, exponential or quadratic model
questions.stem: For $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$, which list of $y$-values is best modeled by a quadratic?
questions.solution: For $2, 5, 10, 17$ the differences are 3, 5, 7 and they change by a constant 2: quadratic. The list 2, 4, 8, 16 doubles (exponential), 2, 4, 6, 8 adds 2 (linear), and 20, 10, 5, 2.5 halves (exponential).

solve.work: 2, 5, 10, 17: first differences 3, 5, 7, second difference 2 constant: quadratic. A linear, B and D exponential.

questions.skill: Outliers
questions.stem: A value is called an outlier if it is greater than $Q_3 + 1.5 \cdot \text{IQR}$. For a data set, $Q_1 = 20$ and $Q_3 = 30$. What is the smallest whole number that would be an outlier?
questions.solution: The IQR is $30 - 20 = 10$, so the upper fence is $30 + 15 = 45$. A value must be greater than 45, so the smallest whole number is 46.

solve.work: IQR = 10; 30 + 15 = 45; strictly greater than 45, smallest whole number 46.

questions.skill: Interpreting a model in context
questions.stem: A quadratic model for the profit, in dollars, from making $x$ items is $P(x) = -x^2 + 40x - 300$. What is the greatest profit that the model predicts, in dollars?
questions.solution: The vertex is at $x = 20$. Then $P(20) = -400 + 800 - 300 = 100$ dollars.

questions.skill: Interpreting a model in context
questions.stem: A model for the number of fish in a pond is $N(t) = 800(0.9)^t$, where $t$ is the time in years. How many fish does the model predict after 2 years?
questions.solution: Each year the number is multiplied by 0.9 (a 10% loss). After 2 years: $800 \times 0.81 = 648$.

questions.skill: Interpreting a model in context
questions.stem: A linear model for the amount of water, in liters, left in a tank after $x$ hours is $y = -1.5x + 30$. After how many hours does the model predict that the tank is empty?

questions.skill: Judging predictions (extrapolation)
questions.stem: A model for a ball's height in feet is $h(t) = -16t^2 + 32t + 4$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. It gives $h(3) = -44$. What does this tell us?
choices: The ball is 44 feet below the ground at 3 seconds, so the ground must be uneven.
The model is correct, because it will give the true height of the ball at any time.
The ball is still rising at 3 seconds, and the minus sign only gives the direction.
The model cannot be used at 3 seconds, because the ball would already have landed.
questions.answer: The model cannot be used at 3 seconds, because the ball would already have landed.
questions.solution: The ball lands when $h = 0$, at about 2.1 seconds. After that the model no longer describes the ball, so the negative height is meaningless.

solve.answer: The model cannot be used at 3 seconds, because the ball would already have landed.
solve.work: h(3) = -144 + 96 + 4 = -44 < 0; ball lands near t = 2.1 s, so the model does not apply at t = 3.

questions.skill: Quadratic regression: finding the model through data
questions.stem: The points $(1, 7)$, $(2, 12)$, $(3, 19)$ and $(4, 28)$ lie exactly on a quadratic curve. What value of $y$ does the curve give at $x = 6$?
questions.solution: The differences 5, 7, 9 change by 2, so $a = 1$. Then $y = x^2 + bx + c$: $1 + b + c = 7$ and $4 + 2b + c = 12$, giving $b = 2$, $c = 4$. At $x = 6$: $36 + 12 + 4 = 52$.

solve.work: Differences 5, 7, 9, second diff 2: y = x^2 + 2x + 4 (checks all four). y(6) = 36 + 12 + 4 = 52.

questions.skill: Residuals (actual minus predicted)
questions.stem: A line is fitted to data at $x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$. The residuals are $2, -1, -3, -1, 3$. Which statement is true?
choices: The residuals do not add to 0, so this line cannot be the least-squares line.
The residuals form a U shape, which suggests that a line is not the best type of model.
The residuals are random, which shows that a line is the best type of model for these data.
The residual at $x = 3$ is the only one that is negative, so it must be an outlier in the data.
questions.answer: The residuals form a U shape, which suggests that a line is not the best type of model.
questions.solution: The residuals are positive, then negative, then positive: a U shape. They do add to $2 - 1 - 3 - 1 + 3 = 0$, and four of the five are within 3 of zero; the U pattern is what matters.

solve.answer: The residuals form a U shape, which suggests that a line is not the best type of model.
solve.work: Residuals 2, -1, -3, -1, 3: sum 0; positive at ends, negative in middle: U shape, so a line is not the best model. A. B false (x=2 and 4 also negative), D false (sum is 0).

questions.skill: Interpreting the correlation coefficient r
questions.stem: The seven points with $x = -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3$ and $y = x^2$ have $r = 0$. Which statement is correct?
choices: There is a perfect curved relationship even though $r = 0$, since $r$ only measures linear relationships.
There is no relationship at all between $x$ and $y$, because the value of $r$ is 0 for these seven points.
The data must contain an error, since a perfect rule for $y$ always gives $r = 1$.
The value $r = 0$ occurs only because $x$ has negative values, so $r$ must be recomputed.
questions.answer: There is a perfect curved relationship even though $r = 0$, since $r$ only measures linear relationships.
questions.solution: $y$ is exactly determined by $x$, but the pattern is a parabola, not a line. $r$ measures only linear association, so it can be 0.

solve.answer: There is a perfect curved relationship even though $r = 0$, since $r$ only measures linear relationships.
solve.work: Symmetric parabola: x values sum to 0 and sum of x*y = sum of x^3 = 0, so r = 0, yet y = x^2 exactly. r measures linear association only. D.

questions.skill: Interpreting r squared
questions.stem: A linear model for a data set has $r^2 = 0.90$, but the residual plot shows a clear curve. What is the best statement?
choices: The high value of $r^2$ proves the line is the best model, so no more checks are needed.
The residual plot should be ignored, because $r^2$ is a more reliable measure of fit than any plot.
The value of $r^2$ must have been computed wrongly, because a curve in the residuals cannot give 0.90.
The line explains much of the variation, but a curved model may still fit the data better.
questions.answer: The line explains much of the variation, but a curved model may still fit the data better.
questions.solution: A high $r^2$ does not rule out a systematic pattern in the residuals. The curve says a different type of model could do better.

solve.answer: The line explains much of the variation, but a curved model may still fit the data better.
solve.work: High r^2 but curved residuals: line explains much variation, a curve may fit better. C.

questions.skill: Reading residual plots
questions.stem: A quadratic model is fitted and its residual plot is an arch: negative at both ends and positive in the middle. What does this suggest?
choices: The model fits well, because the residuals are positive in the middle and negative at the ends.
The model has missed a pattern in the data, so another type of model should be considered.
The data were entered in the wrong order, because the residuals should not be curved.
The points in the middle of the data are outliers, and they should simply be removed from the data.
questions.answer: The model has missed a pattern in the data, so another type of model should be considered.
questions.solution: A good fit leaves random residuals. A clear arch means the model is systematically off.

solve.answer: The model has missed a pattern in the data, so another type of model should be considered.
solve.work: Patterned residuals mean the model missed structure; consider another model. B.

questions.skill: Reading residual plots
questions.stem: Two models are fitted to the same data. The residuals of Model A scatter randomly within 2 of zero. The residuals of Model B also stay within 2 of zero, but form a clear U shape. Which statement is best?
choices: Model B is better, because its U shape shows that it has captured the curve in the data.
The models are equally good, because all of the residuals for both models are within 2 of zero.
Model A is better, because the pattern in Model B's residuals shows that it misses a trend.
Model A is worse, because random residuals mean that the model has explained nothing.
questions.answer: Model A is better, because the pattern in Model B's residuals shows that it misses a trend.
questions.solution: Equal size of residuals is not enough. A pattern in the residuals means the model is missing structure that Model A does not miss.

solve.answer: Model A is better, because the pattern in Model B's residuals shows that it misses a trend.
solve.work: Patterned residuals (U) mean Model B misses a trend; random residuals of A are preferable. C.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: Cities with more police officers tend to have more crime. A mayor says that police officers cause crime. Which response is best?
choices: The correlation shows that hiring more police officers causes crime to rise in a city, as the mayor says.
Correlation is always just coincidence, so there is nothing to explain in the data on police and crime.
More crime may lead cities to hire more police, so the cause could run in the opposite direction.
The correlation cannot be real, because police officers are hired to reduce crime.
questions.answer: More crime may lead cities to hire more police, so the cause could run in the opposite direction.
questions.solution: Reverse causation is possible: crime can cause the hiring of police. A correlation alone does not show which way the cause runs.

solve.answer: More crime may lead cities to hire more police, so the cause could run in the opposite direction.
solve.work: Reverse causation: crime leads to hiring police. B.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: Over ten years, the number of solar panels in a county and the number of electric cars in the county both rose steadily, with $r = 0.98$. Which statement is best?
choices: Both rose over time for their own reasons, so a high $r$ does not show that one causes the other.
Solar panels cause people to buy electric cars, because $r$ is so close to 1.
Electric cars cause people to install solar panels, because $r$ is so close to 1 for the ten years of data.
The value $r = 0.98$ must be a mistake, because no data set has a value so high.
questions.answer: Both rose over time for their own reasons, so a high $r$ does not show that one causes the other.
questions.solution: Two quantities that both trend upward with time will be strongly correlated even with no link. A high $r$ is not evidence of cause.

solve.answer: Both rose over time for their own reasons, so a high $r$ does not show that one causes the other.
solve.work: Both trend with time; high r does not imply causation. B.

questions.skill: Judging predictions (extrapolation)
questions.stem: A line and a quadratic curve both fit data with $x$ from 0 to 10, each with $r^2 = 0.95$. At $x = 30$ the line predicts 85 and the quadratic predicts 190. Which statement is best?
choices: The quadratic prediction is better, because a curve can follow the data more closely than a line can.
Both are far outside the data, so neither prediction can be trusted without further evidence.
The linear prediction is better, because a line is the simplest type of model there is.
The average of the two predictions must be right, because the two errors will cancel each other out.
questions.answer: Both are far outside the data, so neither prediction can be trusted without further evidence.
questions.solution: At $x = 30$ both models are extrapolating three times beyond the data. Equal fit inside the data says nothing about which is right outside.

solve.answer: Both are far outside the data, so neither prediction can be trusted without further evidence.
solve.work: x = 30 is far outside 0-10; both extrapolations untrustworthy. D.

questions.skill: Outliers
questions.stem: Ten points follow a rising line closely, with $r=0.98$. An eleventh point is added far to the right of the others and far below their line. What is the most likely effect?
choices: The value of $r$ stays near 0.98, because one point cannot change a correlation found from ten others
The value of $r$ drops a lot, and the fitted line is pulled noticeably toward the new point
The value of $r$ rises above 0.98, because adding any point to a scatter plot makes the fit stronger
The value of $r$ drops, but the fitted line stays exactly where it was before the new point was added
questions.answer: The value of $r$ drops a lot, and the fitted line is pulled noticeably toward the new point
questions.solution: A point far out in the x-direction and far off the pattern has a lot of pull. It weakens the linear pattern, so $r$ drops, and it drags the fitted line toward itself, so the line moves.

solve.answer: The value of $r$ drops a lot, and the fitted line is pulled noticeably toward the new point
solve.work: A point far to the right is high leverage; far below the line it is also an outlier, so it is influential: it pulls the least-squares line toward itself (lowering slope) and greatly reduces r.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A reporter wants to know how all the students at a school feel about the cafeteria menu. She asks only the students waiting in line at the pizza counter. Why might the results be misleading?
choices: Students waiting for pizza are probably not typical of all students, so the sample is biased.
The sample is not biased, because every single student who was standing in the pizza line was asked.
The sample is large enough to avoid bias, because a pizza line is usually long.
The results are misleading only because she did not also ask the teachers and the school staff.
questions.answer: Students waiting for pizza are probably not typical of all students, so the sample is biased.
questions.solution: A sample must represent the whole group. Students who stand in the pizza line are more likely to like pizza and the menu than other students, so asking only them is a biased way to choose a sample. Asking everyone in the line does not fix that, and a long line does not make it a fair sample.

solve.answer: Students waiting for pizza are probably not typical of all students, so the sample is biased.
solve.work: Pizza-line students are a convenience sample, not representative of all students: selection bias. B wrong (everyone in the line is still not the population), C size does not cure bias, D teachers are not the population.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A student council wants to know how students feel about new library hours. Which survey question is the least biased?
choices: Don't you agree that the wonderful new library hours are a big improvement?
Do you support or oppose the new library hours?
Wouldn't you say the foolish new library hours should be thrown out?
Because the new library hours save money, do you support them?
questions.answer: Do you support or oppose the new library hours?
questions.solution: A fair question uses neutral words and does not push toward an answer. The questions with words like "wonderful" or "foolish", or that give a reason first, steer the answer. "Do you support or oppose the new library hours?" gives both sides equally.

solve.answer: Do you support or oppose the new library hours?
solve.work: Neutral wording, no loaded words or leading reason.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: A school emails a survey to 500 students, and only 125 of them answer. What percent of the students did not answer?
questions.solution: 500 - 125 = 375 students did not answer, and 375 / 500 = 0.75, or 75%. When most people do not answer, the few who did may not be typical, which is a limit on the survey.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: A random sample of 100 students from a large school found that 60 of them walk to school. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Exactly 60% of the students at the school walk to school.
Exactly 60 students at the school walk to school, no more and no fewer.
About 60% of the students at the school probably walk to school.
About 60% of students everywhere probably walk to school each day.
questions.answer: About 60% of the students at the school probably walk to school.
questions.solution: A random sample gives an estimate for the school it came from, not an exact value, and not for other places. The sample proportion is 60 / 100 = 60%, so about 60% of the students at this school probably walk.

solve.answer: About 60% of the students at the school probably walk to school.
solve.work: Random sample 60/100 = 60% estimates the school proportion approximately. Not exact (B, C), not everywhere (D).

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: A town's records show that ice cream sales and sunburn cases both go up in the summer months. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Eating ice cream makes people much more likely to get a sunburn during the summer months.
Getting a sunburn makes people much more likely to buy ice cream during the summer months.
Ice cream sales and sunburn cases are not related at all, since neither one causes the other.
The two rise together, but the data alone do not show that either one causes the other.
questions.answer: The two rise together, but the data alone do not show that either one causes the other.
questions.solution: Two quantities can rise together because of a third factor. Here the hot, sunny weather leads to both more ice cream sales and more sunburns. The data show that they go together, but not that one causes the other.

solve.answer: The two rise together, but the data alone do not show that either one causes the other.
solve.issues: Near-duplicate of Q33 (ice cream and sunburn), though placed under a different standard.
solve.work: Both rise in summer (lurking variable: hot sunny weather). Association without causation. B, D assert causation; C says not related, but they are associated.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: A poll of randomly chosen voters finds that 54% support a new park, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. What is the highest percent of all voters who plausibly support the park?
questions.solution: The margin of error means the percent for all voters is likely within 3 points of 54%. The highest plausible value is 54 + 3 = 57%.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: A news graph about test scores starts its vertical axis at 90 instead of 0. Two bars show scores of 92 and 96. What effect does this have on how the graph looks?
choices: The difference between the two bars looks much larger than it really is.
The difference between the two bars looks smaller than it really is.
The two bars look exactly equal in height, since the scores are so close.
The graph hides the higher of the two scores, so only one bar can be seen.
questions.answer: The difference between the two bars looks much larger than it really is.
questions.solution: With the axis starting at 90, the bars show heights of only 2 and 6, so the taller bar looks three times as tall as the shorter one. In fact 96 is only about 4% more than 92. Starting the axis above zero exaggerates the difference.

solve.answer: The difference between the two bars looks much larger than it really is.
solve.work: Axis from 90: bars drawn 2 and 6 units tall, so the 96 bar looks 3 times the 92 bar though the scores differ by about 4%. Difference exaggerated.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: A class carries out a statistical investigation. Which step should come first?
choices: Make a graph of all of the data that were collected.
Write the conclusion of the report.
Choose the statistics to report.
Ask a question that data can help answer.
questions.answer: Ask a question that data can help answer.
questions.solution: Every investigation starts with a question. The question tells you what data to collect, how to display and analyze it, and what conclusions can be written at the end.

solve.answer: Ask a question that data can help answer.
solve.work: Statistical investigation cycle: formulate question, collect data, analyze, interpret. First is asking a question.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: A report on a student survey must let readers judge how far its results can be trusted. Which detail is most important to include?
choices: How the students were chosen and how many answered.
The names of all the students who answered.
The color used for the bars in the graph.
The writer's opinion about what the results should be.
questions.answer: How the students were chosen and how many answered.
questions.solution: Readers can judge a survey only if they know who was asked, how they were chosen, and how many answered. Names are private and not needed, the color of a graph says nothing about reliability, and the writer's hopes are not evidence.

solve.answer: How the students were chosen and how many answered.
solve.work: Sampling method and sample size determine trustworthiness.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A radio show asks listeners to call in and say whether the city should build a new stadium. Why can the opinions of the callers not be used to describe the whole city?
choices: Phone calls cost money, so the callers must all be wealthier than the rest of the people in the city
A stadium is a topic that cannot be measured by any survey or poll of the people who live in a city
Only people who choose to call take part, and they may feel more strongly than the rest of the city
The callers always answer in the same way, so the calls show nothing about how the city really feels
questions.answer: Only people who choose to call take part, and they may feel more strongly than the rest of the city
questions.solution: The callers chose themselves (voluntary response). People with strong feelings are the most likely to call, so the callers are not typical of the whole city.

solve.answer: Only people who choose to call take part, and they may feel more strongly than the rest of the city
solve.work: Voluntary response: callers self-select and tend to hold strong opinions, so they do not represent the city.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A principal wants to know how all 1,000 students at her school feel about the new schedule. Which way of choosing 100 students is most likely to give a fair picture?
choices: Choose 100 students at random from the list of all 1,000 students at the school
Ask the first 100 students who arrive at the school building on one particular morning
Ask 100 students who belong to the chess club, which meets in the school after classes
Ask the 100 students who stay late each day for the practices of the school's sports teams
questions.answer: Choose 100 students at random from the list of all 1,000 students at the school
questions.solution: A random choice from the list of all students gives every student the same chance of being picked. The other groups are convenient but not typical of the whole school.

solve.answer: Choose 100 students at random from the list of all 1,000 students at the school
solve.work: A simple random sample from the full list of 1,000 gives every student an equal chance.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A phone poll calls only landline numbers. In a town of 5,000 households, 2,000 have no landline. What percent of the households have no chance of being called?
questions.solution: The households with no landline are $\frac{2000}{5000}=0.4$, which is 40 percent. They are left out of the poll completely, which is undercoverage.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: Which of these is an experiment, rather than an observational study?
choices: Researchers record the diets that 40 people already follow and compare the weight each person lost
Researchers assign 40 volunteers to follow a new diet or the old diet and compare weight lost
A survey asks 40 people about the diet that they follow and about the weight that they have lost
Researchers look in the medical records of 40 people to compare the diets and weights of the people
questions.answer: Researchers assign 40 volunteers to follow a new diet or the old diet and compare weight lost
questions.solution: In an experiment, the researchers assign the treatment. In the other three the diets were the people's own choices and were only observed.

solve.answer: Researchers assign 40 volunteers to follow a new diet or the old diet and compare weight lost
solve.work: Researchers assign the treatment (diet) to volunteers: experiment.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: What is the purpose of a control group in an experiment?
choices: It makes sure that every subject gets exactly the same treatment, so that no differences can ever occur
It lets the researchers choose which subjects are expected to do well, so that the result is easier to see
It gives a group that does not get the treatment, so the effect of the treatment can be judged
It makes the experiment larger, so that the number of subjects is always an even number in the groups
questions.answer: It gives a group that does not get the treatment, so the effect of the treatment can be judged
questions.solution: Without a comparison group there is no way to tell whether a change is due to the treatment or would have happened anyway.

solve.answer: It gives a group that does not get the treatment, so the effect of the treatment can be judged
solve.work: Control group provides a baseline without treatment to judge the treatment effect.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: In a study, 90 volunteers are randomly assigned so that the treatment group has twice as many people as the control group. How many people are in the control group?
questions.solution: The treatment group is 2 parts and the control group is 1 part, so there are 3 equal parts. Each part is $90\div 3=30$ people, and the control group is 30.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: A teacher asks every one of the 30 students in her class whether they have a pet, and 18 say yes. Which statement is supported by the data?
choices: 60% of all of the students in the whole school have a pet
60% of the students in this class have a pet
60% of all of the students in the whole country have a pet
Exactly 18 students in every class in the school have a pet
questions.answer: 60% of the students in this class have a pet
questions.solution: She asked the whole class, so the data describe that class exactly: $18\div 30=60\%$. Nothing is said about other classes or other schools.

solve.answer: 60% of the students in this class have a pet
solve.work: 18/30 = 60% of this class only; the class is not a random sample of the school or country.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: A random sample of 25 batteries from a batch of 1,000 finds that 2 are defective. Based on the sample, about how many batteries in the batch are defective?
questions.solution: The sample rate is $\frac{2}{25}=0.08$. Of 1,000 batteries, about $0.08\times 1000=80$ are defective.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: Cities with more libraries tend to have more bookstores. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Building libraries makes new bookstores open in the city during the following year or so
Opening bookstores causes the city to decide to build more libraries in the next years
Libraries and bookstores tend to go together, perhaps because large cities have more of both
Libraries and bookstores are unrelated, since neither one is the cause of the other one
questions.answer: Libraries and bookstores tend to go together, perhaps because large cities have more of both
questions.solution: The data show an association. A hidden variable, the size of the city, may explain both. Neither cause is shown, and an association does exist.

solve.answer: Libraries and bookstores tend to go together, perhaps because large cities have more of both
solve.work: Association only; city size is a plausible lurking variable.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: A poll reports that 35% of adults favor a plan, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. How many percentage points wide is the interval of plausible values?
questions.solution: The interval runs from $35-4=31$ to $35+4=39$ percent, which is $39-31=8$ points wide.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: A poll reports that 62% of voters favor a measure, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Which interval of plausible percents does this give?
choices: From 56% to 68%
From 59% to 62%
From 62% to 65%
From 59% to 65%
questions.answer: From 59% to 65%
questions.solution: Subtract and add the margin: $62-3=59$ and $62+3=65$.

solve.answer: From 59% to 65%

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: What does the margin of error of a poll describe?
choices: How many of the people who were asked refused to take part in the poll when they were called
How far the sample percent may be from the true percent, because of random sampling
How many of the answers were written down by mistake by the people who ran the poll
How far the sample percent is from 100%, which is the largest percent that is possible
questions.answer: How far the sample percent may be from the true percent, because of random sampling
questions.solution: The margin of error describes the expected random difference between the sample result and the whole population's value.

solve.answer: How far the sample percent may be from the true percent, because of random sampling
solve.work: Margin of error: likely distance between sample and true percent due to random sampling.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: To make the margin of error of a poll smaller, what should a pollster do?
choices: Ask only the people who are easy to reach
Ask each person the same question twice
Ask a larger random sample of people
Ask only the people who support the issue
questions.answer: Ask a larger random sample of people
questions.solution: A larger random sample gives a smaller margin of error. The other changes add bias or do not add information.

solve.answer: Ask a larger random sample of people
solve.work: Larger random sample reduces the margin of error.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: An advertisement says, "9 out of 10 users recommend it." Which information is most needed to judge the claim?
choices: What the slogan of the company is, and how long the ad has been shown on television
How long the company has been in business, and in which shops its products are sold
How many people were asked, and how those people were chosen to take part
How much the product costs, and what colors the product comes in when it is sold
questions.answer: How many people were asked, and how those people were chosen to take part
questions.solution: To judge a statistic you need to know the size of the sample and how it was chosen. 9 out of 10 could mean 9 of 10 people chosen by the company.

solve.answer: How many people were asked, and how those people were chosen to take part
solve.work: Need the sample size and how respondents were chosen.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: A news graph shows the temperature for only the last 3 days, and the headline says, "Temperatures are rising dramatically." What should a careful reader ask?
choices: What does the temperature look like over a much longer period of time than three days?
Why does the graph use lines, when a pie chart would show the temperature just as well?
Why are the days shown in order, instead of in a random order across the page of the graph?
How many readers of the news site looked at this graph on the day that it was printed?
questions.answer: What does the temperature look like over a much longer period of time than three days?
questions.solution: Three days is too short to show a trend. A longer record shows whether the rise is unusual or just normal variation.

solve.answer: What does the temperature look like over a much longer period of time than three days?
solve.work: Three days is too short a window; ask about a longer period.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: A headline says, "Prices doubled!" but the price of a notebook rose from 5 dollars to 7 dollars. By what percent did the price actually increase?
questions.solution: The increase is $7-5=2$ dollars. As a percent of the old price: $\frac{2}{5}=0.4$, or 40 percent, not 100 percent.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: People who carry umbrellas are more likely to get wet, so a writer claims that umbrellas make people wet. What is the best critique?
choices: Umbrellas are made of cloth, so they must hold water onto the people who carry them
Rain is a lurking variable: it makes people carry umbrellas and also makes them wet
People who get wet buy umbrellas first, and that is all that the data can ever show
The data cannot show anything, since only people who carry umbrellas were looked at
questions.answer: Rain is a lurking variable: it makes people carry umbrellas and also makes them wet
questions.solution: Rainy weather leads to both carrying an umbrella and getting wet. The link is real but the umbrella is not the cause.

solve.answer: Rain is a lurking variable: it makes people carry umbrellas and also makes them wet
solve.work: Rain is the lurking variable causing both umbrella-carrying and getting wet.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: An ad says, "Our brand is 25% cheaper," and the claim is true. The competitor's price is 40 dollars. What is the price of the advertised brand, in dollars?
questions.solution: 25% of 40 is 10, so the advertised brand costs $40-10=30$ dollars.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: A man says, "My neighbor took vitamin C every day and never got sick, so vitamin C prevents illness." What is the best critique?
choices: The claim is proven, because the neighbor took the vitamin and stayed healthy all of the time
The claim cannot be tested, because illness is never affected by anything that can be taken
One person is not enough evidence; many people, with a comparison group, would be needed
The claim is false, because everyone who takes vitamin C gets sick sooner or later in life
questions.answer: One person is not enough evidence; many people, with a comparison group, would be needed
questions.solution: A single story (an anecdote) cannot show a general effect. A fair test needs many people and a group that did not take the vitamin.

solve.answer: One person is not enough evidence; many people, with a comparison group, would be needed
solve.work: Anecdote of one person: need many subjects and a comparison group.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: A study found that a drug cured an illness in mice, and a headline says, "Drug cures people." What is the best critique?
choices: Results for mice may not hold for people, so the headline goes beyond the study
A drug can cure only mice or only people, and never both kinds of animals at the same time
The headline is correct, because mice and people both can have the same kinds of illness
The study is worthless, because animals may never be used in any kind of study of drugs
questions.answer: Results for mice may not hold for people, so the headline goes beyond the study
questions.solution: The study was done on mice. A claim about people needs a study of people.

solve.answer: Results for mice may not hold for people, so the headline goes beyond the study
solve.work: Mouse results may not generalize to humans; headline overreaches.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: Which part of a report tells readers what the investigation was trying to find out?
choices: The description of the graphs, in the middle of the report
The list of the people who helped, at the end of the report
The color of the cover, on the front page of the report
The statement of the question, near the start of the report
questions.answer: The statement of the question, near the start of the report
questions.solution: A report begins with the question or purpose, so readers know what the data are meant to answer.

solve.answer: The statement of the question, near the start of the report
solve.work: The statistical question stated near the start says what the investigation sought.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: A graph in a report should always include which of these?
choices: A bright background color that matches the cover of the report
A title and labeled axes that give the units
A picture of the people who took part in the study that is shown
The writer's guess about what the next set of data will show
questions.answer: A title and labeled axes that give the units
questions.solution: Without a title, axis labels and units, readers cannot tell what the graph shows.

solve.answer: A title and labeled axes that give the units
solve.work: A title and labeled axes with units.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: Which list puts the stages of a statistical investigation in a sensible order?
choices: Collect data, report conclusions, ask a question, then analyze the data that were found
Analyze the data, ask a question, report conclusions, then collect the data afterward
Ask a question, collect data, analyze the data, then report conclusions and limits
Report conclusions, ask a question, analyze the data, then collect the data at the end
questions.answer: Ask a question, collect data, analyze the data, then report conclusions and limits
questions.solution: The question comes first, then data are collected to answer it, then analyzed, and last the conclusions and their limits are reported.

solve.answer: Ask a question, collect data, analyze the data, then report conclusions and limits
solve.work: Ask a question, collect data, analyze, report conclusions and limits.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: A company ad says, "The typical worker here earns 90,000 dollars a year." The company has 10 workers: 9 earn 40,000 dollars each and the owner earns 540,000 dollars. The 90,000 dollars is the mean pay. What is the best critique of the ad?
choices: The ad is accurate, because the mean is always the best single number for describing the typical pay of workers
The mean can never be used to describe pay, so the claim of the ad has no real meaning at all to readers
The median would be higher than the mean here, so the ad actually understates what a typical worker earns
The owner's high pay pulls the mean up; the median, 40,000 dollars, describes a typical worker better
questions.answer: The owner's high pay pulls the mean up; the median, 40,000 dollars, describes a typical worker better
questions.solution: The mean is (9 x 40,000 + 540,000) / 10 = 90,000, but nine of the ten workers earn 40,000. One very large value pulls the mean up, while the median, 40,000, matches what a typical worker earns.

solve.answer: The owner's high pay pulls the mean up; the median, 40,000 dollars, describes a typical worker better
solve.work: Mean = (9x40,000 + 540,000)/10 = 900,000/10 = 90,000. Median = 40,000 (9 of 10 earn that). The owner's outlier pay pulls the mean up; the median better describes a typical worker.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A shop has 500 customers. It leaves feedback cards at the checkout, and 25 customers fill one in. Of those 25, 20 rate the shop as excellent, and the shop advertises "80% of our customers rate us excellent." What percent of all 500 customers are known to have rated the shop as excellent?
questions.solution: Only 20 of the 500 customers are known to have rated the shop as excellent: 20 / 500 = 0.04, or 4%. The 80% comes only from the 25 people who chose to return a card, and people with strong opinions are the ones most likely to do so. The other 475 customers did not say, so the advertised claim is not supported.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
