questions.stem: A random sample of 150 students from a school of 1,200 students found that 30 of them ride the bus. Based on this sample, about how many of the 1,200 students ride the bus?
questions.solution: In the sample, 30 / 150 = 20% ride the bus. Applying 20% to the whole school gives 0.20 times 1,200 = 240 students, as an estimate.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: In a poll with a margin of error of 4 percentage points, Candidate A has 49% and Candidate B has 46%. Which statement is best supported by the poll?
choices: Candidate A is certainly ahead, because 49% is greater than 46%.
The two ranges overlap, so the poll cannot say for sure who is ahead.
The poll must be wrong, because the two percents do not add up to 100%.
The 4 points means that 4% of the people polled gave a wrong answer.
questions.answer: The two ranges overlap, so the poll cannot say for sure who is ahead.
questions.solution: Candidate A's range is 45% to 53% and Candidate B's range is 42% to 50%. These overlap, so the true values could be in either order, and the poll cannot say who is ahead. The percents need not add to 100% because other people may be undecided or support others.

solve.answer: The two ranges overlap, so the poll cannot say for sure who is ahead.
solve.work: A: 45-53, B: 42-50 overlap; cannot say who leads.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: A poll of 1,000 randomly selected voters finds that 52% support a measure, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Which is the most accurate report?
choices: Exactly 52% of all voters support the measure.
Between 49% and 55% of the 1,000 voters polled support the measure.
Between 49% and 55% of all voters likely support the measure.
The measure will win, because 52% is more than 50%.
questions.answer: Between 49% and 55% of all voters likely support the measure.
questions.solution: The margin of error describes how far the percent for ALL voters may be from the sample percent: 52% - 3% = 49% and 52% + 3% = 55%. The 1,000 people polled supported the measure at exactly 52%, and since the range includes values below 50%, the poll cannot promise a win.

solve.answer: Between 49% and 55% of all voters likely support the measure.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: A bar graph has a vertical axis that starts at 50 instead of 0. One bar reaches 55 and another reaches 60. Measured from the bottom of the graph, the taller bar is how many times as tall as the shorter bar?
questions.solution: Measured from the bottom of the graph at 50, the bars are 55 - 50 = 5 and 60 - 50 = 10 units tall. The taller bar looks 10 / 5 = 2 times as tall, although 60 is only about 9% more than 55.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: An ad says, "Our new tires stop 20% shorter." It does not say what the tires are compared with. What is the best critique?
choices: A percent cannot be used to describe a stopping distance.
Without a comparison, such as the old tires, the 20% has no clear meaning.
The claim is trustworthy, because 20% is such a precise and specific number.
The claim would be believable only if the number were 50% instead of the 20% given.
questions.answer: Without a comparison, such as the old tires, the 20% has no clear meaning.
questions.solution: A percent change is always a change from something. "20% shorter" than which tires, and on what road? Without that information the number cannot be checked. A precise number is not the same as a trustworthy one.

solve.answer: Without a comparison, such as the old tires, the 20% has no clear meaning.
solve.work: "20% shorter" than what? Without a reference (old tires, competitor) the claim is meaningless. A false (percent can describe a distance), C, D irrelevant.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: A town had 2 burglaries last year and 6 this year. A headline says, "Burglaries soared by 200%!" By how many burglaries did the number actually increase?
questions.solution: The number went from 2 to 6, an increase of 6 - 2 = 4 burglaries. A 200% increase is technically correct (4 / 2 = 200%), but it sounds much bigger than 4 more incidents because the starting number is so small.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: A headline says, "Study proves chocolate makes people smarter!" The study had 8 adults who ate chocolate and then solved a puzzle 10% faster, on average, than they did the day before. What is the best critique?
choices: The headline is fair, because the adults solved the puzzle faster after eating chocolate.
There is no comparison group and the sample is tiny, so nothing is proved.
The headline is fair, because a study of any size can prove cause and effect.
The study is flawed only because 10% is too small a change to measure.
questions.answer: There is no comparison group and the sample is tiny, so nothing is proved.
questions.solution: Without a group that did not eat chocolate, the improvement could come from practice, since they had seen the puzzle the day before. And 8 people is a very small sample. Neither supports a claim that chocolate "proves" anything.

solve.answer: There is no comparison group and the sample is tiny, so nothing is proved.
solve.work: No control group, n=8: proves nothing.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: Which survey question is worded so that it pushes people toward answering yes?
choices: Should the school day start later, start earlier, or stay at the same time that it is now?
Do you think that the school day should start later than it does at present at your school, or not?
How would you describe your opinion about the time at which the school day begins each morning?
Since a later start would improve health so much, shouldn't the school day start later?
questions.answer: Since a later start would improve health so much, shouldn't the school day start later?
questions.solution: The first question gives a reason that favors a later start and asks for agreement. The other questions state the options without pushing toward one answer.

solve.answer: Since a later start would improve health so much, shouldn't the school day start later?
solve.work: A presupposes a large health benefit ("shouldn't...?"), a leading question.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A survey is mailed to 1,000 randomly chosen households, but only 90 households send it back. Which statement is best?
choices: The results are free of bias, because the 1,000 households were chosen at random to receive the survey
The results may be biased, because the 90 households that replied may differ from the 910 that did not
The results are certain to be right, because every one of the 90 answers that came back was counted
The results cannot be used, because a survey must always get at least 100 replies to be of any use
questions.answer: The results may be biased, because the 90 households that replied may differ from the 910 that did not
questions.solution: With so many households not replying (nonresponse), the 90 who did may be different from the rest, for example more interested in the topic. Random selection at the start does not fix that.

solve.answer: The results may be biased, because the 90 households that replied may differ from the 910 that did not
solve.work: 9% response rate: nonresponse bias possible; the 90 responders may differ from the 910.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A school has 300 students in each of the grades 9, 10, 11 and 12. A survey about lunch is given only to the students in grade 9. What percent of the school's students had a chance of being surveyed?
questions.solution: There are $4\times 300=1200$ students, and only 300 of them could be surveyed: $\frac{300}{1200}=0.25$, or 25 percent.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: The website of a baseball team runs a poll, "Who is the best team in the league?" Of the votes, 85% are for the home team. What is the best explanation?
choices: The home team must be the best team in the league, because the votes of so many people all agree
The poll was too short, because a poll with only one question can never show what a group thinks
Most visitors to the team's site are its fans, so the voters are not typical of all baseball fans
Fans of the other teams must all have voted at random, which is what makes the percent so large
questions.answer: Most visitors to the team's site are its fans, so the voters are not typical of all baseball fans
questions.solution: The voters chose themselves and mostly visit the site because they support the home team. The sample is biased toward that team's fans.

solve.answer: Most visitors to the team's site are its fans, so the voters are not typical of all baseball fans
solve.work: Voluntary poll on a team website: voters are mostly that team's fans, so the sample is biased.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: A study compares a new cold medicine with a pill that has no medicine in it. The patients do not know which pill they got. Why is this done?
choices: It keeps the patients' expectations from changing how they report their symptoms
It makes sure that the patients cannot tell the doctor how they feel during the length of the study
It makes sure that the medicine works in the same way for every patient who takes the real pills
It lets the researchers use fewer patients, because the patients no longer matter in the study
questions.answer: It keeps the patients' expectations from changing how they report their symptoms
questions.solution: If patients knew they had the real medicine, they might feel better just because they expect to. Not knowing (blinding) removes that effect from the comparison.

solve.answer: It keeps the patients' expectations from changing how they report their symptoms
solve.work: Blinding with a placebo prevents expectations (placebo effect) from affecting reported symptoms.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: A study of 5,000 adults found that dog owners have lower blood pressure than adults without dogs. The researchers did not give anyone a dog. Which is the most important limitation?
choices: It has too many adults, because a study of this kind can have at most 1,000 people in it
Blood pressure cannot be used to compare any groups of people with one another at all
It has no limitation, since both groups are large and the size of the study is so big
It is observational, so dog owners may differ in other ways, such as how active they are
questions.answer: It is observational, so dog owners may differ in other ways, such as how active they are
questions.solution: Nobody was assigned to own a dog, so the owners may differ from the others in activity, age or income. Those differences, not the dog, may explain the blood pressure.

solve.answer: It is observational, so dog owners may differ in other ways, such as how active they are
solve.work: Observational: confounders such as activity level may explain the difference; no causation.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: A teacher wants to test a new method on 40 students: 24 girls and 16 boys. She randomly assigns half of the girls and half of the boys to the new method (blocking by gender). How many girls get the new method?
questions.solution: Half of the 24 girls get the new method: $24\div 2=12$. (Half of the 16 boys, 8, also get it, for 20 in all.)

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: Records show that the more fire trucks are sent to a fire, the more damage the fire does. What is the most likely confounding variable?
choices: The color of the fire trucks, since the color of the trucks can change how a fire burns
The size of the fire, since big fires need more trucks and also cause more damage
The name of the street where the fire started, since street names affect both of the counts
The number of people who watch, since crowds always attract more trucks and cause damage
questions.answer: The size of the fire, since big fires need more trucks and also cause more damage
questions.solution: A confounding variable is linked to both of the things being compared. A bigger fire leads to more trucks and to more damage, so the trucks do not cause the damage.

solve.answer: The size of the fire, since big fires need more trucks and also cause more damage
solve.work: Fire size drives both the number of trucks and the damage.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: Students who take music lessons have higher math scores than those who do not, in an observational study. Which statement do the data support?
choices: Students with music lessons tended to have higher scores here, which alone does not show a cause
Music lessons raise the math scores of any student who takes them, as the study has shown
Students with music lessons tended to have lower scores here, because the lessons take time
Music lessons and math scores are unrelated, since the study did not assign the lessons to students
questions.answer: Students with music lessons tended to have higher scores here, which alone does not show a cause
questions.solution: The data show higher scores for the music group, an association. Because the lessons were not assigned, a cause is not shown.

solve.answer: Students with music lessons tended to have higher scores here, which alone does not show a cause
solve.work: Observational: music-lesson students scored higher here, but no cause is shown.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: A random sample of 200 customers finds that they spend 30 dollars per visit on average. The store has 5,000 visits per week. Based on the sample, about how many dollars are spent in a week?
questions.solution: The average is about 30 dollars per visit, so 5,000 visits come to about $30\times 5000=150000$ dollars.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: In a random sample of 400 teens, 240 use social media for at least 3 hours a day. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: All of the teens in the population use social media for at least 3 hours every single day
Exactly 240 of the teens in the whole population use it for at least 3 hours each day
Social media use for 3 hours a day makes teens in the population feel better each day
More than half of all teens in the population probably use it for at least 3 hours a day
questions.answer: More than half of all teens in the population probably use it for at least 3 hours a day
questions.solution: In the sample, $\frac{240}{400}=60\%$ use it that much. For a random sample this size, the population share is probably above half. Nothing more can be concluded.

solve.answer: More than half of all teens in the population probably use it for at least 3 hours a day
solve.work: 240/400 = 60%, so more than half of the population probably do.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: A random sample of 200 students from the high schools of one city has an average commute of 22 minutes. To which group can the conclusion fairly be applied?
choices: Students at all high schools in the whole country
Students at the high schools of that city
All of the residents of the city, of every age
Only the 200 students in the sample, and no one else
questions.answer: Students at the high schools of that city
questions.solution: A random sample supports conclusions about the group it was drawn from: the high school students of that city. It does not reach other places or other age groups.

solve.answer: Students at the high schools of that city
solve.work: Sample drawn from the city's high-school students generalizes to that population only.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: A poll of randomly chosen voters has a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Candidate X has 52% and candidate Y has 45%. Which statement is best supported?
choices: X's range, 49% to 55%, is above Y's range, 42% to 48%, so X is probably ahead
The race is too close to call, because the two percents are within 10 points of each other
X is certainly ahead, because no poll that gives a margin of error can ever be wrong at all
The ranges overlap, so the poll cannot say who is ahead among all voters in the population
questions.answer: X's range, 49% to 55%, is above Y's range, 42% to 48%, so X is probably ahead
questions.solution: X: $52\pm 3$ gives 49 to 55. Y: $45\pm 3$ gives 42 to 48. The ranges do not overlap, so X is probably ahead.

solve.answer: X's range, 49% to 55%, is above Y's range, 42% to 48%, so X is probably ahead
solve.work: X: 49-55, Y: 42-48. No overlap, X probably ahead.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: A poll has a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Last month a senator's approval was 43% and this month it is 49%. Each percent gives an interval of plausible values. By how many percentage points do the two intervals overlap?
questions.solution: Last month: 39 to 47. This month: 45 to 53. The intervals overlap from 45 to 47, which is $47-45=2$ points.

solve.work: Last month 39-47, this month 45-53; overlap 45 to 47 = 2 points.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: A website lets visitors vote on a question, and it reports "a margin of error of 1 point" for its 20,000 votes. Which statement is correct?
choices: With 20,000 votes, the result is certainly within 1 point of the opinion of all of the people
The margin of error is too small to be real, since no poll can have a margin below 3 points
The margin of error shows that the voters are a random sample of all of the people in the area
The margin covers only random sampling variation, so it cannot fix a biased way of choosing voters
questions.answer: The margin covers only random sampling variation, so it cannot fix a biased way of choosing voters
questions.solution: The margin of error describes chance variation in a random sample. Visitors who vote on their own are not a random sample, and the margin cannot repair that.

solve.answer: The margin covers only random sampling variation, so it cannot fix a biased way of choosing voters
solve.work: Margin of error covers only random sampling error; a self-selected sample remains biased.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: The unemployment rate rose from 4% to 6%. Which statement is correct?
choices: It rose by 2 percent, which is the same thing as a rise of 2 percentage points
It rose by 6 percent, because 6% is the new rate for all of the workers
It rose by 50 percentage points, which is the same as a 2% change in the rate
It rose by 2 percentage points, which is a 50% increase in the rate
questions.answer: It rose by 2 percentage points, which is a 50% increase in the rate
questions.solution: The difference is $6-4=2$ percentage points. Compared with the old rate, $\frac{2}{4}=50\%$ is the relative increase. The two are different measures.

solve.answer: It rose by 2 percentage points, which is a 50% increase in the rate

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: A company's profit rose 10% in year 1 and then fell 10% in year 2. It started at 100 thousand dollars. What is the profit after year 2, in thousands of dollars?
questions.solution: After year 1: $100\times 1.1=110$. After year 2: $110\times 0.9=99$. A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall does not return to the start.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: A poll asks students to name their reasons for choosing a college. The percents for the five reasons in a bar graph add up to 130%. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The graph must be wrong, because percents of a group always add up to exactly 100% in any graph
Students could choose more than one reason, so the percents do not have to add up to 100%
Some of the percents were rounded up by a large amount, which added 30 points to the total
The sample was larger than the whole population, which makes the percents add to more than 100%
questions.answer: Students could choose more than one reason, so the percents do not have to add up to 100%
questions.solution: When people may pick several answers, each percent is out of all the students, so the total can pass 100%.

solve.answer: Students could choose more than one reason, so the percents do not have to add up to 100%
solve.work: Multiple responses allowed, so percents can exceed 100%.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: Cities with more police officers tend to have more crime, and a writer concludes that police cause crime. Why is the conclusion not supported?
choices: Police officers never affect crime in any way, so no link at all can be seen in the data
The data come from cities, and one city can never be compared with another city in a study
More crime can only be found in cities in which the police officers are new to their jobs
Cities with more crime may hire more police, so the cause could run in the other direction
questions.answer: Cities with more crime may hire more police, so the cause could run in the other direction
questions.solution: A link does not show which variable causes which. High crime can lead a city to hire more police (reverse causation).

solve.answer: Cities with more crime may hire more police, so the cause could run in the other direction
solve.work: Reverse causation: high-crime cities hire more police (also city size).

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: A headline says, "Teen smoking cut in half!" In one town, smokers fell from 8 of every 100 teens to 4 of every 100 teens. The town has 5,000 teens. How many fewer teens smoke now?
questions.solution: The rate fell by $8-4=4$ per 100, which is 0.04. Of 5,000 teens, $0.04\times 5000=200$ fewer smoke.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: In an elementary school, shoe size and reading score have a correlation of 0.9, and a writer says that bigger feet make children read better. What is the most likely hidden variable?
choices: The brand of the shoes, since some brands are sold only to children who are good readers
Age: older children have bigger feet and also read better
The color of the shoes, since the colors of shoes are known to change reading scores
The number of letters in each name, since long names give children more practice reading
questions.answer: Age: older children have bigger feet and also read better
questions.solution: Older children have larger feet and have also had more years of learning. Age explains both, so the feet do not cause the reading.

solve.answer: Age: older children have bigger feet and also read better
solve.work: Age drives both foot size and reading ability.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: Which sentence is the best statement of a limitation in a report on a school survey?
choices: Only seniors were surveyed, so the results may not describe the other grades
The survey was long, so the writer was tired when the data were put into the computer
Seniors are the best students, so the results of the survey are right for everyone
Some students do not like surveys, so the report should not be believed at all
questions.answer: Only seniors were surveyed, so the results may not describe the other grades
questions.solution: A limitation says who or what the results may not describe and why. Only the first does that clearly.

solve.answer: Only seniors were surveyed, so the results may not describe the other grades
solve.work: A genuine limitation: sample covers only seniors, so results may not generalize to other grades.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: A report on household incomes in a town has a few very high incomes. Which statistic should it use to describe a typical household?
choices: The mean, because it uses every value, and so it is always the best choice for a report
The range, because it shows the lowest income and the highest income at the same time
The maximum, because it shows the biggest value, which is the one that people read first
The median, because a few very high incomes pull the mean up and distort it
questions.answer: The median, because a few very high incomes pull the mean up and distort it
questions.solution: A few very high incomes raise the mean above what most households earn. The median is not pulled up by them.

solve.answer: The median, because a few very high incomes pull the mean up and distort it
solve.work: Skewed by a few high incomes: the median is the resistant typical value.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: A school starts a new reading program. Students' average score rises from 62 in the fall to 71 in the spring, and the school announces that the program raised scores. Which is the most important limitation of this comparison?
choices: Scores from a fall test and a spring test can never be compared, because the tests are given in different seasons
The gain is too small to matter, because any rise in scores over a year is caused only by chance variation
The program cannot have worked, because the scores of some individual students went down during the year
There was no comparison group, so normal growth over a school year may explain some or all of the gain
questions.answer: There was no comparison group, so normal growth over a school year may explain some or all of the gain
questions.solution: Students usually improve over a school year even without a new program. With no group that skipped the program, we cannot tell how much of the 9-point gain the program caused.

solve.answer: There was no comparison group, so normal growth over a school year may explain some or all of the gain
solve.work: A before/after comparison with no control group cannot separate the program's effect from ordinary growth across a school year. The other options are false generalisations.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: Chen surveyed a random sample of 200 adults in her city. Of them, 56% favor a new bus line, with a margin of error of about 7 percentage points. Her draft says, "A majority of adults in the city favor the bus line." Which sentence is the best revision?
choices: Exactly 56% of all adults in the city favor the line, because the sample of adults was chosen at random
More than half of the adults in the city favor the line, because 56% is greater than 50% in the sample
In the sample, 56% favored the line, but a 7-point margin of error leaves a majority uncertain
The poll shows that 56% of the city wants the line built, so the city should go ahead and build it right away
questions.answer: In the sample, 56% favored the line, but a 7-point margin of error leaves a majority uncertain
questions.solution: With a margin of error of 7 points, the city's true percent could be anywhere from about 49% to 63%, which includes values below 50%. A good report states the sample result and says a majority is not certain.

solve.answer: In the sample, 56% favored the line, but a 7-point margin of error leaves a majority uncertain
solve.work: 56% +/- 7 gives roughly 49% to 63%, which includes values below 50%, so a majority is not established. Best revision reports the sample result and the uncertainty.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A county gym surveys 200 randomly chosen teenage members about their weekly exercise and reports, "Teenagers in our county exercise 9 hours a week on average." Which statement about this conclusion is correct?
choices: It applies to all teenagers in the county, because the 200 members were chosen at random.
It applies to no one, because 200 members is far too small a sample for any conclusion to be drawn.
It applies at most to teenagers who are members of the gym, not to all teenagers in the county.
It applies to all people in the county, because teenagers at the gym represent everyone who lives there.
questions.answer: It applies at most to teenagers who are members of the gym, not to all teenagers in the county.
questions.solution: A random sample from gym members represents gym members only. Teenagers who belong to a gym may exercise more than other teenagers in the county, so the conclusion cannot safely be stretched to all of them. The sample size of 200 is not the problem; the group it was drawn from is.

solve.answer: It applies at most to teenagers who are members of the gym, not to all teenagers in the county.
solve.work: Random sample of teenage gym members generalizes at most to teenage gym members; members likely exercise more than non-members. B/C/D overreach or wrong.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: A gardener puts a new fertilizer on 3 tomato plants and no fertilizer on 3 other plants. The fertilized plants produce more tomatoes. What is the best advice for her report?
choices: Report that the fertilizer is proven to work, because the fertilized plants produced more.
Say that only 6 plants were used, so the result is weak evidence and more plants should be tested.
Report that the result must be due to chance alone, because only 6 plants were used in the whole test.
Report that the number of plants does not matter, because plants of one kind grow alike.
questions.answer: Say that only 6 plants were used, so the result is weak evidence and more plants should be tested.
questions.solution: With so few plants, differences between individual plants could easily explain the result. A careful report states the small sample as a limit and calls for a larger test. It neither proves the fertilizer works nor claims the result must be chance.

solve.answer: Say that only 6 plants were used, so the result is weak evidence and more plants should be tested.
solve.work: 3 vs 3 plants is a tiny sample; the difference could be chance, so it is weak evidence and should be replicated. A overclaims, B says must be chance (overclaims), D false.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: A poll of 2,000 randomly chosen adults from a city of 60,000 adults found that 35% favor a new bike lane, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Using the top of the margin of error, what is the greatest number of the city's 60,000 adults who could plausibly favor the bike lane?
questions.solution: The plausible range for the percent in the whole city is 35% plus or minus 3 points, so it runs from 32% to 38%. The top is 38%, and 0.38 times 60,000 = 22,800 adults.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: In an experiment, 80 volunteers were randomly assigned to follow a new stretching routine or not. After a month, the stretching group had fewer back-pain days on average, and the difference was too large to be explained by chance alone. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The routine likely reduces back-pain days for people like these volunteers.
The routine reduces back-pain days for every person in the country.
The routine has no effect, because the volunteers were not chosen at random from everyone.
The difference is probably due to chance, so the routine has no effect.
questions.answer: The routine likely reduces back-pain days for people like these volunteers.
questions.solution: Random assignment and a difference too large for chance support the claim that the routine caused the improvement in these volunteers. Because the volunteers were not a random sample, the claim should be limited to people like them, not to everyone.

solve.answer: The routine likely reduces back-pain days for people like these volunteers.
solve.work: Randomized experiment supports causal conclusion for volunteers like these.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: Two polls of the same population find mayor approval rates of 46% and 49%. Each has a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Which statement is best?
choices: The polls disagree, so at least one of them must have been done wrong.
The polls are consistent only because they have the same margin of error.
The polls disagree, because the true approval cannot be both 46% and 49%.
The polls are consistent, because the two ranges overlap.
questions.answer: The polls are consistent, because the two ranges overlap.
questions.solution: The first poll gives a range of 43% to 49% and the second gives 46% to 52%. These ranges overlap from 46% to 49%, so one true approval rate could fit both polls. Sample results naturally vary a little from poll to poll.

solve.answer: The polls are consistent, because the two ranges overlap.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: A company says, "Our average salary is 85,000 dollars." The company has 10 employees: 9 earn 40,000 dollars each and the owner earns 490,000 dollars. Which statement is correct?
choices: The mean is 85,000 dollars, and it is the best description of a typical employee.
The median is 85,000 dollars, so the company's claim is accurate for a typical employee at the company.
The mean is 85,000 dollars, but the median, 40,000 dollars, better describes a typical employee.
The mean is 40,000 dollars, because most of the employees earn that amount and only one earns more.
questions.answer: The mean is 85,000 dollars, but the median, 40,000 dollars, better describes a typical employee.
questions.solution: The mean is (9 times 40,000 + 490,000) / 10 = 850,000 / 10 = 85,000 dollars, so the claim is true as a mean. But the owner's large salary pulls the mean up. The median is 40,000 dollars, which is much closer to what a typical employee earns.

solve.answer: The mean is 85,000 dollars, but the median, 40,000 dollars, better describes a typical employee.
solve.work: Mean = (9*40000 + 490000)/10 = 850000/10 = 85000. Median of nine 40000s and one 490000 = 40000. The mean is skewed by the owner; the median is typical. C.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: A student fits a line to the last 6 months of a store's sales and uses it to predict sales 5 years from now, getting a number 10 times larger than any month so far. What should her report say about this prediction?
choices: It is reliable, because the line fits the last 6 months of the store's sales data very closely.
It is reliable, because a straight line can always be extended to any future time that is needed.
It goes far beyond the time period of the data, so it is unreliable and the limit should be stated.
It should not be reported at all, because a model can never be used to predict anything about the future.
questions.answer: It goes far beyond the time period of the data, so it is unreliable and the limit should be stated.
questions.solution: A model is built from data over a certain range. Predicting far outside that range (extrapolating) is risky, since sales rarely keep growing along a straight line for years. A good report says what range the model covers and warns that a distant prediction is unreliable.

solve.answer: It goes far beyond the time period of the data, so it is unreliable and the limit should be stated.
solve.work: Extrapolating 5 years from 6 months of data is far outside the data range; unreliable, limit should be stated. A.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A city surveys residents twice. The question "Do you support a tax to help the city's schoolchildren?" gets 72% yes. The question "Do you support raising your taxes?" gets 31% yes. What is the best explanation?
choices: The wording of a question can change the answers, so each result depends on how the question was asked
One of the surveys must have had a much larger sample than the other, since the results differ so much
Residents change their opinions each day, so any two surveys will disagree by about this much
The 72% result is the correct one and the 31% result is wrong, since a tax for children is a good thing
questions.answer: The wording of a question can change the answers, so each result depends on how the question was asked
questions.solution: The two questions describe the same tax in different words, one with an appealing purpose. This is wording bias: the answers depend on how the question is framed.

solve.answer: The wording of a question can change the answers, so each result depends on how the question was asked
solve.work: Wording effects: framing (schoolchildren vs your taxes) changes the answers.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A website invites visitors to answer a poll about a new law, and 50,000 people respond. A random sample of 500 residents is also surveyed. Which is the better basis for describing all of the residents?
choices: The 50,000 responses, because a larger sample is always more trustworthy than a smaller sample
Neither one, because no sample of any size can ever say anything about all of the residents of a city
Both are equally good, because the number of responses never matters in any survey or any poll of people
The random sample of 500, since even a huge voluntary sample can be biased and size cannot fix that
questions.answer: The random sample of 500, since even a huge voluntary sample can be biased and size cannot fix that
questions.solution: Size reduces random error but not bias. The visitors chose themselves, so their answers may be far from the views of all residents, while a random sample of 500 is fair.

solve.answer: The random sample of 500, since even a huge voluntary sample can be biased and size cannot fix that
solve.work: A random sample of 500 is better; a large voluntary sample stays biased.

questions.skill: Identify bias in a sample or a survey question
questions.stem: A survey reaches only households with internet access, which is 70% of the households in a region. Of those households, 63% support a plan. Suppose the households without internet support it at a rate of 40%. What percent of ALL households in the region support the plan?
questions.solution: The households with internet give $0.7\times 63=44.1$ points. The others give $0.3\times 40=12$ points. Together: $44.1+12=56.1$ percent, lower than the 63% the survey would report.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: A study reports that a difference between a treatment group and a control group is "statistically significant." What does this mean?
choices: The treatment is certain to work for every person who takes it, whenever it is used in the future
The difference between the groups is big enough to matter in daily life for every person alike
A difference this large would be unlikely by chance alone if the treatment had no effect
The study had no flaws, so there is no need to ask how the subjects were chosen at the start
questions.answer: A difference this large would be unlikely by chance alone if the treatment had no effect
questions.solution: Significance means the result is hard to explain by chance alone. It does not mean the effect is large, certain, or free of other problems.

solve.answer: A difference this large would be unlikely by chance alone if the treatment had no effect
solve.work: Statistically significant: a difference this large would be unlikely by chance if there were no effect.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: A random sample of 300 adults from a town is asked about sleep and mood. Those who sleep more report better moods. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: It can describe adults in that town, but it cannot show that more sleep causes better moods
It shows that more sleep causes better moods for every adult in the world, since the sample was random
It tells nothing about adults in the town, because only 300 of the adults in the town were asked
It shows that better moods cause more sleep, since the people who are happy go to bed early
questions.answer: It can describe adults in that town, but it cannot show that more sleep causes better moods
questions.solution: Random selection lets the results apply to the town. But sleep was not assigned, so the study shows an association only, not a cause.

solve.answer: It can describe adults in that town, but it cannot show that more sleep causes better moods
solve.work: Random sample allows generalizing to the town's adults; observational, so no causation.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: A school tests a new reading program. The best teacher in the school teaches the group that uses the new program, and a new teacher teaches the group that uses the old program. The new-program group scores higher. Which statement is correct?
choices: The new program caused the higher scores, because the two groups took the very same test at the same time
The groups cannot be compared at all, because a study can use only one teacher for both of the groups
The old program caused the lower scores, because the new teacher has less experience than the other
The teacher and the program are mixed together, so the study cannot tell which caused the higher scores
questions.answer: The teacher and the program are mixed together, so the study cannot tell which caused the higher scores
questions.solution: The two groups differ in two ways at once, the program and the teacher, so either could explain the difference. This is confounding.

solve.answer: The teacher and the program are mixed together, so the study cannot tell which caused the higher scores
solve.work: Teacher is confounded with program; cannot separate the causes.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: In an experiment, 40 volunteers were randomly split into two groups, and the treated group's average score was 4 points higher. In 1,000 computer reshufflings of the same scores into two random groups, a difference of 4 points or more happened only 12 times. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: A difference this large happens often by chance, so there is no evidence of an effect at all
The treatment is proven to work for everyone, since 12 is much smaller than the 1,000 reshufflings
A difference this large rarely happens by chance, so there is evidence of an effect of the treatment
The result is meaningless, since the reshufflings were done by a computer and not by a person doing it
questions.answer: A difference this large rarely happens by chance, so there is evidence of an effect of the treatment
questions.solution: Chance alone gave such a difference in only 12 of 1,000 shuffles (about 1.2%). That is unusual, so the treatment probably had an effect for people like these volunteers.

solve.answer: A difference this large rarely happens by chance, so there is evidence of an effect of the treatment
solve.work: 12/1000 = 1.2% by chance: rare, so evidence of a treatment effect (not proof).

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: Hospital A has a higher overall survival rate than hospital B. But for mild cases, and for severe cases, taken separately, hospital B has the higher survival rate. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Overall rates can mislead if the hospitals treat different mixes of cases, so compare similar cases only
Hospital A is better, because the overall rate is the only rate that matters for any decision to be made
The data must contain an error, because a hospital cannot be better in both groups and worse overall
Hospital B is better for mild cases only, since severe cases are too unusual to be counted at all
questions.answer: Overall rates can mislead if the hospitals treat different mixes of cases, so compare similar cases only
questions.solution: This can happen when one hospital treats many more severe cases. The combined rate hides the difference between the types of cases, so the groups must be compared separately.

solve.answer: Overall rates can mislead if the hospitals treat different mixes of cases, so compare similar cases only
solve.work: Simpson's paradox: different case mixes; compare within severity groups.

questions.skill: State a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: In a random sample, 120 of 300 adults in town A and 150 of 300 adults in town B favor a proposal. Town A has 12,000 adults and town B has 8,000 adults. Assuming each sample represents its town, about how many adults in the two towns together favor the proposal?

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: A poll of 400 randomly chosen people has a margin of error of 6 percentage points. A pollster instead surveys 1,600 randomly chosen people. The margin of error is proportional to 1 divided by the square root of the sample size. What is the new margin of error, in percentage points?
questions.solution: The sample is 4 times as large, and $\sqrt{4}=2$, so the margin shrinks to half: $6\div 2=3$ points.

solve.work: n multiplied by 4 -> MOE divided by sqrt(4) = 2: 6/2 = 3.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: A poll reports "a 95% confidence level and a margin of error of 3 points." Which is the best way to understand the 95%?
choices: There is a 95% chance that any one person in the poll gave the answer that was written down for them
If the poll were repeated many times with random samples, about 95% of the intervals would hold the truth
The poll is 95% free of bias, so only 5% of the voters were chosen in an unfair way for the poll
The true percent is certain to be within 95 points of the percent that was reported from the sample
questions.answer: If the poll were repeated many times with random samples, about 95% of the intervals would hold the truth
questions.solution: The confidence level describes the method: with repeated random samples, about 95% of the intervals built this way capture the true percent.

solve.answer: If the poll were repeated many times with random samples, about 95% of the intervals would hold the truth
solve.work: Confidence level: in repeated random sampling, about 95% of such intervals contain the true value.

questions.skill: Report uncertainty and margin of error
questions.stem: In a random sample of 400 people, the sample proportion is 0.80, and the standard error is $\sqrt{\frac{0.8\times 0.2}{400}}=0.02$. A margin of error is 2 standard errors. What is the lowest plausible percent for the whole population?
questions.solution: The margin of error is $2\times 0.02=0.04$, or 4 points. The lowest plausible percent is $80-4=76$.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: A news story says, "Of the 100 drivers hurt in crashes, 60 were wearing seat belts, so seat belts do not protect drivers." What is the best critique?
choices: It uses 100 drivers, and a sample of exactly 100 drivers can never show anything about seat belts
It cannot be critiqued, since 60 out of 100 drivers is a majority, and a majority is always proof
It does not say what share of all drivers wear seat belts; if most do, 60 of 100 is normal
It shows that seat belts help, because the 60 drivers were hurt less than the other 40 were
questions.answer: It does not say what share of all drivers wear seat belts; if most do, 60 of 100 is normal
questions.solution: If, say, 90% of all drivers wear belts, then 60% of the hurt drivers wearing them is much lower than expected, which suggests belts help. The count means little without the base rate.

solve.answer: It does not say what share of all drivers wear seat belts; if most do, 60 of 100 is normal
solve.work: Base rate missing: if most drivers wear belts, 60 of 100 hurt is expected or even favorable for belts.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: Town A has 300 crimes and 60,000 residents. Town B has 80 crimes and 10,000 residents. How many more crimes per 1,000 residents does the town with the higher rate have than the other town?
questions.solution: Town A: $\frac{300}{60000}\times 1000=5$ per 1,000. Town B: $\frac{80}{10000}\times 1000=8$ per 1,000. Town B is higher by $8-5=3$.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: A graph shows the total number of cases of an illness to date, which rises every day. The headline says, "The number of new cases each day keeps getting bigger." What is the best critique?
choices: A running total can never go down, so a rising line does not show that new cases each day are growing
A rising line always shows that the new cases each day are growing, so the headline must be correct
Totals should never be graphed, because only the cases for one day at a time can be graphed
The graph is wrong, because a graph of cases must go up and down across the days that it shows
questions.answer: A running total can never go down, so a rising line does not show that new cases each day are growing
questions.solution: A cumulative total rises even if the daily count is steady or falling. To judge the daily count, look at how steeply the total rises, or graph the daily numbers.

solve.answer: A running total can never go down, so a rising line does not show that new cases each day are growing
solve.work: Cumulative totals always rise when there are any new cases; growth of daily new cases would need the slope to increase.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: Product A has an average rating of 4.8 stars from 5 reviews. Product B has 4.5 stars from 2,000 reviews. An ad says, "Product A is rated higher, so it is better." What is the best critique?
choices: Averages cannot be compared across different products, since each product has its own set of buyers
Product B must be better, since 2,000 is a larger number than 5 and its rating is a big one
The ad is fair, because 4.8 is greater than 4.5 and a higher rating always means a better product
An average of only 5 reviews is much less reliable than an average of 2,000 reviews
questions.answer: An average of only 5 reviews is much less reliable than an average of 2,000 reviews
questions.solution: An average of 5 reviews can swing a lot with one extra review. The average of 2,000 reviews is far steadier, so 4.8 versus 4.5 proves little.

solve.answer: An average of only 5 reviews is much less reliable than an average of 2,000 reviews
solve.work: 5 reviews give a far less reliable average than 2,000.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: Class A has 10 students with an average score of 80. Class B has 30 students with an average of 60. A report says, "The average of the two classes together is 70." What is the correct average of all 40 students?
questions.solution: Total points: $10\times 80+30\times 60=800+1800=2600$. Divide by 40 students: $2600\div 40=65$. The report averaged the two averages without weighing the class sizes.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: A researcher tests 20 unrelated foods for a link with acne, using a 5% significance level. One food shows a significant link, and the headline says, "Food X causes acne!" What is the best critique?
choices: A significance level of 5% proves that the food is the cause of the acne in every person who eats it
Only foods that are tested one at a time can ever be linked to a health problem like acne
With 20 tests, about one is expected to look significant by chance alone, so the link may be a fluke
The 19 other foods prove that Food X is the cause, since they showed no link of any kind
questions.answer: With 20 tests, about one is expected to look significant by chance alone, so the link may be a fluke
questions.solution: At the 5% level, about 1 test in 20 will look significant even when nothing is going on. A single hit among many tests is weak evidence.

solve.answer: With 20 tests, about one is expected to look significant by chance alone, so the link may be a fluke
solve.work: Multiple comparisons: 20 tests at 5% expect about 1 false positive.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: Analysts study the planes that returned from missions and find most bullet holes on the wings. They conclude that the wings should get extra armor. What is the best critique?
choices: They studied only planes that survived, so planes hit in other places may never have returned
They counted too many holes, because a study of bullet holes can use at most a few planes
The wings are hit most often, so the wings must also be the part of a plane that matters least
Armor can never be added to a plane, so the study of bullet holes is of no use to the analysts
questions.answer: They studied only planes that survived, so planes hit in other places may never have returned
questions.solution: This is survivorship bias. Planes hit in the engines or cockpit did not come back, so the returning planes show only the harmless places to be hit.

solve.answer: They studied only planes that survived, so planes hit in other places may never have returned
solve.work: Survivorship bias: planes hit elsewhere did not return; armor where returning planes were NOT hit.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: A class collects the commute times of 40 students. Three students have times far longer than the rest, because they ride a ferry. What should the report do about these three values?
choices: Delete them without any comment, since values that are far from the rest never matter
Show them, say why they are unusual, and report the results with them and without them
Keep them but never mention them, since readers prefer a short report with fewer details
Replace them with the mean of the other times, so that the graph looks neater to the reader
questions.answer: Show them, say why they are unusual, and report the results with them and without them
questions.solution: Unusual values may be real. A good report is open about them: it explains them and shows how much they change the results.

solve.answer: Show them, say why they are unusual, and report the results with them and without them
solve.work: Report the outliers, explain them, and give results with and without them.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: A study of a new teaching method found no significant difference between the new and the old method. Which sentence in the report is best?
choices: The study proved that the new method and the old method work equally well for every student
The study proved that the new method is worse, because it did not show a gain over the old method
The study did not find convincing evidence of a difference, which does not show the methods are equal
The study was a failure, since a good study must always find a difference between two groups
questions.answer: The study did not find convincing evidence of a difference, which does not show the methods are equal
questions.solution: Not finding a difference is not proof that there is none: the study may have been too small to see it. The report should say so.

solve.answer: The study did not find convincing evidence of a difference, which does not show the methods are equal
solve.work: Failure to find a significant difference is not evidence of equality.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: A report says, "Of the 250 students surveyed, 60% like pizza, 45% like tacos and 25% like neither." How many of the 250 students like both?
questions.solution: The students who like at least one are $100-25=75\%$. Adding 60% and 45% counts the students who like both twice: $60+45-75=30\%$ like both. $30\%$ of 250 is 75.

questions.skill: Order and content of a statistical report
questions.stem: A report on a survey about grades lists each student's name next to his or her score. What is the main problem?
choices: It shows private information; results should be given for groups, without names
It uses too many names, since a report may name at most five of the people who took part
It lists the scores in the wrong order, since scores should be listed in alphabetical order
It gives the exact scores, when a report must give only the percents of all of the scores
questions.answer: It shows private information; results should be given for groups, without names
questions.solution: People's names and individual scores are private. A report should protect the people who took part and show summaries of groups.

solve.answer: It shows private information; results should be given for groups, without names
solve.work: Names with scores expose private information; report group results anonymously.

questions.skill: Evaluate a study design and its limits
questions.stem: A researcher asks 100 people about 20 different foods and tests each food for a link with acne, using a 5% significance level. One food shows a statistically significant link. Which is the best interpretation?
choices: With 20 tests, one hit is expected by chance alone, so the finding needs to be confirmed in a new study
The finding proves that the food causes acne, because a 5% chance of a false alarm is far too small to matter
The finding is worthless, because no result from a study that runs many tests at once can ever be real
The other 19 foods are shown to have no link with acne, because their results were not statistically significant
questions.answer: With 20 tests, one hit is expected by chance alone, so the finding needs to be confirmed in a new study
questions.solution: At the 5% level, each test on an unrelated food has about a 1-in-20 chance of looking significant. Across 20 tests, one such result is expected even if no food matters, so one hit is weak evidence until a new study confirms it.

solve.answer: With 20 tests, one hit is expected by chance alone, so the finding needs to be confirmed in a new study
solve.work: 20 tests at the 5% level: expected false positives = 20 x 0.05 = 1. One significant result is what chance alone predicts, so it needs confirmation in a new study. Non-significance does not prove no link; significance does not prove causation.

questions.skill: Critique a graph or statistic in the media
questions.stem: A news graphic says, "City A had 300 burglaries last year and City B had 150, so City A is twice as dangerous." City A has 600,000 residents and City B has 100,000. What is the best critique of the claim?
choices: Counts are the fairest way to compare cities, so City A really does have twice the burglary problem
Burglaries cannot be compared between cities, because every city defines the crime in its own way
Raw counts ignore population: per 1,000 residents, City B has 1.5 burglaries and City A only 0.5
City B must be safer, because fewer burglaries were reported there than in City A overall in the year
questions.answer: Raw counts ignore population: per 1,000 residents, City B has 1.5 burglaries and City A only 0.5
questions.solution: A fair comparison uses a rate. City A: 300 / 600,000 = 0.5 per 1,000 residents. City B: 150 / 100,000 = 1.5 per 1,000 residents. So a resident of City B faces three times the rate, the opposite of the claim.

solve.answer: Raw counts ignore population: per 1,000 residents, City B has 1.5 burglaries and City A only 0.5
solve.work: Rates: A = 300/600,000 = 0.5 per 1,000; B = 150/100,000 = 1.5 per 1,000. Raw counts ignore population; B has the higher rate.

questions.skill: Critique a causal or numerical claim
questions.stem: A condition affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test is positive for 99% of the people who have it and also for 1% of the people who do not. A headline says, "If you test positive, you are 99% likely to have the condition." What is the best response?
choices: Correct: the test is positive for 99% of the people who have the condition, so a positive result means 99%
Wrong: of about 1,100 positives per 100,000 people, only 99 are real, which is about 9% of them
Wrong: a positive result means a 1% chance, because the test is wrong for 1% of the people it checks
Wrong: a positive result means a 50% chance, because each result is either right or wrong, nothing more
questions.answer: Wrong: of about 1,100 positives per 100,000 people, only 99 are real, which is about 9% of them
questions.solution: Take 100,000 people. About 100 have the condition and 99 of them test positive. Of the 99,900 who do not, 1%, about 999, also test positive. Of about 1,098 positives, only 99 are real, which is about 9%.

solve.answer: Wrong: of about 1,100 positives per 100,000 people, only 99 are real, which is about 9% of them
solve.work: Per 100,000: 100 have it, 99 test positive; 99,900 do not, 1% = 999 false positives. Positives = 1,098 (about 1,100). P(have | +) = 99/1,098 = about 9.0%.
